Chaos is properly called a species of the abyss; for in its very center, a fiery nature is contained with a watery one, and a watery nature with an earthy one, observed in no particular order. This will be very easy to discern from a Cabalistic <note>Cabalistic refers to Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that interprets the Hebrew alphabet and scriptures as containing hidden divine secrets. Christian scholars in the Renaissance often adapted these ideas.</note> inspection of the characters of its name, a subject we shall discuss more extensively in the following chapter. Under this species of darkness can also be included that Egyptian darkness of which it is written in *Exodus 10:23*: *The darkness of the Egyptians was so great that one person could not see another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days.* Furthermore, this darkness was sensible, or palpable, over the land of Egypt, so that anyone could feel it. And such was also that darkness which occurred from the sixth hour until the ninth during the passion of the Savior, *Matthew 27:45* <note>The text reads 47, but refers to the darkness at the Crucifixion described in Matthew 27:45.</note>. The reason for this is clear: namely, because God—who is the unique light of the world—turned away His brightness, first from the region of Egypt, and then universally from the kingdom of the Jews for the space of three days in one place and three hours in the other. He permitted the true darkness of the abyss to creep into the air or the lower waters in the same manner as they existed in the beginning of the Lord, before the light had fully shone upon the world. And so, <term>תהו</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tohu*, meaning formless, chaotic, or "vanity."</note>, deprived of all light, rendered the darkness of the Egyptians palpable. In the other instance, however, the darkness was not so palpable, but rather truly wondrous and arisen in a supernatural way. Concerning this, Saint Lucian of Antioch, the Martyr, while placed in the torment of his passion and death, cried out to the judges standing by him in his torture: *Search in your annals, and you will find that in the times of Pilate, while Christ was suffering, the day was interrupted by darkness, even with the Sun having been put to flight.* <note>original: "Perquirite in annalibus vestris, & invenietis, temporibus Pilati, patiente Christo, etjam fugato Sole tenebris diem fuisse interruptum."</note> Certainly, this eclipse was not without the remarkable finger of God, or a manifest turning away of His face from the iniquity of the deed, as if He were unwilling to look upon such a crime. For three miracles accompanied it: first (which is marvelous to say), it happened contrary to the common natural order of eclipses, as they never occur during a full moon—that is, when the Moon is in opposition to the Sun—yet this happened immediately after the Sun's opposition. Second, the part of the Sun toward the East was shaded first, and that same part also recovered its light first afterward, which is likewise known to happen contrary to the common disposition of nature. Finally (which may be considered the most prodigious and almost incredible of all), in the hour of the eclipse, the Moon traveled against its natural course—namely from East to West—when its natural motion is contrary to this; and then, immediately after the eclipse ended, it hurried back by its natural motion toward its usual goal, from the setting, I say, toward the rising. Furthermore, this eclipse was *universal*, whereas common experience teaches us that others are merely particular. Wherefore it is manifest that Jehovah God, in a wondrous and ineffable way, turned away the saving light of His countenance for the space of three hours from the lower region of the world, in which those darknesses persisted throughout that entire interval between the sixth and ninth hours, in the lowest heaven, like the first abyss. Under this species was also that gloom of which Joshua speaks in *Joshua 24:7*: *He put gloom between you and the Egyptians;* although this species of darkness can also be very aptly referred to the arrangement of Chaos.

# ON THE PRIMARY ELEMENTS OF NATURE

The third principle of darkness [arises] from its material source <note>original: "hyloso," from the Greek *hyle*, meaning matter</note>, gaping from the beginning; from which source its shapeless substance flowed out. There are, however, others who define it as the formless matter of heaven and earth. But yet these people (unless I am mistaken) erred in this: that they took Chaos to be its mother, the abyss. Or at least this opinion of theirs can agree with Chaos, if it is taken for the lowest species of the abyss. For this reason Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure viewed as the author of the *Hermetica*, a body of texts blending philosophy, magic, and religion.</note> also said in the *Pimander*, book 3: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss; moreover, water and a thin intellectual spirit were present in Chaos through divine power.* 

In this passage, however, he seems to distinguish the darkness of the abyss from Chaos, because he says that the infinite shadow or infinite darkness is in the abyss. He understands, by that reasoning, the whole of *hyle* <note>primordial matter</note> as the void and empty, and Chaos as all that formless matter which is not empty—which contained within itself the water and the intellectual spirit through divine power (that is, the hidden shaping by the divine light). This divine power is symbolized by the Sun <note>The symbol ☉ represents the Sun or the divine spark.</note> in the center. Or even in that place, this whole can be signified by *Tehom* <note>Hebrew: תהום, meaning "the deep" or "abyss."</note> or the abyss; in which word *Tehom*, he argues for the infinite darkness of matter, insofar as it denotes, in the dimension of the world, the ultimate end of the diameter, or the principle of empty and void matter of infinite *hyle*. Hence he said: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss, etc.* 

And by "water" and by "intellectual spirit," he understands the Tetragrammaton <note>original: יהוה (YHWH), the four-letter ineffable name of God.</note>, which is the character of the ineffable name. But now, as God puts aside His veil and dark cloak, and looks forth into the world on the third day—and thus the moist nature reveals itself with the form of all things—the ultimate and lowest mass of darkness was brought forth into the light, as will be declared below. 

But, so that we may reveal our mind's opinion concerning the abyss and Chaos in this place, we say (having considered these same things again and again, not without purpose) that it is manifest that the Archetypal God—whom Hermes Trismegistus calls "Pimander" and the "Divine Mind"—did not first act with His fiery spirit from the center of the world's abyss, but rather from the circumference. This is consistent with the saying that *the universal Spirit of Elohim <note>God</note> was carried over the waters*, not *in* the waters. 

Hence, this spirit was the first emanation from the luminous *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often associated with the number 1 and the divine unity.</note> or the *Jod* <note>The letter י (Yod), the first letter of the divine name YHWH.</note> of the Tetragrammaton. And all the waters over which it was carried were not inwardly formed, but were still shapeless and overwhelmed by darkness, being nothing other than the true, murky abyss of the universal world. On its spherical surface, the bare watery spirit of the abyss appeared, with the darkness gradually stripped away and driven downward by an oblique revolution. 

This entire mass of darkness, I say, from the womb of the resting exterior matter, is called *Tehom* <note>תהום</note>. Here, through *Tehom*, the spirit is potentially covered by darkness, represented by the letter *Kaph* <note>The author refers to the final letter of the word, which he identifies as ך (final Kaph). He notes it stands in place of a final Aleph or the number 1000, signifying the deep abyss or the Greek "Omega," the end.</note>. 

But indeed, its more central spherical part—in which God [Elohim] established the world and over which the spirit brooded with a circular motion—is called the "abyss" or the "deep," separated from its mother *Hyle* by the luminous power of the fiery spirit. Upon its face there was darkness; or, according to Hermes Trismegistus: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss.* This means darkness was everywhere upon the face of the abyss. From its superficial face, however, as the light itself flashed from the face of the *Jod* <note>י</note>, the water suddenly began to appear in an obscure way—that is, at the very moment of the appearance of the spirit of Elohim. 

Hence, the name of God <note>יהוה</note> is turned into the Abyss <note>תהום</note>; that is, the name is already beginning to be manifested in potentiality, and is turned into the "obscure abyss"—which means it is still closed and not yet opened. Thus, the letter *Mem* <note>ם</note> is the final *Mem*, signifying the finishing of the abyss itself by the presence of the spirit which was carried over the *Mem* [the waters]. 

Then, by the unconquered power of the acting Holy Spirit, the horrendous shadows—or the curtain, or the dark skin of the waters—pushed downward, are lifted little by little and step by step, and the waters are purified. Thus, by the first appearance of the spirit, the first day was made, and the work of the first day: namely, the purification of the spirit, or of the subtle waters, from their third deformity and dark filth. From the elements of the spirit thus purified (which are distinguished according to the greater or lesser dominion of the fiery nature), the creatures of the nine orders were created, according to the opinion of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential theologian who described the nine choirs of angels.</note>. 

And so the darkness or shadows of the abyss were driven downward by one more degree; in that way, the darkness was strengthened in the compression of the lower abyss. Then, by the second appearance of the spirit, the second day was made, in which the darkness of the abyss was driven downward by another degree. Thus the waters or spirits of the middle region were revealed; and by the retraction of the spirit within the cloud or its own segregated seat, the second night followed. By that reasoning, all this darkness descended into the lowest abyss, where the darkness was greatly contracted and made compact by compression. 

Thus, by diligent observation, one may now see how the four elements are gathered into this dark mass, and of what substance and nature they consist. First, therefore, it must be understood that all parts of the formless abyss were homogeneous and of the same nature in density and potential being, insofar as it had no fiery power within it, by whose greater or lesser virtue one part might be thicker or subtler than another. 

But it happened differently after the revelation of the uncreated spirit from the light. For where there was a greater presence of the spirit, there the substance of the matter or waters was subtler, purer, and in a smaller quantity, just as has been clearly and exactly demonstrated in my booklet *On Pyramidal Physics*. From this it follows that, because of the greater presence of the spirit in the highest heavens, the substance of the abyss (now revealed in the spiritual form of the waters, which was the same in potential as the rest) became very thin in quantity. And from this it happens that its denser part is reverberated downward with the darkness in the form of a shadow. This indeed cannot happen so subtly that no sparks of the eternal light, enclosed by the thicker spirit, are snatched away into the portion of the darkness of that place. Hence this spirit [takes] a more worthy place in Chaos...

## CHAPTER VII.
### Concerning the third kingdom of darkness, which is called Chaos.

That Chaos is a third degree of darkness, distinct from the two higher ones, we can elicit and observe from the living characters of its name; namely: חֹשֶׁךְ <note>Hebrew: *Choshekh*, meaning darkness.</note>, that is, darkness or Chaos. But as this Chaos exists in its own proper nature, it is defined as a raw, undigested, dark mass, in which all things are confused and poorly placed. This was the prin- <note>original: "prin-", catchword for the next page's first word, "principium" (beginning).</note>

And so the darkness or shadows were thrust downward by one more degree; and in that way, the darkness was strengthened in the compression of the lower abyss.

Then, by the second appearance of the spirit, the second day was made, in which the darkness of the abyss was thrust downward by another degree; and so, after its waters were segregated, the second night followed; and by that reasoning, all these darknesses descended into the lowest abyss, where the darknesses were greatly contracted and compacted by compression. Thus, by diligent observation, one may now see how the four elements are gathered into this dark mass, and of what substance and nature they exist.

First, therefore, it must be understood that all parts of the unformed abyss were homogeneous and of the same nature in density and potential existence; insofar as it had no fiery force in itself, by whose greater or lesser virtue one part of it might be thicker or subtler than another. But the matter stood differently after the revelation of the uncreated spirit from the light: for where there was a greater presence of the spirit, there the substance of the matter or waters was subtler, purer, and in smaller quantity, just as has been clearly and exactly demonstrated in my booklet, *On the Pyramidal Physical Art* <note>original: "de arte phyſica pyramidalis," a reference to Fludd's own work where he uses intersecting pyramids of light and shadow to explain the density of the universe.</note>. Whence it follows that, because of the greater presence of the spirit in the highest heavens, the substance of the abyss already revealed in the spiritual form of the waters (which was the same in potential as the rest in quantity) was made very thin. And from this, it happens that its denser part is reverberated downward with the darkness in the form of a shadow; which cannot happen so subtly without some sparks of eternal light, enclosed by the thicker spirit, being snatched away into the portion of darkness in 그 place. Whence this spirit [finds] a worthier place in Chaos...

Nevertheless, these substances are so confused, so intermixed with litigious and discordant darkness, that no order of nature is observed in them; for Fire contends with water, and moist air is confounded with dry earth, and thus all things are subverted in a tumult, until the Word of the Lord, bringing forth the third day with the fiery Spirit, well disposed all things on that day, and bound all things to one another with the bonds of peace, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pimander*, chapter 1: *Finally they were moved by the spiritual Word, which was carried over them, sounding around their ears, etc.* <note>Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary founder of Hermeticism; the *Pimander* is a core text describing the creation of the world.</note> It follows, therefore, that this heap of darkness, and the discordant and mutually litigating elements—indeed, even enclosing a portion of divine light in their belly—are called Chaos; which is that gloomy darkness called *Choshech* <note>original: חשך (Hebrew for darkness)</note>. For the letter *Shin* <note>original: ש</note>, that is, fire, is included in its center in a triple spirit in a confused manner, just as fire is enclosed in a dense cloud. Whence Chaos was most rightly defined as raw, undigested, and confused matter, gaping from the beginning. And now at last, I shall betake myself with a hasty step and pace to the disposition of the earth, after the complete opening of the universal waters and the cleansing from the dense darkness; that is, after the completion of the heavens.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->On the last grade of Darkness, namely the element of earth; and first on the meaning of the living characters of its name.<-

The darkness of the abyss having been reduced through the double circulation of the lucid spirit into 그 disposition which we have called Chaos, or *Choshech* <note>original: חשך</note>, finally by the third appearance of that spirit, both heaven and earth were completed, and all things were weighed and disposed by the true proportion of numbers and the most fitting scales of justice, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pimander*, chapter 3: *The holy splendor flourished, which led the elements forth under the sand and moist nature, etc.* And since the light things had been indistinct, they afterwards flew forth into the high region; the heavy things settled under the moist sand. In this way, therefore, you see both the earth and heaven procreated; we intend to deal specifically with the earth here. The primary characters of its name are of this sort, and are thus disposed: *Eretz* <note>original: ארץ (Hebrew for Earth)</note>; where the lack of light in the center is signified by the letter *Tzade* <note>original: ץ (the final form of the letter Tzade)</note>, and the external fertility of the earth is proven by the letter *Aleph* <note>original: א</note>, which is now the source of light, insofar as it is external and lucid, and the origin of darkness, insofar as it is resting and dark, and hidden in the belly of matter <note>original: "hylæ"</note>. In this mystery of *Eretz* <note>original: ארץ</note>, therefore, day and night are first declared, insofar as *Aleph* [א] is placed first, which is a lucid and formal letter; and *Tzade* [ץ] is placed last, which is a material letter, found among the tens in the numbers of the Alphabet. For *Tzade* [ץ] denotes the material elements. Furthermore, *Aleph* [א] on one side denotes the uncreated light on the surface of the darkness; and *Tzade* [ץ] on the other denotes the elements of fire, air, water, and earth, arguing from this that from the earthy mass or the first dark matter, the four elements leaped forth. Furthermore, *Aleph* [א] can indicate the animal kingdom, in which there is more of the fiery and divine; *Tzade* [ץ] truly indicates the vegetable kingdom, in which air predominates, and there is not as much light; and *Resh* <note>original: ר</note> denotes the mineral kingdom, in which dense water has dominion, and light is at its least, as it moves slowly and sluggishly in the mineral body because of the compression of matter. Moreover, *Aleph* [א] proves the supreme darkness, immediately illuminated by the *Aleph*, from which are the bodies of animals; *Tzade* [ץ] designates the middle darkness vivified by the intermediate light, from which are the bodies of vegetables; and *Resh* [ר] denotes the lowest darkness made into essence by the lowest light, from which the bodies of minerals are compacted. And the column and support of all these, hidden in the center of the *Tzade* [ץ], by which the whole obscure mass is established, is the Word of God, or that cornerstone, about which Job 38, verse 4 says: *Where were you, when...*

ON THE PRIMARY ELEMENTS OF NATURE.

*Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Who marked off its dimensions, surely you know? Or who stretched a measuring line across it? On what were its footings set, or who laid its cornerstone?* <note>original: "quando fundabam terram...?" citing Job 38:4-6</note> From this also *Proverbs 3:19*: **By wisdom the Lord laid the earth’s foundations, by understanding he set the heavens in place.** In a similar way, like a Carbuncle <note>A "carbuncle" is a legendary deep-red gemstone thought to glow with its own internal light; here it represents the spiritual fire of the Sun.</note> sent forth by divine breath, the Sun was established in its place. This Sun is the foundational stone of that divine tabernacle which Jehovah placed in the Sun. This stone, therefore, is that true "central Sun," the <term>Archaeus: The vital, formative principle of nature in Paracelsian alchemy, acting like a celestial craftsman.</term> of divine nature, or the power of the <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH), considered to hold the power of creation.</term> walking in the darkness (according to *Ecclesiasticus 24*: Wisdom walked in the depth of the abysses, etc.). By this power, the earth—which before creation was empty and void—is now observed to be full of fertility and overflowing with a seeding and multiplying virtue. Indeed, the very Earth—<note>original: "ארץ" (Eretz)</note> Earth—draws to itself daily and in great abundance a significant portion of the beauty of the whole world, both material and formal, through the virtue and power of that God-like magnet.

However, that this Earth is, in and of itself, a most evident portion of substantial darkness, is taught to us by many testimonies of the sacred letters. For first, in *Job 17:12*, he seems to call the Earth a *sepulcher* (which is also translated as *hell* according to Jerome’s translation); and he also calls it darkness itself, saying: *In darkness I have spread my bed; that is, I prepare my grave in the earth.* It is also called the seat of the Prince of Darkness. Furthermore, it is called *dust, ashes, mud, an opaque body, etc.* Similarly, night is derived from this dark Being, according to *Job 17:11: Night is near because of its darkness.* From this, night is defined as nothing other than the positioning of the opaque earth between the two hemispheres. Thus, in *Job 4:9*, he calls the human body the *dark house of the internal man*; and in *Wisdom 5:15*, he calls the *opaque body, infected by corruption,* an *earthly dwelling.* And in *John 1*, it is said that *Life is in the darkness, that is, in a dark prison.* Finally, Job best describes the opacity of the earth in *Job 10:21* with these words: *Before I go, never to return, to the land of gloom and deep shadow, to the land of utter darkness, like the shadow of death, and without order, where even the light is like darkness.* From these things—if experience itself did not warn us—we might see by the light of the sacred scriptures that the earth is a mass of the thickest darkness, just as the heaven is a gathering of clear and bright waters in the spherical sea of the world.

# CHAPTER IX.

->*On the origin, hardness, opacity, location, composition, shape, immobility, foundation, and use of the earth.*<-

In the preceding sections, it was said that the mass and matter of the earth come from the darkness of <term>Hyle: A Greek term for "prime matter," the raw, unformed substance of the universe.</term>. But truly, because according to the teaching of Saint Peter in *2 Peter 3:6*, the heavens and the earth are said to have existed previously from water, and to consist through water in the Word of God, some might object that the earth was created from water and not from a dark substance. To these people one may respond that the earth itself is like the dregs and sediment of that entire immense water that was once unformed and called the "Abyss." We have seen this, for example, from the muddy and turbid Tiber river in Rome: thick, opaque, and non-transparent water is drawn out, which, after resting in a small vessel for 24 hours, finally becomes clear, transparent, and bright as the opaque and muddy matter settles to the bottom. We perceive that muddy matter residing at the bottom to be the compact, dense, and globular substance of the earth.

In exactly the same way, God, by the power of the Word, fashioned the dark earth from the immense storehouse and jumble of water. For we see that from pure and most clear water, crystals and other transparent gems are usually generated by natural operation. But truly, if transparent earth is generated from clear water, there is no doubt that opaque and dark earth can also be brought into the light from the dark, turbid Abyss (or the substance of unformed water) through a certain cold coagulation. Furthermore, it is a common axiom among Philosophers that every material thing, through true resolution, is reduced back into its primordial matter or substance from which it first arose. Common experience teaches us that the earth of any nature can be converted into water. For if you take a clod of earth, or even a piece of stone, and burn it until it becomes lime or ashes, and pour water onto those ashes and pass it through a linen cloth several times—separating it from the ashes in that way—a very sharp <term>Lixivium: A solution of alkaline salts leached from ashes; lye.</term> will be made from it. If you distill this several times through an <term>Alembic: A chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling liquids.</term> or by another method, and gradually cook it at the end and allow it to evaporate, you will find Salt at the bottom. If you grind this finely and place it on marble or glass in a somewhat humid place, it will resolve into water; thus you may conclude from this that earth comes from water. What remains of that earth is like an empty and void earth, in which the force of darkness abounds; and that is the cause of the extreme darkness in the body. This is not unsuitably named the "impious" and "damned" earth among the <term>Chymists: An early term for alchemists or early chemists who studied the transformation of matter.</term>. And yet, nothing is so impossible for God that He cannot make even this dark and useless body transparent and healthy by some medicinal "menstruum" <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent or substance used to dissolve or transform solids.</note> coming from His breath. Thus we can be taught that all those things can be held as good and useful before God which seem to us evil, perverse, and placed beyond any hope or possibility of salvation. For the Spirit of God (says John) blows where it wills, and by its invincible spirit, it attempts to convert all things into its own nature. For so sweet is the spirit of wisdom, and endowed with such great kindness. We conclude therefore from these things, that water is the source of both earth and...

We gather this from the words of the Psalmist as if from upright foundations: *God founded the earth upon its bases, so that it should not be moved forever, and he covered it with the abyss as with a garment.* <note>citing Psalm 104:5-6</note>

Regarding the geometric figure of this huge mass or bulk, we must understand that God extended and created the heaven, the stars, the sun, and the moon, and likewise the transparent elements, in a spherical shape and likeness. From this it follows, as if granted, that the earth itself is of the same form and likeness. Indeed, this thing is crafted with such accurate roundness that no corner at all is found in it; and thus this total globe has an equal roundness on every side, to such an extent that whatever part you touch, you always encounter its middle point there. That the earth has the form of a globe is related to us by David in many places in the Psalms, where he mentions the "orb of the lands" <note>original: "orbis terrarum," often translated as "the world."</note>. And truly, the round form is more suitable, convenient, fit, and accommodated for use than all others; for the circle, orb, or globe contains within itself a perfect and absolute work. Indeed, if we wish to inspect other created things diligently, we shall find them also to be round—namely animals, as well as vegetables and minerals. 

Finally, regarding the use of this terrestrial globe, we find that just as the heaven is the receptacle of invisible spirits, so also the earth is the storehouse and "perfume-cabinet" <note>original: "myrothecium," a container for ointments or oils, implying the earth holds the precious essences of life.</note> of all visible animals. It is also like a chest, abundantly filled with riches, such that they could not be described even in many centuries. It is, I say, a certain treasury-chest of God, filled with riches for the use of men and for divine honor. Lastly, regarding its duration, we are taught in *Ecclesiastes 1:4* that the earth is to remain forever.

These, then, are those subtle waters of which it is said in *Genesis 1* that *God separated the firmament from the lower waters.* 

Next, just as we can elicit a "fifth essence" from wine, so also God extracted the nature of the firmament in the second place from the universal mass of water. By its mediation, the pure and spiritual waters are separated from the coarse and material ones. This firmament He also called "Heaven," in which He later arranged the two great lights and the remaining stars. Finally, in the third place and order, He extracted a fourth essence, in which there was a very small portion of divine action and essence. For this stood in relation to the upper heavens as the phlegm of wine stands to its various degrees of spirit; for the more the spirit is mixed with phlegmatic water, the weaker, unworthier, and worse it becomes. A similar logic holds in the production of the three heavens; the purest of these is made from the first circulation of the universal water in the great <term>Macrocosmic: Relating to the "great world" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "microcosm" of the human being.</term> Philosophical Egg. This circulation occurs by the movement of the uncreated light's spirit over the waters at that instant which is called "Day." However (as it appears to me in my secret contemplation), all seven days of creation were completed and encompassed within a single day. Nor do I speak thoughtlessly, since Holy Scripture also seems to assert this same thing in *Genesis chapter 2*, where it is read: *These are the generations of the heaven and the earth in the day that Jehovah Elohim made the earth and the heaven.* The Hebrew words are <note>original Hebrew: ביום</note> *in the day*, not "in the days." By this it seems to be implied that the seven days of creation are to be understood in a mystical way by the <term>Antistite: A high priest or overseer; here likely referring to a master of mysteries or the Creator acting as the chief architect.</term>. This fact surely cannot remain hidden from those who have immersed themselves more deeply into the delightful sea of divine mysteries.

But returning to our subject, we say that the earth is the dregs of the entire extraction and the gathering of darkness, separated from the clear divine aid. It is a casting down from heaven to the bottom—from the circumference and top of the mundane egg, as if from a <term>cap: The top part of an alchemical still (alembic) where vapors condense.</term> or <term>alembic: A chemical apparatus used for distillation.</term>, to the center and, as it were, to the base and bottom of the <term>cucurbit: The gourd-shaped lower vessel of a distillation apparatus that holds the liquid to be heated.</term>. Yet, in these dregs, an admirable virtue is hidden: namely, **Salt, Tincture, and Mercury**. By these, the seeds enclosed in the earth are multiplied, and the nurseries of heaven are naturally conceived in the matrix of that universal female. They are kindly preserved and nourished as if by menstrual blood, so that they increase and grow step by step in the general womb, until at last they rise high from the earth in vegetable form, or are exalted in mineral form with splendor and perfection. Or even, as this universal mother takes on an animal form, they are born and produced in the figure and substance of animals—both upon her mass and in her very bosom, as well as in the sea, the waters, and likewise in the air. 

But here a mystery lies hidden from many: how it is possible for these three species of propagation, so different in nature and disposition, to be produced from one and the same mother. For her mineral son is fixed, without any manifest life, heavier than the other two, of a coarser, more compact, rebellious, hard, and dense substance. It never comes forth from its matrix except by force; it is most friendly to rest, hiding around the center and veins of its mother, imbued with a small amount of heavenly heat, etc. Meanwhile, on the other hand, her other sons—namely the vegetable and the animal—behave in a completely different and contrary manner. They hasten toward maturity in the maternal womb and hurry to emerge at the appointed time. In their substance, material parts, and nature, they are softer, more obedient to the action of light, and more ready for refinement (in which they constantly exercise themselves). They are more vivid in spirit, fuller of light and soul, and richer in natural heat, so that their substance is seen to obey its actions. Similarly, there seems to be as much difference between her vegetable and animal son as there is between the mineral and the vegetable. For the vegetable offspring of the earth rises from a seed cast into the earthen matrix; its substance is very watery and does not abound much in heat because of the abundance of cold water. Its body is very compact when mature, it is held in the earth by roots, it lacks sense, and it does not move from place to place, etc. Meanwhile, the animal son of the earth behaves in a completely different way; for the species of the earth take on a certain form for its generation. Thus the earth and mud are accustomed to bring forth their animal sons, who are most rich in fiery heat, endowed with sense and local motion by the celestial spirit...

# SECTION I. PORTION I. PART II. BOOK I.

...drenched, and raised up by the dignity of the highest earthly kingdom. The reason for these three types, if we are not mistaken (for what mortal, in such a difficult and doubtful matter, would consider himself entirely free from error?), proceeds from a threefold diversity of darkness. This darkness was reflected in stages during the three days of creation, with a corresponding spirit enclosed within each, divided by order.

For first, the darkness was propelled downward from the highest face of the abyss along with a great portion of the spirit of that same heaven—or the subtle waters. Because these were viscous and tenacious, and hungry for the divine and virgin light by which they might be formed, they snatched up and claimed for themselves infinite sparks of that light which were pursuing the dark shadow. Thus, the dignity of the darkness—or the dark spirit of this heaven—is as much more eminent than the two lower portions of darkness as the honor of the spirit remaining in the <term>Empyrean heaven: The highest part of heaven in ancient cosmology, believed to be the realm of pure fire and the dwelling place of God.</term> is raised in place and essence above the middle and lowest spirit. For we see this in nature: the spirit of wine <note>original: "spiritus vini"; in alchemy, this refers to distilled alcohol or the "essence" of the wine.</note> by natural instinct floats upon its own oil, and that oil in turn floats upon its watery <term>phlegm: A term used in early chemistry and alchemy to describe the watery, tasteless residue left after distillation.</term>.

The reason why the dignity of the highest darkness is above the others is that it participates in the immediate ray and emanation proceeding from **God Jod** <note>original: "Deo Jod"; Jod (or Yod) is the first letter of the Hebrew Divine Name, often used in mystical philosophy to represent the point of origin or the creative power of God.</note>. However, because the spirit of the middle darkness snatches for itself a ray of secondary light—which is a portion of *created* light—its light is not as noble; for the former is a ray of God, while the latter is a ray of Nature. Finally, the third light, whose sparks the spirit of the lower darkness snatches and adopts for itself, is composed of a double light—namely, of God and of Nature—which is immersed in a double spirit. From this, the matter of that darkness is rebellious against this composite light.

It follows, therefore, that since among the spirits of each heaven one is found worthier and higher in place than another (according to the greater or lesser proximity of its light to the divine nature), it is also necessary that the darkness must maintain this same dignity and exaltation within its own dark world or terrestrial globe. For because of this divine light held within the darkness of the earth, God is said to be as much in the earth as in the heaven; it is said that *Wisdom is upon the earth*, and it is said that *the earth is the footstool of Jehovah’s feet*, just as the heaven is recorded in Holy Scripture to be His throne. Indeed, in every respect, this opaque terrestrial globe behaves like that transparent celestial globe. 

Now, we find three regions in the <term>diaphanous: Transparent or translucent.</term> world, the middle of which, according to the sense of the sacred text, separates the lowest from the highest. Therefore, in the dark machine of the earth, there are undoubtedly also three regions, the highest of which is distinguished from the lowest by that middle region from which the vegetable power emerges.

It follows, then, as probable, that the **mineral nature** belongs to that region of the earth which is the lowest, both because it occupies a deeper place and has a denser and harder substance, and also because it possesses a soul from a weaker light. Hence, it is more given to rest and is enveloped in foul darkness at the center of the whole; thus, because of its immense weight, it attempts to strive further downward toward the lowest abyss. From these things it is clearly evident that this species of creature belongs to the dark kingdom of the lowest darkness, where the efficacy of light is found to be lesser and meaner due to the abundance of rebellious matter; thus, it is recognized that earth and water abound more in minerals.

By a similar proportion, the opaque **vegetable composition** is related to the kingdom of the middle darkness; for we perceive that vegetables sprout and rise up from the middle part or region of the earth—that is, the part closer to the upper and superficial region. By comparing the <term>ether: The clear sky or the higher regions of air above the clouds.</term> with this region, do we not also see that the Sun, the Emperor of the ethereal kingdom, and likewise the other stars, are the cause of growth and multiplication?

As for the kingdom of the opaque **animal creature**, we find that it was formed from mud and earth—specifically, from the highest region of the earth. Thus, it is perceived to be warmer and stronger than the others in fire and air; so it happens that it possesses not only local motion, but also sensation. Indeed, what is greater is that **Adam** himself with his kind—a noble animal—was formed from the mud and clay of this kingdom in his external part, yet participates in reason and intellect. 

The reason for this is ready at hand: the element of **fire** was made from the superfluous spirit leaping out from the first darkness and adorned with the dignity of the highest light; hence, because of the dominion of light, it is called hot and dry. So the element of **air** draws its origin from the superfluous spirit of the middle heaven; thus it is hot and moist, because of the equal tempering of spirit and light. The element of **water**, however, proceeds from the superfluous spirit and the weak light of the lowest darkness; and this is the reason why waters and springs are so frequent in the innermost bowels of the earth. Hence, because of the lack of heat in that kingdom, the waters are called cold and moist—namely, because of the moist nature of their thinner part. But concerning these things, we shall speak more clearly in their proper place below.

We see, therefore, that the **mineral kingdom**, as it is the lowest portion of darkness, consists of water and the lowest darkness; the **vegetable kingdom** of air and the middle darkness; and the **animal kingdom** of fire and the highest darkness. Consider, I pray, that the mineral is fused from an opaque body and a conforming spirit; similarly, that the vegetable covers an opaque body with a lighter spirit; and finally, that animals possess their opaque veil with a most free spirit. Hence, these bodies differ from one another only by the varying nature of the earth, as you yourselves admit that the character of different spirits proceeds from the diversity of the elements, one of which is exalted in dignity above another.

Similarly, a vegetable is more easily ignited and catches flame more quickly than a mineral; for the mineral resists the violence of fire because of the stubbornness of its compact substance. Since, therefore, every sublunary creature is composed of body and spirit, it is necessary that the body itself corresponds to the spirit in its proportions of darkness. And this is the reason why there is such a great difference between species and species, and between genera and genera. But we shall discuss these kingdoms more fully in the *following chapter*.

### CHAPTER XI.

->*A clearer and more ample declaration of the threefold sublunary creature; namely, the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral.*<-

For the reason alleged in the preceding chapter, the difference between the intelligences created on the first day arose. In these lower things, we say that animals differ from plants because of the diversity of darkness—namely, those in which fire more greatly abounds—and that plants or vegetables differ from minerals insofar as air is more exuberant in them. And in this way we see that the darkness, which wove together and covered the spirits of the first heaven (or the thin waters) before creation, was first driven downward by the act of the appearing Divine Spirit and cast out, as if into exile. In the bowels of this darkness, there was undoubtedly hidden a certain thick and dense Spirit, greedily attracting and seizing for itself a no small portion of the sparks of light emitted immediately from the face of the Founder. Having snatched this light, the Spirit held it firmly by its own viscosity, as if vehemently desiring to be liberated from its foul prison and captivity by the immense power of that light. From this it happens that some portions of that Spirit are liberated because of the suitable quantity of light adhering to them; by the power of their incorruptible fire, they are raised up in the manner of their own artificial power into the concavity of the <term>eighth heaven: The sphere of the fixed stars, situated above the seven planetary spheres in the traditional geocentric model of the universe.</term>, and there, frozen by the cold of the waters, they constitute the innumerable fixed stars. Or else, because of the smallness of the sparks they possess, they dwell forever in darkness; from these were produced those opaque bodies on the fifth and sixth days of creation, which are called animals. For insofar as the spirits hidden in darkness received form and a spark of splendor emanating immediately from the divinity, it is necessary that they act within the darkness, and lead it here and there according to their will and appetite.

<margin>Wisdom 9:15</margin>
Furthermore, since that enclosed light flows immediately from God, the fountain of light and life, it follows necessarily that this form, by its own efficacy, procreates a nobler kind of creature from the lower things: namely, the animal. We see, therefore, a reason not only probable, but also, as I think, sufficiently manifest, why souls were from the beginning enclosed in opaque bodies, and that the body is almost nothing other than a prison, weighing down the spirit and the light enclosed within it, according to that saying of the <note>original: "Sapiens"; referring to the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha.</note> Wise Man:

> *For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthy tabernacle presses down the mind that muses upon many things, etc.*

Here, then, the reason offers itself freely as to why the animal body is mortal and subject to passions and changes; namely, because it is a mass of darkness or earth, which is always ready to resist the actions of light, to oppose motion, to be an adversary to life, and to afflict the soul and spirit with every sadness (if indeed divine light can ever be subjected to affliction). From here comes the origin of diseases and death; from here the misfortune of animal life, and its deadly enemy. And yet, if the vigor of the vital spark is sufficient, and the <term>fluid: In the original "latex," referring to the spiritual moisture or fuel that feeds the internal fire of life.</term> of its food or Spirit corresponds to its flame, that foul and obscure element of the animal is made obedient and is compelled to perform the functions of life by force. But if it perceives any defect in the spirit, or in its light (mystically dwelling in the divine word), it immediately attacks the light with injuries in a treacherous manner, ardently and violently, and attempts to root it out and extinguish it on the spot. And so, in this contrary motion, disease for the most part precedes in the first place—just as battle and war precede victory—and finally death and destruction succeed, unless nature is aided by prompt medicines and, with its strengths wonderfully gathered, emerging at last as the victor in this conflict, it recovers and newly acquires the former health of its life. This is just as the light of the middle heaven—which is called the <term>Act of Nature: A secondary level of divine power that governs the natural growth and mechanical processes of the world.</term>—is not as effective as that of the supreme heaven, which is called the <term>Act of God: The primary, immediate power of the Creator, representing the highest form of spiritual energy.</term>, or the first and immediate emanation of light from the divine source. This primary light is of ineffable efficacy and wondrous virtue, insofar as it is most fully replenished by the essence of the Holy Word. 

And from this it follows that the light of animals, although it is enclosed within an internal spirit and surrounded by a dark body, nevertheless shines forth from its own darkness. It perceives external things from a distance, remembers past events, thinks about things far removed by a certain instinct of reason, and gazes upon them as if with spiritual eyes. And although it cannot sublimate the spirit in which it is enclosed—by example and imitation of the fixed stars—up to the "sieve and diaphragm" of the starry heaven, nevertheless the rays of its enclosed light are dispersed far and wide in a circular fashion. They act no differently than the flames of a lamp or a candle, whose root adheres fixedly to the wick. Indeed, this light in man is so excellent and distinguished that, by its own subtlety, it is accustomed to penetrate continually even to the throne of the <term>Archetype: The original divine model or blueprint of the universe in the mind of God.</term> itself. Nor can any physical barrier of the body hinder its act in any way from being able to observe and perceive the furthest reaches of the earth and sea, as well as those things which are above in the heavens. 

In other animals, however, the brightness of light does not expand so greatly; yet it is also granted to them to ascend to the stars themselves through vision. Furthermore, such is the liveliness of this spark that the animal is accustomed to spring upward from the earth in a light leap, as may be seen in the lion, the cat, the dog, the deer, the serpent, man, and others of this kind. Do we not also notice by daily experience in the vegetable that the bright spark within the "middle darkness" <note>original: "tenebrarum mediarum"</note> attempts and strives with all its might to redeem itself, as if captured, by the help of the celestial rays or its own "brothers" (the stars)? Hence, that spark in its plant, rising out of the earth and seeking flight from the opaque body, tends upward. It carries up with it the fiery nature—which is bound to it by a natural bond, as one participating in the nature of the <term>quintessence: The "fifth element," a celestial substance purer than the four earthly elements.</term>. 

But, because air is bound to fire by the same logic, the air itself ascends together with the fire. By a similar concatenation, water is carried upward with the air; and finally, the earth itself, in a manner not unlike water, is joined by a firm bond and the laws of nature. It holds that wretched fugitive (the spark) in the corruptible and changeable region by means of a fixed root, and prevents it from ascending higher toward its fatherland. This is exactly how the opaque and terrestrial animal body is found to guard the soul detained within it, holding it by earthly force and bonds in its "putrid belly"—a place hateful and entirely opposed to the perfections of the soul. 

From these things, it is discerned that the fiery nature of the vegetable is not as effective in its operations as that of the animal. This is because the animal nature is derived immediately from the rays of God, or the brightness of the "primary emanation," whereas the vegetable is derived from the rays of nature—that is, from the rays of the "secondary emanation." Hence, the rays of the vegetable spirits enclosed in the middle or secondary darkness are weaker in action than the sparks of the spirits imprisoned in the primary darkness. 

From this, therefore, it happens that the nature of the primary darkness—those shadows thrust downward on the first day, from which the external bodies of animals consist—and the complexion of the spirits retained in them (which make up the internal animal matter) and the essence-making light of the primary emanation (by whose presence the animal genus is brought into being) is exalted in dignity above the vegetable nature. This is in the same way that the vegetable nature is exalted above the nature of minerals, which were created into the condition of opaque bodies from the "tertiary light" and the darkness of the lowest region of the world, along with their enclosed spirit. 

And so we see the reason why animal and vegetable creatures were produced into the disposition and nature of opaque and dark bodies. It remains now, in the last place, to tell why mineral bodies obtain the final place in creation, and to treat precisely of their property and dignity. 

As we have said, the external part of animals was fashioned from the darkness beaten downward from the first heaven on the first day of creation, and their internal part from the "superfluous spirit" of that same heaven and the sparks of light clinging to that spirit. (From this, the animal genus differs according to the diversity of the proportions: first of light, then of spirit, and finally of the quantity of darkness. First, they differ in dignity and liveliness because of the abundance of light, as in **man**; next, in lightness and speed because of the abundance of spirit, as in **birds**, the **cat**, and similar creatures; and finally, in slowness and magnitude because of the abundance of darkness, as in the **Elephant** and the **Whale**. Similarly, where there is an abundance of darkness with an abundance of light, there **terrestrial animals** are born; but where there is an abundance of darkness with an abundance of thin spirit and a sufficient quantity of light, from those come the **winged creatures** of the sky. If there is an abundance of gross spirit with a paucity of light in various quantities of darkness, **aquatic creatures** arise therefrom. But if there is a great quantity of light in a small but thin spirit, **Salamanders** and **serpents** are generated, to whom "subtlety" is attributed by the testimony of the Holy Scriptures. However, if the spirit is gross along with such darkness, then comes forth the **toad**, etc., all of which are reckoned among the genera of **reptiles**.) 

Similarly, as we have said, the external part of vegetables was fashioned from the darkness beaten downward on the second day of creation from the second heaven (or middle region of the world), and their internal part from the spirit of those same regions—which is a denser and more "superfluous" part of the ethereal spirit, thrust downward in creation with the darkness of that heaven—and from a portion of such light, namely the secondary emanation, which we have called the "Act of Nature." Just as (I say) these two kinds of creatures <note>animals and plants</note> have arisen from a portion of the two superior darknesses, so it also seems likely that the external part of minerals is from the darkness of the third and lowest heaven, which was reflected back to the center of the spherical machine upon the completion of the third day of creation, and there reduced and gathered into a murky mass. Their internal part, however, is composed of a gross, heavy, and compact spirit, and a weak, meager light, oppressed by the mixed burden of matter (which is the effect of the third and final emanation) enclosed in the aforementioned rebellious and horrendous darkness. 

A large proportion of light with an equal amount of spirit and darkness produces **Gold**; hence it is called the **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*</note> by the Alchemists. A large proportion of spirit, a smaller amount of light, and a minimal amount of darkness brings **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> into the light. A greater portion of darkness constrains that spirit of Mercury into **Lead** <note>associated with Saturn</note>; to which, if a greater faculty of light is added, it changes the gloomy **Saturn** into a more lucid and **Jovial** <note>pertaining to Jupiter, or Tin</note> nature, and **Tin** is produced. If this light is even more eminent and finds a spirit sufficiently clean, purified enough from darkness and polished, it soon causes **Silver** to come forth. But if the spirit is defective and the light eminent, **Copper** is usually produced; and so on with the rest. Moreover, if the dark nature holds dominion, it tends to produce and provide the lesser and brittle <note>original: *triabilia*, likely a corruption of *friabilia*</note> minerals, such as **Antimony**, **Arsenic**, and various kinds of **Salts**; about which we shall also dispute more fully elsewhere. 

But these things are also declared by the position and site of every kind of composite creature. For, as we ought primarily to observe that there are three heavens, so there are also three principal elements to which the nature of these heavens is referred; and likewise three kinds of composites which correspond to the said elements. 

*   The **Empyrean heaven** <note>the highest, fiery heaven</note> is referred to the nature of **Fire**; whence it is called Empyrean, that is, "fiery." And therefore we must consider that, just as fire is placed before the other lower elements in dignity and nobility, so the supreme heaven excels the lower in glory, place, subtlety, and beauty. For this reason also, all **Animals**—being fashioned from the darkness, superfluous spirit, and light of that same heaven—hold dominion, power, and excellence over vegetables and minerals, insofar as they possess a greater quantity of light among opaque composite bodies and are of a more excellent lineage, like sparks of the first divine emanation. 
*   Likewise, the **Middle heaven** is not unsuitably compared to **Air**, since it is composed of an ethereal spirit; its substance is nothing other than incorruptible air, called the <term>Quinta essentia: The "fifth essence" or ether, a pure, celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</term>. From this it is gathered that air is placed before water. Thus this heaven seems to excel the lowest heaven (the third region of the world) in dignity, purity, and subtlety. Consequently, the opaque **Vegetable** composite—born from the darkness of that same heaven and the secondary spirit and light enclosed within them—is preferred in dignity to minerals. 
*   From this it is clear that the efficacy of light is greatest in animals, lesser in vegetables, and least in minerals. 

And here the ancient Philosophers seem to support our opinion; their judgment was that in sensitive creatures <note>animals</note> **Fire and Air** dominate; in vegetative creatures **Air and Water** (though by "air" they seem to signify a diminution of fire); but in minerals, although they consist of all elements, **Earth and Water** have the preeminence. For what else do they mean, other than that in the animal region, Fire and Air have their exaltation (namely, the spirit with the primary light of the Empyrean heaven contiguous to the ethereal heaven); in vegetables, Air and Water (that is, the ether, in which there is a smaller part of light, and the air of the ethereal region contiguous with the aerial heaven); and in minerals, Water and Earth (or the lowest heaven, in which there is the smallest part of the sixth essence <note>original: *sextæ essentiæ*, likely a typo for *quintæ* (fifth) given the context of the quintessence</note> or light, which is contiguous to the earth). 

But let us look more closely still at the site and position of these darknesses, reflected into the center of the world and constituting the earth; we shall perceive from the effect that the matter stands exactly as I have indicated to you. For we see that minerals themselves, because of the gravity and thickness of their darkness (or rather the spirit enclosed in them), are placed and found in the veins of the earth and further down toward the center. From this it may be observed that, according to their position, they were fashioned and created from the darkness of the lowest heaven, and are subject in dignity to the other two creatures. ...[perfec]tion <note>original: "tiam," the end of a word like *perfectionem* from the previous page</note>, we see happening; for it is observed that its spirit raises itself upward every year. Next, we perceive that, in the natural order, the vegetable kingdom is placed above the mineral; and from this it follows that its summits are found to rise from the surface of the earth, out of the center of its region, and to emerge from the realm of the middle darkness situated within the earth. This is because their spirit is more obedient to the actions of light than the spirit of minerals, and their sparks of light are more effective. 

As for animals, the subtler part—and, as it were, the cream of the entire earth <note>original: *cremor terræ*</note>—concurs in their composition; and this is further confirmed because we read that man, the most excellent of all animals, was made from mud or dust. Here also, in the consideration of animal nature, it must especially be observed that, just as the dark part of other creatures, with its enclosed coarse spirit, is bound by a natural bond to the earth and cannot live without adhering to it, so it is the nature of animals that their root is free and detached from the earth. Thus, they can pass from one part to another and move here and there according to their own pleasure and will. 

The reason for this, as it seems to me, is readily apparent: for first, as the earth is bound to water by a certain natural bond so that no vacuum may intervene—and also water to air, and air to fire—so it is manifest that a mineral body cannot be separated from the earth in its natural life and existence; indeed, it is submerged more deeply in the bowels of the earth because it is more friendly and familiar to the terrestrial nature. Similarly, because the ether is linked and glued with a natural glue to fire, and fire to air, and air to water, and water to earth, therefore the earth retains the ethereal darkness through its kinship with the ether, just as is observed in vegetables; for their roots are so fixed to the earth that they are prohibited from ascending higher toward their homeland. 

But in animals, the matter is different: for because the region of the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or ether, which was thought to compose the celestial bodies</note>—which is called the middle heaven or firmament, separating the upper waters from the lower—is placed between the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven of pure light and fire</note> and the lowest so-called Elementary realm, therefore the composition of an animal (consisting of darkness, Spirit, and the light of the Empyrean heaven) is not joined by a necessary bond of nature to the earth. Instead, it is free, so that it can swim in water, fly in air, and leap and breathe in it, as is seen in fish, birds, and land animals.

But if these things do not suffice for you as confirmation of our opinion, I shall proceed with you in another way: From where, I ask, comes this darkness and opacity of composite creatures? To this objection, you will undoubtedly (and not ineptly, I confess) answer: from the earth, mud, dust, or ashes; since we read in Holy Scripture that Adam’s external part, which is his dark part, was created from such an opaque substance. Or, speaking with the Philosophers, you might say it comes from the four elements united together in composition. However, we boldly say—trusting in the Holy Bible—that this assertion of the Philosophers is incorrect, since the other three elements are transparent and clear in themselves, and in no way opaque, and they constitute that lowest heaven of the world. This is what Moses understood in Genesis 2:20: *And Adam called all the animals and the birds of the heaven, etc.* These elements, in that they constitute heaven, are contrary to the earth itself and to opacity, according to that passage in *Genesis 1: God created the heaven and the earth.* Hence, the opacity of bodies comes from the earth, and not from any other thing; for nothing besides the earth itself is called opaque. For although the stars are the denser parts of their spheres, they do not possess their own darkness, but rather a profound transparency; otherwise, light could not have penetrated them any more than the rays of the Sun can penetrate the earth itself. 

These things being thus granted to your wishes—namely, that the darkness of composite creatures comes from the earth—another question arises: from where does the dark condition of the earth itself come? To this, I think it must be answered that it comes from the darkness and gloom, or the shadow of Chaos itself, sliding beneath by a gradually oblique revolution (to use the words of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: *Merc. Trism.*</note>). These shadows are distinguished threefold according to the threefold region of the world, from which they were reverberated downward step by step during the first three days of the creation. They must behave no differently here on earth (constituted by their gathering) than the three regions of the world or the waters themselves, of which one is more excellent and worthy than another. And just as the highest of these three regions corresponds to the element of fire, whose nature is to seek a more eminent place in the world, so also its darkness, reflected into the center of the orbicular machine, undoubtedly occupies the highest part of the earth. This is because, through the vitality of light and the multitude of Spirit enclosed in the darkness, it rises like the cream of milk to the peak and summit of the mass. 

That these shadows are more excellent than the other two is declared by this very fact: that their spirit is more abundant, and the primary light inherent in them is more excellent and powerful in virtue than the other two types of light; for it was the first emanation from the most holy fountain of unity and <term>supersubstantial light</term> <note>A term for the divine light that exists beyond material substance</note>. Moreover, that its spirit is more abundant and subtle than the spirit of the lower things is argued from the fact that the multitude of light of the first heaven requires only a single portion of spirit out of four. Hence it happens that this wondrous light, or the act of God, has so refined that spirit that out of its four parts, it reserved only a single one for itself; and consequently, it struck back its three superfluous portions with their darkness downward. But the darkness of the middle heaven, because of the mediocrity of the light in that place, embraced only two parts of spirit, with which they fell downward toward the center, fleeing from the face of the following light. And finally, although three portions of the lowest spirit are present in the darkness of the lowest heaven, yet because they are very heavy, dense, and unchanged by the tertiary light (which was too meager and therefore weak), they were subjected to such great changes and claimed for themselves the place nearest the center—that is, the lowest place.

# OF THE PRIMARY ELEMENTS OF NATURE.

...insofar as that is the true seat of coldness, which is found to be entirely contrary to the heat of light. But all these things are more clearly declared by our adaptation and description of the double pyramid—namely, the material and the formal—just as it has been more fully demonstrated in our book, the *Treatise on Pyramids* <note>original: "de pyramidum Tractatu"</note>, and in many places in our treatise on the *History of the Macro- and Microcosm* <note>original: "Physica Macro- & Microcosmi historia"</note>. Similarly, the highest darknesses are far more abundant than the others in regard to the fullness of the light above; and the middle darknesses more so than the lowest. By these things we are clearly taught that, just as fire occupies the highest region of the world because of the perfection of its condition, so also the darknesses of that region in the earth float upon the remaining lower ones; insofar as it possesses three portions of subtle spirit, by which it is carried into a higher place of the earth through the aid of the light implanted in them. And as the Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters, so the Empyrean spirit of this dross-filled matter <note>original: "fæculentæ materiæ," referring to the heavy, sedimentary material of the physical world</note>, illuminated and stirred up by the light of that place, is carried over the remaining lower darknesses. By a similar reason, the middle darknesses, which are related to the air, possess a middle place in the earth, no differently than air sits between fire and water, or the ether between the Empyrean and elemental heavens. Finally, the lowest darknesses of Chaos, compared to the waters, possess the lowest place. Do we not perceive here an evident difference between the regions of the earth, by which region is seen to differ from region, no less than the Empyrean spirit from the Aethereal, and the Aethereal from the elemental, or the fiery spirit from the aerial, and the aerial from the aqueous? For, just as water, when more purified of its darkness through thinning, becomes invisible air, and that air is further turned into fire by the operation of light, so also the matter stands in the changes of the parts of the earth. Is it not dealt with in plainly the same way with the mineral, the vegetable, and the animal? For we gather, taught by experience, that minerals are turned into vegetables by purification, and vegetables into animals: a point which is also confirmed by Artephius <note>A famous medieval alchemist, often cited by Fludd as an authority on the transformation of matter.</note> in his book called the *Key of Wisdom* <note>original: "Clavis sapientiæ"</note>. But, returning to the matter, do we not perceive the greatest difference between these three constitutions and conditions of dark creatures—namely, between the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral? What other reason, I ask, can we find, or what more probable and manifest argument, for such a great discrepancy between these three kinds of dark creatures than that which was alleged by us above? Namely, that three species of darkness are shown to be distinct in nature, dignity, condition, and motion, and that just as many kinds of dark creatures are clearly different from one another. Of these, that which is animal is preferred to vegetables by the same dignity as the Empyrean heaven is to the Aethereal; and the vegetable is preferred to the mineral, just as the Aethereal heaven is to the elemental. But truly, because the spirits of these kinds of heavens have cast off their earthly garments and are found naked and invisible, it must be understood that those creatures adorned with a dark cloak are likened to these heavens in their internal part; but in their external part, they are likened to the dark rags which the spirits cast off. Thus the spirit hidden in the animal, on account of its sense, memory, and a certain reason, is related to the Empyrean spirit; yet its body has a relation to the darkness of that same place. But since those darknesses could not fall downward unless they descended through the middle region, it is therefore from that region that they received a portion of their life. Let it not, therefore, seem strange to you, O Kind Readers, that we bring this opinion of ours—which is entirely new and unheard of before this day—so boldly and confidently here into the light. For (as I entirely believe), if you will consider with strenuous contemplation these things now indicated by us, you will find immediately and without delay (unless I am mistaken) that they are the root and foundation of the knowledge of all visible things. For the Creator <term>Opifex: Literally "the worker" or "craftsman," a term Fludd uses for God as the architect of the universe.</term> produced nothing into the light in vain; but God produced into the world both darkness and light, both night and day, both privation and position, both the origin of death and the principle of life, both the reason of the body and of the soul, both the garment and the one clothed, both the Evil Demon <note>original: "Cacodæmonem"</note> and the Good Angel, and finally both evil itself and good. The medium of these is the universal spirit, which is subjected to the aforementioned contrary actions; for this is that which draws health and life from the light, but attracts and suffers sickness and eventually death itself from the darkness. For the external thing and its spirit are what suffer and are rendered subject to death, while its internal part cannot perish. But concerning these things, we shall discourse copiously and clearly hereafter.

## CHAPTER XII.

### *Concerning the substantial quality that emerges from darkness and necessarily concurs in the constitution of the terrestrial mass and the sphere of moisture.*

Darkness has, and light has, a certain essential quality most proper to themselves, by which the latter acts upon the former, and the former first suffers the actions, and then afterward, in an instant, are said to react by resisting. Yet neither of these qualities has a name or an existence without the presence of the other, just as there is no action without passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>, or vice versa; hence both have received their names from mutual action and passion. That which first suffers and then is said to react belongs to darkness; that is, it rises out of the obscure whirlpool of darkness and is called coldness <note>original: "frigiditas"</note>. But that which leaped out of the light, and first revealed the effects of coldness in the world-bringing waters, is called heat <note>original: "caliditas"</note>; of which we shall make mention below in its proper place. Coldness, therefore, is so called insofar as something is found in the bowels of matter <note>original: "hylæ," from the Greek word for "wood" or "raw matter."</note> and darkness that is adverse to the nature of heat. For, just as darkness is entirely contrary to the nature of light, so also its quality—immediately after the appearance of light upon the dark face of the abyss—produced effects contrary to the action of light. Coldness is therefore a sluggish quality, naturally devoted to rest...
