...given over, by the excitation and agitation of light—that is, incidentally—and provoked to a motion against its own nature, plunging itself into the density of dark matter as if into its own proper place; it is opposed to motion, the origin of rest, the enemy of life, and the lethal minister of death; the companion of the body and the enemy of the soul, dulling the senses with stupor, withdrawing them from their natural function. It is familiar in minerals, yet likewise a disease in animals and vegetables, and finally their destruction and avoidance, gathering together different types of things and joining contraries to one another. And this is, finally, that always-attached disposition of matter through which so many changes and alterations are accustomed to happen in the elementary world, and often occur so suddenly and unexpectedly. The origin of this, I say, is in the belly of the <term>hyle<gloss>The Greek word 'hyle' refers to the raw, unformed primordial matter of the universe.</gloss></term>, or the <term>abyss<gloss>The 'abyss' refers to the chaotic, bottomless void existing before the ordering of the world.</gloss></term>, in which the dark <note>original: א (Aleph, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here used to represent the primary Divine Principle or Spirit)</note> is said to lurk and hide its rays and its acts within itself. And thus even coldness, preserved in a deformed manner within the deformed nature of the hyle, was within the power of Almighty God beyond all human imagination; the coldness of the hidden <note>original: א</note>, which quality was nevertheless revealed out of the darkness by the effective power of its light when the <note>original: א</note> appeared. And although the <note>original: א</note>, covered in darkness and revealing its power only to itself, seems plainly dark to human understanding, yet in a hidden way it was then able to see and discern all things that were in the darkness. Thus, it was also able to distinguish the quality of the cold, which was then latent, resting, and existing only in potential, as if in its hiding place; for to Him, as Witnessed in **Psalm 139:11**, the darkness cannot be so darkened but that He foresees; for the night shines for Him as the day, and the darkness to Him is as the light itself. Therefore, cold is a disposition of God's hiding place, dispersed here and there by His breath according to His will, either for the benefit of a creature or for its punishment. And this cold in its highest degree is always joined with a remarkable aridity or dryness; that is, it is separated from all fellowship with moisture. Whence, by its congealing property, it is accustomed to gather diverse things together. This also seems to be confirmed by the words of David in **Psalm 147:17**: *God casts forth His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold?* To which **Job 37:10** <note>original: "Iob. 29. 7." — the author likely miscited the chapter, as the quote corresponds to Job 37:10</note> also seems to agree: *By the breath of the mighty God, frost is produced; when God stands, the ice is congealed.* By these we are taught that coldness is stirred by the breath of God, who is hidden in His dark pavilion, or the dark <note>original: א</note>, inasmuch as cold is accustomed to obey Him as the God of both darkness and light. That dryness also accompanies extreme coldness is proved by the aforementioned testimonies of Holy Scripture, insofar as it produces frost. From this, I leave it to you (judges distinguished by the marks of learning) to determine how foolish is the opinion of both ancient and modern philosophers who assert that the element of water itself is the seat of coldness; since it is evident that its true seat, appropriated or assigned to it from its primary birth, is the dark abyss—indeed, the darkness itself, whose place we find here in the world, as we shall show below. For first, we see that darkness, by the operation of the breath of God, brings to light the congealing property of coldness; thus it is evident that hail and snow proceed from a foul and black cloud, when the spirit of <note>original: א</note> or Jehovah stands from the North, which is the true region of darkness, as will be said later. Next, we see that water is contiguous with the air; indeed, it is itself a thickened air. Whence it possesses a manifest heat within itself, insofar as it is of the nature of air, which no one will deny is warm. Furthermore, even if the highest coldness were in water, then it would always be coagulated by itself and the whole would be constrained into ice; since this does not happen, it is certain that the nature of cold is derived from a source foreign to the water. Similarly, we see that the icy sea is found in the northern part; this happens not from the nature of the water, but of the place, or from the position of the darkness, or the earth, in which darkness predominates because of the absence of the Sun. And also, among other reasons, this one should not be rejected: that motion and action are evident signs of internal heat. But the water of springs and rivers, as well as of seas, is perceived to move and, as if by a certain life-giving soul existing in heat, to walk (as it were) through ebb and flow. Therefore, it contains within itself a great quantity of heat, and as it were, a most evident living soul; for motion is the companion of heat, being its effect. On the contrary, however, the resting earth, contracted from heterogeneous parts as if into a clod-like disposition in the form of frost, is massed together around the center of the world-machine, which is the place most remote in position, nature, and motion from fire and light—the gathering of the Chaos of darkness, and finally its thickness. By this it is argued clearly enough that the earth itself is the receptacle of the extreme coldness of the whole abyss; its nature is to occupy the seat nearest to rest. What, indeed, is more immobile in the whole world than the earth? For God firmly *founded it upon its bases, that it should not be moved forever,* **Psalm 104:5**. By these things we are clearly taught, I believe—contrary to the opinions of almost all physicians and philosophers—that water is not the coldest thing, but the earth is. For how absurd it would be to assign to so noble a body, which is joined to the heaven as a companion, like a female to a male, a quality so vile as its essential property, such as dryness; which indeed is almost nothing, except the absence of that thing which is not present. For dryness is nothing else than the absence of moisture; and yet we see the earth itself is filled on all sides with water and air, lest a vacuum be admitted into its nature. But I know that some will reply: what then should be said of water, or how do we recognize it to differ from the other elements? To them we answer, that water is nothing but a portion of the moisture of one sphere; whose upper part, namely the air, as it participates with fire, is for that reason called warm, although not so warm as fire; whence it is also called moist. So its lower part, namely water, inasmuch as it is contiguous and as it were continuous with the earth, participates in its coldness; whence it is called cold, but not so cold as the earth, because that which makes a thing such, is more so itself. # CONCERNING THE PRIMARY ELEMENTS OF NATURE.

...it is joined with coldness; so that it may be argued from this that its nature is a mean between the heat of fire and the coldness of the earth. From the action, passion, and reaction of these qualities in the intermediate space, the entire—yet two-part—sphere of humidity is procreated. From this it follows that humidity is found only in the intermediate places between the two extremes; however, in the extremes themselves, it is not found naturally—that is, unless it should come to them accidentally. Hence, because of the absence of humidity, the extremes are called "dry." Therefore, the natural quality of water is the same as that of air: namely, humidity. These two together constitute nothing but a single element, which is called the "sphere of humidity." Thus, we have three primary, universal principles of nature: namely light, water, and darkness. So also we have only three secondary principles of nature appropriate to the elementary world: namely fire, the sphere of humidity, and earth, which refer back to the aforementioned principles, as will be demonstrated below.

From these things, therefore, we conclude that the earth is the true seat of darkness, and consequently the receptacle of intense coldness. Yet, in its intermediate parts, it does not usually demonstrate its force because of the Sun’s constant operation upon it, which is contrary to the coldness hidden within the earth; but in the extremes, and towards the poles, the earth exerts this coldness vehemently. From the North, therefore—as if from a place where darkness is said to predominate perpetually in the open air—cold abounds, and by the breath of divine Wisdom it is dispersed toward the South. 

That there is a place of such darkness in the furthest region of the poles, we are first taught by Olaus Magnus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish writer and archbishop famous for his descriptions of Northern peoples and geography.</note>, a man highly skilled in Northern secrets, as he was born in the farthest borders of Sweden. Indeed, he recounts that there is a great and unknown region obscured by perpetual darkness, in which intense cold, frost, and constant snows abound—just as if this were the truest seat of spiritual darkness, just as the whole earth is the seat of material darkness. From this place, the cold Northern winds and the cause of freezing emanate as if from a fountain or source. Perhaps Olaus could have been mistaken in this: that at the time when that region was revealed in the luminous territories of furthest Biarmia <note>Biarmia was a historical territory in the far north of modern-day Russia and Scandinavia.</note>, the sun, declining toward the opposite pole, left a "great night" (and not just a single night) in those parts for the space of half a year. 

Some have said, moreover, that the location of Paradise itself is in the Hyperborean mountains <note>The "Hyperboreans" were a mythical people of the far North in Greek legend.</note>, where the treasures of Jehovah are enclosed. And I remember hearing a sermon by a certain Jewish Rabbi, speaking in the Prague Synagogue, who said that their Messiah remains on a certain Northern island, surrounded on all sides by ice and snow and rendered inaccessible, staying there with an infinite number of the Holy Israelites. They believe with incredible faith and obstinacy that he will finally come from that place to deliver the Jews from captivity, to renew the entire world, and to subject it to himself. We suspect that they first received this doctrine from a certain Teacher well-versed in profound mysteries; however, it must be understood metaphorically, and thus it does not seem so obvious to common sense that the speech could be understood by everyone immediately. 

But to return to the matter: we believe the mystery of both heat and cold lies hidden in the secret and dark hiding place or "hut" of Jehovah, where His treasures are stored. For the Word of Jehovah said (in 1 Chronicles 6:1)—and therefore it is infallible—that He Himself "dwells in the thick darkness." Furthermore, the certain testimony of the Holy Bible instructs us that the secret of cold also hides in that darkness. For in Job 28:22 <note>Fludd cites Job 28:22, but the text "Have you entered the treasuries of the snow?" is found in Job 38:22.</note>, it is held: *Have you entered into the treasuries of the snow? Or have you seen the treasuries of the hail?* Truly, where the treasuries of snow and hail are, there without doubt is also the fountain of coldness, by whose action water is condensed into snow and hail. 

From the North, or the Boreal part, these cold blasts are sent out to us, as we are taught not only by experience but also by the testimonies of the Divine Word. For, according to Job 37:9: *From the North <note>original: Arcturo</note>—or from the "scatterers" as others interpret it, or according to other translations, from the Northern winds—comes the cold.* But the winds belong to God (Job 37:10), or are the "blasts of the nostrils of Jehovah" (Exodus 15:8). Whence we also read in Job 37:10: *By the breath of God frost is given; and the broad waters are frozen.* From this it follows that since thick and dark clouds are the hiding place of God, "who walks upon the circuit of the heavens" (Job 22:14), cold also proceeds from that hiding place by the power of the breath of Jehovah’s nostrils from the North. 

How the wind proceeds from Jehovah, we shall explain more clearly in the booklet on *Windy Meteors*. We conclude, therefore, that the wind inducing cold, frost, snow, ice, and hail is from the nostrils <note>The OCR reads "natibus" (buttocks), but the context of "flatu" (breath) and the cited verse Exodus 15:8 ("blast of thy nostrils") strongly suggests "naribus" (nostrils) was intended.</note> of Jehovah, by which the waters are strengthened and subsequently constricted more and more. Indeed, the water itself is mixed with the earth—that is, heterogeneous natures are gathered together—and it even converts the clouds themselves into ice and hail by a kind of vitrification <note>Vitrification: the process of turning something into glass or a glass-like substance; here used to describe the hardening of ice.</note>. But on the other hand, by the "shining word" proceeding from His mouth, He liquefies the frozen things again, separates and disperses the heterogeneous parts, and by His warm spirit wonderfully causes the frozen waters to flow. 

If you believe me less in this matter, observe what the Psalmist recounts in Psalm 147:16 in these words: *God gives snow like wool, and scatters the hoarfrost like ashes; He casts forth His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? He sends out His word and melts them; He causes His wind to blow, and the waters flow.* What could be said more clearly or brilliantly? We see, therefore, that the invisible and dark Aleph <note>original: א (The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which Fludd uses to represent the primary Divine Spirit or "Breath" in its hidden/cold state).</note> produces invisible coldness, while the shining and manifest Aleph (the Word) is accustomed to dissolve and vivify it; for the "cold" Aleph has, as it were, deprived it of life and made it rest. And thus Apollo <note>Apollo: here representing the sun and the principle of light/heat.</note> restores by his daily light what Dionysius <note>Dionysius: here representing the night and the principle of cold/constriction.</note> tore apart by his nightly cold or constricted with lethal chill. 

But someone will say: frost or ice occurs even when no cloud or darkness appears in the sky. To him I respond: the fountain of darkness, in which the cold hides and is dispersed from the north by a secret breath, is no less known...

...as the spring of light, by which the actions of cold are dissolved. <note>The author is completing a thought from the previous page, likely contrasting the warmth of the sun with the inherent cold of the earth's depths.</note> But how difficult it is to designate the fountain of darkness, or the origin of light, Job teaches us in chapter 38, verse 19: *Where is the way to where light dwells? And where is the place of darkness?* However, that Jehovah sends forth cold by His <term>Northern winds</term> <note>original: "ventis suis Aquilonaribus." Aquilo was the Roman name for the North Wind, associated with biting cold.</note>, bringing on ice and frost, the passages of the Holy Bible cited above teach us; and that His bright Word is also frequently moved from that quarter of the world is argued by that passage in Job 37:22: *Golden light arrives from the North; for God is terrible in praise.* <note>The author interprets the "gold" of Job 37:22 as a spiritual or celestial light coming from the polar regions.</note> 

Regarding the fact that the earth is called "dry," it must be known that this occurs not in respect to anything of the earth itself, but insofar as in its pure arrangement, all regard for humidity is said to be absent from it; so that for this reason it is even called dust in Job 38:37: *and dust and ashes* in Genesis 18:27. For the earth is one extremity of humidity, where no humidity appears, just as fire is the other extremity; and consequently these two extremes are called "dry," as if one were to say they are positioned outside the limits of humidity or are free from all humidity. Hence it is said in Psalm 95:5: *The dry land God made and fashioned;* and in Genesis 1:10: *God called the dry land Earth;* similarly <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Corpus Hermeticum," a foundation of Western alchemy and mysticism.</note> in the *Pimander*, book 3: *The heavy things settled beneath the moist sand, etc.* 

We say, therefore, that aridity or dryness itself is nothing other than the absence of humidity. From this it follows that humidity is that region situated between these two extremes—namely, between the cold and the hot, or between earth and fire. And so, clearly enough, though briefly and succinctly, we have spoken concerning the four types of darkness according to the limits of our understanding. Now, we shall further **advance** our step to the first birth of darkness, which is the universal moist nature, which the Ancients imagined to be the God **Pan**, and St. Peter called **water**, and the Cabalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that assigns deep cosmological meaning to Hebrew letters.</note> named the **Mother**, **Mem** מ <note>In the "Sefer Yetzirah," Mem is one of the three "Mother Letters," representing water (Mayim).</note>, which is the symbol of the waters and the pattern of the ineffable name <term>Jehovah</term> <note>original: יהוה (The Tetragrammaton). The author links the Hebrew name of God to the physical structure of the elements.</note> itself.

### CHAPTER I.

-> *Concerning water, or the universal spirit, without any regard for light or formal shaping.* <-

The substance of the waters enclosed within the womb of <term>hyle</term> <note>original: "hylę" – a term from Greek philosophy referring to the primordial, unformed matter of the universe.</note> was nothing, or rather something between Being and Nothing; and thus it was "Non-being," but held the potential for being. This is because all "Being" derives its existence from the presence of an informing light. Hence, these waters—existing only in potential and covered by the veil of primary darkness—were called "prime and most remote matter" by the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>; they described it as something in potentiality, but nothing in actual existence. Nor could their darkness be called a "privation" by these philosophers, insofar as no form had preceded it which might cause them to exist. Instead, from the beginning, they existed as unformed, uncultivated, void, and empty within the vast whirlpool of the hyle, since <term>Aleph</term> <note>original: א - the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here by the author to represent God or the First Cause.</note> or Jehovah had not yet illuminated them, nor looked out from His center upon their deformity. In this way, the waters are to be considered as nothing—indeed, scarcely anything imaginable—but rather a substance in potentiality constituting the empty hyle, or the void and "imaginary" earth. 

However, when Aleph looked out from His center upon the deformity of things, then the spirit of His mouth and the rays of His countenance were carried over the dark face of the Deep. Upon the outer face of this deep, the deformed waters, which had been hidden, now appeared outwardly with a perceptible form and appearance of water. For this reason, the word for "the deep," <term>Tehom</term> <note>original: תהום - the Hebrew word for the primordial abyss.</note>, is written as it is, insofar as it was enclosed by the presence or first appearance of the uncreated spirit. For although the first face of the waters was revealed by a sudden gaze of light, His rays did not yet penetrate into their depths. Hence it is said that "the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters," and not yet that it was *in* the waters. 

Therefore, after the manifestation of the upper waters, the first creature—namely, light—was established. That is to say, the highest portion of the waters was illuminated. This creature, the most noble of all, is composed of the eternal rays of the uncreated spirit and the most subtle water, as will be explained later in its proper place. By the power of this uncreated light, the shadows of the abyss retreated in a slanted revolution, first to the middle and then to the lowest region of the universal machine; for the dark abysses feared the presence of the Lord and were troubled (Psalm 77:17 <note>original: "Psalm. 77. 17." - In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 77:16: "The waters saw thee, O God... the depths also were troubled."</note>). In this context, the name "abyss" is taken for the deformed and not-yet-illuminated waters. But after the reverberation of their denser parts toward the center of the machine (in which density, indeed, blackness and gloom consist), the upper waters emerged transparent, subtle, and more noble, according to their greater or lesser participation with the light. The Wise Man describes this most excellently in Proverbs 8:24-29 with these words:

> When Jehovah strengthened the upper clouds above, when he made firm the fountains of the deep, when he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass the commandment of his mouth; when he appointed the foundations of the earth: then I, Wisdom, was with him, rejoicing before him at all times.

In this passage, he argues that the "upper waters" signify the regions of the higher heavens, and the "fountains of the deep" signify the springs of the dense and dark waters, etc., where the divine light or the power of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>, which is Wisdom...

That divine nature or the Word, of which the wise man speaks, is the cause of their illumination through its entrance into the entire mass of the water: For *Wisdom went around the circuit of the heavens, and walked in the depths of the abyss, in the waves of the sea, and in all the earth. (Ecclesiasticus 24:5-6).* <note>The author cites this as Ecclesiast. 1. 4., but the text corresponds to the Wisdom of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus chapter 24.</note> From these things it is also clear that the axiom of Saint Peter is most true *(2 Peter 3:5)*: *that the heavens and the earth itself were of old from water, and through water, consisting by the word of God.* These are the same waters that God, through that same Word, suspended in different regions by measure, and established a law for them throughout the universe. Therefore, we do not take "water" here to mean merely the visible water of the clouds or the sea, but rather every moist nature, counting from the <term>supersubstantial heaven</term> <note>A celestial realm existing above the physical substances of the world.</note> down to the lowest abyss of the earth itself. Thus, Holy Scripture divides this entire mass of water into three: namely, into the heaven—which is like a <term>Quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth element," a pure, celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> and its exalted part, which is the Sixth Essence; into the sea, which is like its <term>phlegm</term> <note>In alchemy, the watery, tasteless, and inactive part of a substance.</note>; and into the earth, which is like the dregs or sediment of the whole. Hence the Royal Psalmist says: *Let the heaven, the earth, and the seas, and everything that dwells in them, praise God.* And again in *Psalm 146: God preserves the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, constantly forever.*

For this reason, in many places in our work, we have called these waters the **Universal Spirit**; which we later divided into two parts: namely, the gross and the subtle. We have called "gross" everything that is visible, namely the earth—which is nothing other than thick water—and the thick water itself, which is nothing other than the substance of the abyss, or a subtle earth. We call "subtle" all that is invisible, which is called heaven. And so it is said that Jehovah made the heaven and the earth, that is, the subtle and invisible, and the thick and visible; of which the latter is his footstool, and the former his throne, as we read in *Matthew 5:34-35.* And yet these two are nothing but a single water, divided into two differing parts; one of which is dark, the other bright; one thick, the other thin; one spiritual, the other corporeal. Yet the gross is nothing other than the subtle [condensed], nor is the subtle anything other than the gross [refined], since that which is gross will become the same as the subtle through thinning, as we see in the burning of wood; and that which is subtle is rendered gross by thickening, as is shown by the conversion of air into mist, mist into a dense cloud, and cloud into hail, ice, and even into the bolt of a lightning-strike. By these examples, that obscurity of the assertion of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy and Hermeticism is attributed.</note> found in the *Emerald Tablet* is revealed, where he says: *That which is above is like that which is below, etc.*

We conclude, therefore, that this material element is signified by the "second mother" of Abraham in the <term>Yetzirah</term> <note>Refers to the *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Creation), an early foundational text of Jewish mysticism/Cabala.</note>: For **מ** <note>The Hebrew letter Mem.</note> is that Hebrew hieroglyph which signifies the waters brought forth into the light, just as **ש** <note>The Hebrew letter Shin, associated with fire or the spirit.</note> is the character or symbol of the dark and darkness. And hence it is that the Hebrew word for "water" is formed from the doubling of that character; in the middle of which characters the letter **י** <note>The Hebrew letter Jod.</note>—the formal or bright letter—is found, like a Sun illuminating both the upper and lower waters, in this manner: **מים** (*Maym*), that is, **Water**; where the preceding **מ** (*Mem*), which is open at the base, denotes the bright waters, through whose open base the spirit flows into nature through the **י** (*Jod*). And the final, closed **ם** (*Mem*) indicates the lower waters, which end with the darkness of the earth. And the **י** (*Jod*) in the middle stands in place of the Sun, in the midst of the firmament dividing the waters from the waters. Thus, you have a brief explanation, according to the reasoning of the Cabalists, of the living and primary name for water, **מים**: in which, through living letters or characters, the symbol of the substance of the waters—as well as that of Jehovah God who informs them—is explained as hiding in their center, and from the center illuminating and informing them on all sides.

### CHAPTER II.

->That water is the mother of all things.<-

Just as Abraham in his *Yetzirah* made the obscure **א** (*Aleph*), or darkness, the one and first unformed mother or prime matter; so also he not unsuitably established **מ** (*Mem*)—which is the symbol of water gushing from the womb of the dark *Aleph*—as the fruitful mother, or the fertile matter of things, from which the substance of heaven and earth and all things found in them are derived. For in the beginning, it was not heaven but water that was created, and then afterwards the heaven and the earth were made from water; as if from its abundance God finally created all things and separated them from one another, such as the heaven of immense height, depth, and breadth, the earth, fire, air, and water. All these were reduced and compacted into such harmony and unity that even in each of these separated bodies those four essential matters are found; namely, Air, hot and moist, containing within itself water, fire, and even earth; Water, cold and moist, containing in itself air and earth (whose shadow appears, whence it is called the Abyss). Earth, embracing in itself water, fire, and air; But water also comprehends in itself the earth, from which it also has its form, and by the same reasoning fire, which lies hidden in the earth, and air, from which it has its softness and mobility. And all these things, I say, are from water, through water, and in that immense water, which is the first mother, whose character or hieroglyph is **מ**; in which so many regions or species are found, like different types of a single genus, because of the greater or lesser presence of the uncreated light within them.

We see, therefore, that water itself is the first matter of all things in potentiality, and consequently...

...consequently the first mother of all things, and as it were a <term>storehouse</term> <note>original: "penus" — a pantry or store of provisions; here used to describe a source from which all creation is drawn.</note>, from which all things, both visible and invisible, were taken and separated. Yet this must not be understood or interpreted as if God made all things from a single mother who existed from eternity—such as, for example, from water—and that for this reason water is the "first being" of all things. For, as has been said elsewhere at length, the first mother and storehouse from which God created water was "Nothing"; that is, the Darkness and <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "hyla" — from the Greek word for "wood" or "matter," referring to the raw, unformed substance of the universe before creation.</note> signified by the <margin>k</margin> first mother. From her matrix, through the mediation and emanation of divine light, there came forth <margin>l</margin> <term>Mem</term> <note>The Hebrew letter representing water.</note> or water. However, this must be understood in a human way: that God created water out of Nothing. And this is rightly said, since in the "Beginning" or the *Hyle* there was nothing visible, nothing formed, but mere deformity; out of which—as if from a "nothingness" in being, and consequently something unimaginable, invisible, and even imperceptible—God <term>Elohim</term> <note>The Hebrew name for God used in the creation narrative of Genesis.</note> created and brought forth the waters into the light. Furthermore, if we wish to contemplate truly and beyond the human capacity how water has its true origin, it cannot be denied that in the creation of water there was a certain unformed matter (as I have said) in the "Greatest Mystery" or *Hyle* which existed in the divine will. From that storehouse, as from a mystery, the waters flowed forth during creation; this seems too obscure, even incredible, to the human grasp. For we, who are born of the flesh, both perceive and speak of such things carnally; but if once, by the preceding divine grace, we are reborn of the spirit, we shall understand such mysteries to our satisfaction, and we shall know the origin and first beginning of water, which was made visible from the highest invisible and unformed mystery, and from which all other principles thereafter arose. And thus can this water now well be called the "matter of all things": namely, the invisible water of invisible things, such as the heavens and their intelligences; and the visible water of visible things, namely the earth and the sea, fresh waters, and those things which dwell within them. Whence it is reasonably concluded that water is the second mother, or the secondary matter of all things, both celestial and terrestrial; and consequently, that the entire world, including heaven and earth, is nothing other than water altered and changed in various ways, according to the different measure of the <term>luminous act</term> <note>The action of Divine Light upon matter.</note> working differently upon it. For we see that one part of the same river can be stained with ink, another with blood, another with saffron; and its edge with milk or lime, while in the meantime it remains one and the same water in its species and continuity. Finally, we have sufficient testimony of this matter from the Apostle in the place cited before, namely *2 Peter 3*, stating that in the first times the heaven was even as the earth, consisting of water through the Word of God. Therefore, it appears from what was said above that the water *Mem*, which is the first mother of things, is simple and mixed with nothing else. It is also quite clear that it encompasses the principles of the remaining three elements within itself, and contains the seeds of all things, both visible and invisible, insofar as out of it and in it God founded heaven, earth, and all their contents, both visible and invisible; and consequently He also placed the four elements and their "nurseries" within it. Wherefore it is also certain that the elements themselves were made from water, as will be demonstrated in the following chapter.

### CHAPTER III.

->*How water is the mother of the heavens and of all the elements, and the "glue" by which, through the mediation of the divine act, they are connected in composition.*<-

In the preceding sections, it was declared that the substance of the unformed darkness was waters or spirits, and that from this it follows that one kind of gloom is preferred over another: namely, that which belongs to the higher heaven over that of the middle heaven, and again that of the middle over the lowest. This is certainly in respect to the mobility of the location of that light whose sparks those dark spirits snatched for themselves as something opposite to them; while the superfluous spirit of any heaven was gradually driven downward toward the center with its dark veil. For although that barely imaginable matter, *Hyle*, which now through the revelation of the <term>fiery spirit</term> <note>Divine light or the Holy Spirit.</note> appears and is named "water," was equally dispersed through the vast and infinite whirlpool or abyss of the *Hyle* (since all inequality was made by a "diverse act" which did not manifest itself before the beginning in the *Hyle*, insofar as its source <term>Aleph</term> <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing the Monad or the One God.</note> had not yet revealed itself), it must nevertheless now be understood that this equality is turned into inequality by the appearance of the uncreated light. For where the presence and effect of light is more clear and abundant, there, because of its thinning and refining nature, those spirits in which that clear light dwells are made more subtle and rare. Whence, the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest part of heaven, believed in ancient cosmology to be composed of pure fire or light.</note> having been purged of its superfluous dark spirits, that superfluity was forced to glide downward like a horrendous shadow by the gaze of Jehovah. Indeed, that whole mass was greatly disturbed, according to *Psalm 77:16*: *The depths feared the presence of Jehovah and were troubled.* And <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetica are attributed.</note> in the *Pimander*, Book 1: *At the presence of the immense light of the revealed Pimander, a horrendous shadow glided downward in an oblique revolution*; that is, the shadow—meaning the denser part of the unformed spirits—inclined itself toward the center in the presence of the uncreated light, while the thinner portion of the same, purified from darkness, was carried by the uncreated light to the place...

This same order was observed by the surplus portion of the dark spirit of the middle region; for, having left a sufficient part of its substance for the "fecundating light" (whose vehicle it is), it was likewise pushed downward by the power of those rays of nature. And so the substance of the **ethereal heaven** was procreated from the universal mother-water; and the remaining surplus of that heaven, seizing for itself infinite rays of nature or secondary light, fell downward into the nature of the general **Chaos**. Thus, we have three portions of unformed waters or spirits remaining from the aforementioned heavens, mixed in a confused way with the darkness of the lowest kingdom. Finally, from their enclosed subtle spirits—extracted by the <term>alchemy of nature</term> <note>The natural process of refining, separating, and perfecting substances, viewed as a divine chemical process.</note>, brought to a transparent form by the third-level light, and purged of impurity and dross—the three elements are produced: those simple, clear, and pure things by which the vacuum of the lower heaven is filled. And, from the dregs and opaque part of the universal Chaos, the three kingdoms of opaque creatures arise; from which we say the whole earth is composed (and for this reason it is divided into three regions, corresponding to those regions of the heavens to which their dregs are related). Thus we see that spirit of wine, because of the presence of the worthier light it possesses, floats upon oil.

Similarly, the second portion of darkness, which belongs to the middle heaven, emits its own subtle part through compression, and occupies the place of the middle light as the **element of air**. Do we not also see that air agrees in all things with the ether, and fire with the Empyrean spirit; except that these are coarser spirits and consequently placed in the lowest part of the world, while those are more subtle because they exist in the higher parts? Nevertheless, we say that insofar as fire proceeds from the darkness of the Empyrean heaven, and air from the dark spirit of the ethereal heaven, fire behaves in the highest sphere of the lowest heaven just as the intellectual spirit behaves in the highest heaven of the world; similarly, air in the middle region of the lowest heaven is as ether is in the middle heaven of the world. Furthermore, by the compression of the lowest darkness (or the lowest heaven), the **element of visible water** is made, which is nothing other than subtle and transparent earth, as is sufficiently shown in ice or in a clear gemstone. And as spirit of wine floats on oil, and oil on <term>phlegm</term> <note>A term used in early medicine and chemistry to refer to a watery, dull, or inert residue.</note>, so likewise fire floats on air, and air on water. Many testimonies have marked the probability of this matter for us; for first, in the writings of Hermes Trismegistus, we read thus in the *Pymander*, book 1:

> *The true Word, standing by the moist nature, cherished it; and from the bowels of the moist nature, a pure and light fire immediately sought the heights. Here, therefore, he argues how, by the mediation of the Word and the luminous emanation, all these things of the water are bound together in harmonious peace and arranged according to their greater or lesser dignity. He teaches us that all these things were done in the same place immediately after the movement of the horrifying shadows that slipped downward. From this, it seems likely that the substances of these elements were extracted from the shadow of each worldly region (which excelled each other in dignity and excellence) through the mediation of the Word, or the light, and the super-celestial fire. Similarly, the same author declares this best elsewhere, namely in his *Third Sermon*:

> *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss; water, moreover, and a thin intellectual spirit were in Chaos by divine power. But a holy splendor flourished, which led the elements forth from under the sand and the moist nature. And when they had been indistinct, the light things afterward flew up into the high region, and the heavy things settled under the moist sand.*

Once the things carried by the fiery spirit were distinguished and balanced, the heaven shone out into seven circles.

From this, therefore, he seems to hint that not only the element of fire (as a fourth essence) was expelled from the dark spirit of the Empyrean region, but also the very flower of the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or ether, the purest substance of the celestial bodies.</note>, the Solar one, or the <term>Heliotropion</term> <note>original: "Heliotropion" — literally "sun-turner," here referring to the luminous body of the sun itself.</note>—namely, the luminous solar body—arose from the same, from whose power and luminous fountain the remaining wandering stars [planets] receive their light, as was demonstrated in the first Treatise of the first Volume. The fiery spirit was carried over the face of the waters, both in the higher heaven of the world, where light reigns, and in the higher sphere of the elements. *Concerning the air, or the invisible elementary spirit, Ecclesiastes 1:5-6 speaks thus:* *The air or spirit goes round and hastens according to the motion of the Sun from the east to the west, and returns according to its circuits.* <note>The author is interpreting the biblical "wind" (spiritus) as the alchemical element of Air.</note> Similarly, whenever the sacred scriptures mention the winds, they understand the air to be driven by the power of **Jehovah**. Water also signifies an element in *Psalm 104:6* <note>The text cites Psalm 33:7, but the quote "You covered the earth with the deep as with a garment" is from Psalm 104:6.</note> when it says: *Jehovah covered the earth with the abyss, as if with a garment.* From these things, therefore, we see that all elements are in water and come from water, and consequently, that water is the mother of all elements.

However, we shall now show that this very water is also the fountain and origin of opaque bodies in the three kingdoms of composition. Just as there are three heavens in the world, it was clearly explained above that there are also three kingdoms of darkness on the earth. The highest of these corresponds to the highest heaven of the world and the highest element of the lower region—namely, fire—and to the **animal** kind of composition. 

From this, the more skilled in Philosophy have perceived it as certain that animals—in respect to a certain reason (which they treat as metaphorical in irrational beasts, or call truly intellectual in man)—and similarly by consideration of memory and sense, participate in some way in the higher or rational heaven. They also perceive that in the composition of animals, fire holds dominion over the air. By this it is declared that the dark animal body (which is nothing other than **condensed water**) comes from the darkness of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most celestial part of the universe, associated with pure fire and light.</note>, or rather, from the first appearance of the divine spirit reflected downward; from which the element of fire leapt forth through compression. 

Hence, the animal body very easily allures a nature similar to itself into its composition by its magnetic attracting power. And from this it happens that animals, being fiery in nature, surpass vegetables, just as vegetables surpass minerals. Similarly, vegetables—with respect to their growth and multiplication which proceeds from the solar realm or the ethereal heaven—derive their opaque bodies from the darkness of that heaven; and in their composition, they participate in the spirit of the element of air along with water, which arose from that same darkness. 

In exactly the same way, the matter stands in minerals, whose bodies are compacted from the darkness of the lowest heaven, and participate most greatly in the nature of water with earth. This element of thin water was squeezed out through compression by the power of the Word or divine fire, and was extracted by <term>true chemistry</term> <note>original: "chymia vera" — refers to "alchemy" as a sacred, natural-supernatural science of creation.</note> in both a supernatural and natural way. From this it follows that animals are more subtle and soft than vegetables, and minerals are denser, harder, and more compacted than both. But we shall deal with these in a clearer discourse in the third Section of this work, where we shall speak of the medicines of the three opaque kingdoms.

We conclude, therefore, from these things, that **Water** is the <term>materia prima</term> <note>The "first matter" or the fundamental substance from which all things are created.</note>, and the mother, and as it were the storehouse of all things, both invisible and visible, both simple and composite, both transparent and opaque; and that opacity or darkness is nothing other than **condensed water**. This is the source of the "thick cloud," which is also called "gloom" in the sacred scriptures. 

Nor, certainly, is air anything other than subtle water, and consequently, when thickened, it becomes water. Finally, fire is nothing other than rarefied air; which, when condensed, becomes air; and that air again becomes a flashing cloud because of the fire enclosed within it and contracted by thickening; and that cloud is even accustomed to be congealed into earth and stone. 

Hence, we see that the "thick" is nothing other than the "subtle," nor is the "subtle" anything else than the "thick"; *that is, the lower is just like that which is above, and vice versa* <note>original: "inferius est sicut & illud, quod est superius" — A direct reference to the famous Hermetic maxim from the Emerald Tablet.</note>. Consequently, whatever exists in the world is nothing other than water, subtle or thick; and the thick is subtle in potential, just as the subtle has the power of turning into the thick. 

However, that which distinguishes and alters all these things is the **Word** and the shining power of **Jehovah**; by His greater action the thick becomes subtle, and by His lesser action the subtle becomes thick. And thus that saying of the Psalmist is understood: *By the Word of Jehovah the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit from His mouth.* In water, from water, and through water—with the Word operating—the subtle and thick, the transparent and opaque, heaven and earth, and all creatures composed of them were made. 

In heaven, therefore, water is a very precious thing: transparent, liquid, subtle, spiritual, and simple, penetrating both visible and invisible things, and connecting all essential bodies like a **glue** by the power of the light acting within it. So much so that without water, no thing, as it was created by itself, could be contained or cling together; but outside of this clear water, bodies would fall apart like dust or ashes. 

This is indeed proven in wood; for as soon as the aqueous liquor is expelled from its composition by the force of fire, it immediately returns to dust and ashes—that is, into its dark portion, from which it had its opacity. For it is impossible for any animal, vegetable, or mineral creature to be able to subsist in its composition without its **essential water**; which is its <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum radicale" — in alchemy, the vital fluid or "innate balm" that preserves life and prevents the body from becoming brittle or decaying.</note>, or balsam, by which its parts are preserved and compacted together as if by a certain glue. 

What this radical moisture does in the curing of the body, we shall explain in its own place and time. Conversely, the "dark water" is like the base and foundation upon which the more liquid and subtle waters are established to form the image of a species and are covered by opacity. Thus ashes, mud, clay, earth, shadow, and gloom are called the foundations of the **external man**, as sacred monuments declare in many places. 

You see, therefore, O Earth-born, that you are water; you live in water, you feed in water, you sleep through water, you feel in water, you understand in water; finally, from water, in water, and through water you are sustained and you breathe. You are affected by joy and health, and are drenched in gladness by the thin and clear spirit of water; but you are afflicted by sadness and sorrow, and a miserable life and disease, through a draught of thick and dark water. Finally, in St. Peter's...

Yet, all that water which is visible is called the "element of water," just as invisible water encompasses air, fire, and the heavens.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Concerning the manifold division of waters, and especially into the visible and the invisible.*<-

Next, we shall briefly say a few words regarding the division of the universal water into its particular parts. In <margin>Genesis 1</margin> we read that the waters were divided into the "expanse"—which part is indeed the firmament or heaven—and into the "gathered part," which is named the sea. This is the exact division of the clear waters, which seems to imply the same thing as the distinction of water into visible and invisible, discussed below. Again, water is divided into an upper and a lower part; thus, the firmament is said to have distinguished the upper waters (which are subtle and spiritual) from the lower waters (which are gross and material). The firmament itself, or the middle heaven, participates in both, and its waters are moderately thin and moderately thick. Hence, the "sphere of equality" is said to pass through the center of the middle heaven. 

Again, in <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> water is divided into the upper clouds above, the springs of the abyss, and the sea. These are the words: *When **Jehovah** established the upper clouds above, when he strengthened the fountains of the deep, when he imposed his decree upon the sea and the waters, lest they should escape the command of his mouth, when he established the foundations of the earth; I, **Wisdom**, was with him.* By "upper clouds above," he understood the heavens themselves, according to <margin>Psalm 104:3</margin>, *The upper heavens are covered with waters by God;* and <margin>Job 25:5</margin> <note>Likely referring to Job 35:5: "Look at the heavens and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you."</note> *Look to the heaven, and contemplate the upper clouds, how they are high above you.* Similarly, in <margin>Psalm 89:7</margin> <note>The author likely means Psalm 89:6 or 37 in older numbering.</note> the heaven is called the "upper clouds," and in <margin>Psalm 89:9</margin>, *Who is considered equal to **Jehovah** God in the upper cloud?* 

By the "springs of the abyss," he meant fresh water; by the "sea," salt water; and by the "earth," he meant opaque water, which was the dregs <note>original: *fæx*; the sediment or leftover material from a process</note> remaining from the creation of the universal clear waters. But elsewhere, he seems to include all visible waters under the name of the sea; namely in <margin>Psalm 146</margin>: *God constantly preserves the heaven, the earth, the sea, and whatever is in them, forever.* In <margin>Genesis 7:24</margin>, clear water is distinguished into the springs of the deep and the floodgates of heaven. And in <margin>Deuteronomy 4:18</margin>, visible waters are divided into waters under the earth and above the earth. 

Likewise, the visible and sensible upper waters are divided into cloud, mist, vapor, and exhalation, mention of which is made in <margin>Psalms 104 and 105:39</margin>, <margin>Psalm 135:7</margin>, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:3</margin>, and in infinite other places. These same waters are also divided into liquid and condensed forms, such as snow, hail, ice, manna, and so on. Similarly, the visible lower waters are distinguished into fresh, salt, acidic, bitter, sulfurous, hot, and currently cold. Furthermore, waters are either "living"—which **Christ** Himself said would take away thirst forever in <margin>John 4:13</margin>—or common waters, which do not extinguish thirst permanently. 

But among all other divisions of water, we prefer this one: that which is made into the **spiritual and invisible**, and into the **material or visible**. Furthermore, the spiritual waters are divided into natural and supernatural; the natural into ethereal and elementary; and similarly, the material or visible waters are divided into the limpid (namely, the element of water) and the opaque (or earth). Regarding this kind of division of water, we shall discourse in this place. 

Accordingly, it must be known that in the beginning, water was invisible. Truly, so that humans and other animals might see it, God dressed it in a kind of transparent garment; just as all visible things were invisible from the beginning, and only afterward were dressed in a visible form, as if in a garment, so that they might be seen and perceived by bodily eyes. And so water will persist in this visible essence until its prefixed end, at which point it will return again into a clear, invisible, and purely spiritual essence—concerning which the great Psalmist of Israel sings in <margin>Psalm 102</margin>. Moreover, the Holy Scripture testifies in <margin>Hebrews 11</margin> that God created visible things from invisible things: *By faith we recognize that it has always been so with the world through the **Word of God**, so that from those things which could not be seen, those things which can be seen were made.* 

Invisible, therefore, was the water in the beginning, from which all visible things were created. Even a noble creature, so that it may be seen, is accustomed to put on a garment or a shell. Thus indeed we see the invisible air put on a garment of thick and visible cloud; and even sometimes the heaven, containing the "best treasure of **Jehovah**," is made visible to man according to <margin>Deuteronomy 28:12</margin>. If anyone, however, should know the method and art of capturing and collecting the **true invisible water**, the Sages say he possesses a most excellent balsam <term>a medicinal or alchemical substance capable of healing and preservation</term> that heals every kind of infirmity; which I shall explain more clearly in its own time, as I have received it from trustworthy authors.

### CHAPTER V.

->*On the measure of the waters; and whether water was created sweet or salty.*<-

Although the body of the created water is of such vast magnitude that no mortal can grasp its scale through reason, nevertheless, God has measured it with His own hand, as seen in *Isaiah 40*, for He is the one who grants to every thing its own measure, number, and weight, as in *Wisdom 11*. Indeed, this Master Craftsman <term>original: *artifex*; a term often used to describe God as the Divine Architect or Alchemist</term> measured the created water in such a way that He holds its measure by number—specifically, how many thousands of handfuls of it exist. Furthermore, the weight of the water was tested by the most exact scale of God, and thus the most certain number of pounds or weights has been recorded. This measure, number, and weight of the water are joined in such harmony and equality that the entire body cannot move upward, downward, or even to the sides without the permission of the Creator; rather, it persists so constantly in its measure, number, and weight that not even a single drop of it perishes. For in whatever way we use water—whether for washing or by pouring it onto the ground—nothing of it is lost; instead, it returns either to the waters of the earth or into the air, for water exists there as well. Thus, nothing at all passes away, but it is always preserved in its measure, number, and weight without any decrease. Nor should this be said only of common water; the same must be understood of the earth, of visible water, of air, of clouds, of fire, of the ether, and of the Empyrean spirit, which are indeed various species of the most general "universal water." For concerning the measure of the earth (which is the dregs of water, or opaque water), it is written in *Psalm 95:4*: "The deepest tracks of the earth are in the hand of God," with whom are the heights of the mountains, etc. And in *Psalm 104:5*: "God founded the earth upon its bases, that it should not be moved forever." Similarly, *Job 26:7*: "God hangs the earth upon nothing"; and *Proverbs 3:19*: "God founded the earth by wisdom"; and *Job 38:37*: "Who made those things which descend from the heavens to rest? When the dust descended into that hardness, and the clods cleaved fast together?" We find it written likewise concerning the measure of visible water in *Job 26:10*: "He has surrounded the waters with a boundary, or marked out the surface of the waters with a decree"; and in the same book, *28:25*: "God weighs the waters in a measure." Similarly, speaking of the proportion of the clouds, *Job 28:26* says: "He set a law for the rains, and a way for the sounding storms"; and *Proverbs 8:28*: "When Jehovah strengthened the upper clouds above," etc. Regarding the number of the heavens, it is said in *Job 38:37*: "Who numbered the heavens in Wisdom?" and in *Job 26:7*: "God stretched out the north over the empty space"; and *Proverbs 3:19*: "God established the heavens by understanding," etc. From these passages, one may see that God ordained every species of universal water with just scales and due measure from the beginning, and has perpetually observed such perfection of arrangement.

Now, as for the quality of the water—whether sweet or salty—a significant doubt may arise as to whether the universal water, or indeed the sea, was salty or sweet from the origin of its creation. To answer this in one word: we say that the universal water, and consequently all its particles, were sweet from the beginning; and also possessed a sweetness and scent so pleasant that nothing similar can be found in the entire world. Indeed, this "best water," as a miraculous, holy, and unique creature of God, was of a scent and flavor so pleasant, sweet, and healthy that the human tongue cannot express it. But since God clothed this work of His in a certain transparent shell, garment, or husk <term>original: *putamen*; a shell or covering, used here to mean the material exterior that hides a spiritual essence</term>, and enclosed within it its sweetness, flavor, and that most delightful and healthy scent, it is certainly a task of no small skill to remove that husk from it—as from other things in which noble balsams lie hidden—and to extract the uniform and invisible essence from it. But "here is the labor, here is the work" <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*: *hoc opus, hic labor est*, referring to a difficult task</note>. I know indeed that it must be done, yet I cannot accomplish it. 

But to return to the reason for the saltiness of water: we say that on the second day, when the waters were separated from the waters by the interposition of the firmament, all the water gathered below the firmament into one place and was called the "sea." This water became salty immediately and in that very hour, and nothing in it was left without salt. Hence it was called "The Salt" in *Genesis 14* and *Numbers 34*. On this occasion, it is also worth noting that salt is found in all the fruits of the earth, trees, herbs, animals, minerals, and indeed in all visible things that exist in the entire world, as can be demonstrated by the daily examples of the Chemists <term>original: *Chymicorum*; referring to practitioners of alchemy and early chemistry</term>. The reason is readily apparent why salt is found in every composite creature: namely, because every composite body is made from the dregs or ashes of dark water. Since gross water concurs with the "ashes of darkness" to form the composition of a creature, it follows that the creature contains salt in its composition, because the water of its composition resembles sea water. This is why we perceive urine in animals to be tainted with salt, and why lye <term>original: *lixivium*; an alkaline solution leached from wood ashes</term> is easily made from wood, and tartar <term>original: *tartarus*; the potassium bitartrate sediment found in wine casks</term> from wine. Therefore, we see that in the beginning, universal water was sweet and of a pleasant flavor; but after its separation and its union with the earth—like common water mixing with ashes—that water began to extract the salty nature of the terrestrial ashes, and thus it became salty immediately. However, the waters of springs and rivers behave differently; for although their origin is from the sea and they return again to the sea according to *Ecclesiastes 1:7*: "The rivers hasten to the sea, yet the sea is not full" (which proves they come from the sea), they are nevertheless purged and purified of their saltiness through their constant filtration or passage through the pores of the earth, and they are made sweet once more.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*Whether water possesses sense within itself or not?*<-

But here a question of no small importance arises: namely, whether this universal creature <note>referring to the primordial element of water</note> has been endowed and gifted by God with sense and intellect? To this, answering in the affirmative, we say that first in water, and then in all other creatures fashioned from it, there is as much sense and intelligence present as is sufficient for them to listen to and hear the voice of God, so that they may tremble at it and obey it. For the Spirit of the Lord, which was "carried over the waters," mixed His own fiery and intellectual nature into them in such a way that—with the Uncreated Spirit <note>original: *Spiritu increato*; the Holy Spirit</note> acting as the mover and director—the created spirits, or the waters, acting as the passive element, might understand the sense and will of God and always show themselves obedient to Him. 

Indeed, because of the presence of the luminous Spirit, the universal waters possessed life; they were called the Messiah, or the power of the Tetragrammaton <note>original: *virtus Tetragrammati*; the power of the four-letter divine name of God, YHWH</note>, and in the realms of nature, they are called Metatron <note>A high-ranking mediator or celestial scribe in Kabbalistic tradition, often associated with the governance of the natural world</note>. From this came that Paradisiacal and mystical water, which is, as it were, the vital spirit of the entire mass; it is called "living water" in many places of the Sacred Scriptures. For God commands that they pour "living water" over the ashes (*Deuteronomy 19*) <note>The author likely refers to the ritual of the Red Heifer found in Numbers 19, though he cites Deuteronomy</note>. It is by this same reasoning that David speaks of the water "seeing" Jehovah and "fearing" Him, and the depths being "troubled" (*Psalm 77:16*). And at Christ’s command, the waters obeyed, so that its tumultuous or raging waves suddenly submitted to His voice (*Matthew 8:26*). 

In these passages, it is confirmed that there is some sense and intellect in water, such that it sees, hears, and fears. Furthermore, in *Psalm 148:4*, it is said that the "waters above the heavens" praise God. And elsewhere: "The heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and whatever dwells in them, shall praise God." Moreover, water also hears and sees the malice of men, and bears it patiently. Indeed, the waters are even said to speak; hence it is said that the "heavens declare the praise and glory of God," and that the "firmament of heaven announces the works He has made with His hands." 

However, men cannot obtain this or perform this as a punishment for their sins—that is, to have the waters obey them as they obeyed Moses, Joshua, Elijah, Elisha, and Christ, when they crossed through the Red Sea with dry feet (*Exodus 14:21*), through the Jordan (*Joshua 3:16* and *2 Kings 2*), and walked upon the sea, as in the place cited before. This is despite the fact that God subjected all His visible creatures to men, so that men might command them, and they, in turn, might obey them with fear and trembling (*Genesis 1:28*). 

But this "hearing, seeing, fearing, and speaking" which we have said exists in water, rises above all the *Physics of the Pagans* <note>original: *Physica Ethnicorum*; referring to Greek and Roman philosophical texts, particularly those of Aristotle</note>; nothing of this sort is found in their books. Truly, they knew neither the true God nor His creatures, but ridiculously fashioned for themselves a certain "god" and "world" of their own. From this, they fell into those blind errors in which the world—and this current age of ours judging the world—still remains stuck. 

And certainly, I submit myself to their opinions in some way, though with a kind of forced will, lest I be called a "critical introducer of new opinions" or a "vain attacker of ancient doctrine" if I depart too far from common error right at the beginning. For would it not seem foolish and ridiculous to some overwhelmed by ignorance if it were asserted among them that the Empyrean and Ethereal Heaven—the seat of God—is just as much in the elementary world as in the highest? Or that heaven is in the earth, and earth is in heaven; likewise that God is in man, and man is in God; and that the Sun, Moon, and Planets descend? 

And yet we boldly affirm that all these things can be proven and confirmed by the clearest testimonies of Sacred Scripture, however much they may lose their credibility when recounted to the ignorant. Therefore, I desire to lead you through the ancient way and through human, fictitious wisdom toward the divine and true gate of wisdom—that is, to direct and entice you from Aristotelian foundations toward the Elysian Fields <note>The mythical "blessed lands," here used to represent the lush spiritual truths of the Bible</note> of the Word of God, following the paths of the Holy Bible through similar principles. In these alone is the one and only truth, and outside of them, there is none. For it is not fitting to desert the fountain of all Wisdom and seek art, science, and intellect in foreign regions, as did the Hagarenes <note>original: *Agareni*; a biblical term for descendants of Hagar, often used to refer to outsiders or those lacking the true covenant</note> and those who were in Teman; for they never recognized the way of true wisdom (*Baruch 3*). Indeed, this fountain alone possesses the "Key of David," which opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens (*Isaiah 22*).

### CHAPTER VII.

->*On the greatest mysteries which are in water.*<-

Jehovah placed truly magnificent mysteries in this general water of His. Indeed, He has enclosed the hidden property, power, operation, and motion of every creature—both visible and invisible—within the water, albeit in an invisible manner. Thus, the "seed" of all things lies hidden within it. Consequently, according to our preceding doctrine, this is the universal mother of all things, since the seeds of things are contained in her womb—namely, the seeds of the heavens, the stars, the animals, the plants, the gems, and the metals; concerning which we shall speak at length in the Section *On Medicines*. ...[it is] also the food and nourishment of all living things in every kingdom, and likewise the glue and connection of all elements and tangible things composed of the elements. The most expert Sages have also said that it is the most excellent medicine that can be found anywhere under the Sun, between heaven and earth. And finally, it is the greatest mystery of all: that God made all the stars—and indeed the Sun, the Moon, and the other planets—as well as the entire air and the angels and spirits dwelling within it, and finally the terrestrial globe itself with everything existing upon it, out of water. He enclosed them in water in a wondrous way, and sealed them firmly within it by His living and omnipotent word; and thus each of these things perseveres constantly in the order originally established, performing its duty without intermission for the praise and honor of God and for the benefit of the human race.

We see, therefore, that heaven is, as it were, mere water; and that all the stars swim in it just like wood in water. And yet, if that wood were to be dissolved, we find it to be nothing other than water; just as the compact bodies of the stars themselves are nothing other than condensed water gathered into a globe. The remaining spiritual mysteries contained within this created water are gathered from the Biblical writings and even from the New Testament: namely, by what means Jesus Christ came through water and blood; not through water alone, but through water and blood. <note>original: "Christus Jesus venerit per aquam & sanguinem; non per aquam solummodo, sed per aquam & sanguinem"</note> *There are three witnesses on earth: namely the water, the spirit, and the blood, and these three are one. 1 John 5.* <note>original: "Tres esse testes in terra; nimirum aquam, spiritum, & sanguinem, & tria illa esse unum, 1. We also read in many places of the New Testament regarding Baptism by water, spirit, and fire, not without stupendous mystery. Similarly, mention is frequently made in Holy Scripture of the living water and the fountain of life in Paradise, both the celestial and the lower, and other things of this kind. So too do the books of Moses speak of the pillar of fire and cloud, and Ezekiel speaks of the spiritual wheels in heaven before Jehovah, and of the sapphire and amber-colored waters similar to Him. Finally, as to what concerns the end of the waters—namely, what will become of water on the last day, and whether it is all to perish or not—we have declared this sufficiently in the *First Treatise, Volume 2*. # CHAPTER VIII.
### That visible water cleanses all things, and even purges itself.

So precious is this mother of all things, and so necessary for the use of whatever things are procreated from her, that man—the prince of visible creatures—cannot do without it in temples, at home, or abroad. For whatever has become depraved, rotten, or moldy, or is otherwise impure, polluted, or stained and defiled, all of this is washed and cleansed by water. Insofar as it cleanses impure things by drawing all impurity to itself, it carries everything away to the appropriate and destined places, so that nothing can hinder or offend mankind. When we see water in the butcher shops and kitchens stained with blood, muddy in the workshops of potters, black, blue, or green at the dyers', infected with manure in the stables, and so foul in the latrines that you cannot even bear it because of the excessive stench, but must carry it out and pour it away for that reason—even then, it possesses such virtue that it removes such uncleanness from itself. It purges and cleanses itself again in such a way that you can no longer detect any fault in it, but may use it healthfully again for drinking and in the kitchen. From secret places, the dung and filth of the heated rooms and dining chambers are cast into the water, so much so that the water is rendered entirely impure and contaminated by such dregs; yet it has hardly carried all those things even for two hundred stadia <note>original: "ducenta stadia"; a stadium was an ancient unit of length, roughly 185 meters. 200 stadia is about 23 miles or 37 kilometers.</note> before it has again deposited all that impurity, purified itself most excellently, and corrected every taste, so that it may be of use for drinking and other necessities. And although it usually happens that the water of rivers, and indeed even of springs, is observed to corrupt and rot through a long stay in vessels, so that it cannot be kept in ships or houses without detriment to health, it must nevertheless be known that water in its nature is a holy, clean, and pure thing, and that by no means can it rot or be corrupted, but it always persists in its healthy and pure essence. As for the fact that it contracts such an unpleasant odor in some vessels, this happens not from the nature of the water—as if the water itself were putrefied—but rather because the water assumes the odor from the wood, metal, or earthenware in which it is kept, and attracts and increases it more and more until it is finally poured out, and then it drives that rot of the vessel away from itself. Furthermore, the hidden nature of the earth in the place from which this water is drawn can be the cause of that stench; hence it happens that one water rots more quickly in the same vessels than another. For water, by its succession in motion, removes the cause of corruption, which is more likely to happen when the elements are at rest, as they are not naturally quiescent. For thus, when a humor in the body is outside its natural seat,

### CHAPTER IX.

->*Concerning that portion of the lower water which is called the sphere, or element, of humidity; and concerning the most proper quality of water.*<-

That portion of the lower waters which is situated between two extremes—namely, between fire and earth—is called the **sphere of humidity**. This is nothing other than those two elements which Philosophy <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to "Natural Philosophy," the precursor to modern science.</note> has called "water" and "air," that is, visible water and invisible water, or dense and subtle water. For this sphere is distinguished into two parts, differing in nature and location from each other, because of the proximity of the two extremes to each of them. Thus, the lowest portion of the sphere of humidity is rendered visible and dense because of the dominion of the earth’s coldness within it, whose property it is to condense. The upper part, however, is invisible and rare <note>The term "rare" or "rarefied" describes a substance that is thin or less dense, like air.</note> because of its partnership with the heat of the neighboring fire, whose property it is to thin, and by thinning, to make invisible.

Earth is therefore the lowest water, which is the universal extremity and the dark tabernacle of cold; fire, however, is the highest summit and peak of the lower waters; while water and air, which are called the single sphere of humidity, are suspended between these two. Their origin, as was said in the preceding sections, is derived from the lowest darkness and the middle of heaven. For by the compression of this darkness around the center of the universe, certain spirits <note>In alchemical texts, "spirits" often refers to volatile vapors or the life-force within matter.</note> poured over the soul and other sparks enclosed within them are either exalted more sublimely or submerged more deeply, according to the dignity of the light which is carried in them.

But truly, the sparks of secondary light or nature, immersed in the spirit of the middle darkness reflected downwards, are more worthy and more lively than those third-rank sparks which are infused into the spirit of the lowest darkness. Therefore, the latter fills the place of the sea and visible water, while the former fills the vast capacity of the air, and both complete the entire sphere of equality.

But here a great doubt may arise: namely, why—since both the element of earth and the element of fire are portions of water—are both of these said to be not "moist," but on the contrary "dry," given that humidity is always accustomed to accompany the condition and nature of fire by origin?

To which we respond in the first place: although the earth is said to be arid because of the condensing and constricting presence of immense cold, it nevertheless has within itself a hidden humidity of water. This can be seen in the nature of salt, found in the middle of any portion of earth; it can be seen that through the mediation of actual humidity with heat, salt is reduced into water. From this it is clear that the earth itself, in a hidden way and as if in potentiality, has humidity within it. But because of the congealing act of dry cold itself, the effect of that humidity is removed; nevertheless, that humidity hides in the earth in the meantime and exists in potential.

From this, therefore, it is that humidity is said by us to be absent from the earth, so that it is called "dry" and "arid"—not because it is truly and centrally so, but because, as far as human sensation is concerned, humidity does not seem to have dominion in the earth, insofar as its entire mass appears arid <margin>Genesis 1</margin> in the midst of the waters, as is held in Genesis 1. And yet, if we look into the matter as it is with the eyes of the intellect, we find humidity here centrally; but, insofar as it is congealed by the force of cold, it is called not "humidity" but "aridity." Humidity is said to be absent for this reason, and this absence of humidity in the earth is called "dryness."

For a not dissimilar reason, humidity is found in the element of fire; for it is, as it were, the vehicle of essential light. Nevertheless, because of the thinning nature of fire, it is so attenuated—namely, with the spirit receiving the fiery power—that no sign of humidity appears in it. Consequently, this member of the "water" is called dry, insofar as, because of the hiding and imperceptibility of humidity, its contrary appears to be present, namely aridity, as we shall declare more broadly in the description of the final principle, namely light.

There is therefore a cone of a material pyramid <note>The author uses the "interlaced pyramids" of light and darkness (fire and earth) to explain the structure of the universe.</note> packed and suffused with imperceptible spirit; and thus humidity is thought by the senses to be absent from that place, and dryness is said to predominate. But in the base of that same pyramid, the aqueous spirit is found abundantly, but it is congealed by cold into a hard and dry mass, and the act of humidity is removed and changed into aridity.

But, to return to the point, we say that the intermediate sphere, which contains water and air, is made from the proportional conflict of the opposite qualities of the two extremes—namely Earth and Fire. This comes from the action of heat upon the cold of the earth, and the similar and corresponding passion, reaction, and resistance of terrestrial cold against the nature of the pursuing fire. Therefore, the diameter of the fiery pyramid passes and descends from its base (located in the element of fire) to its cone (which ends in the earth); and vice versa, the diameter of the terrestrial pyramid ascends from its terrestrial base to its cone...
