### SECTION I. PORTION II. PART II.

...by [distillation] it becomes so subtle that it is sublimated to the head of the whole **human Alembic** <note>original: "Alembici humani." An alembic is a chemical vessel used for distillation; here, the author views the body as a laboratory where fluids are heated and refined.</note> in the manner of a smoke or vapor that is excessively hot and light, which is carried upward into the middle region of the air. And thus, when that vapor reaches the brain, it is condensed by the coldness of that place into a watery substance, generating **catarrh** <note>original: "catharrum," excessive discharge or mucus.</note> or distillation or rheum, which descends through the nostrils, eyes, and mouth, and sometimes even into the lungs. Indeed, it even returns to the "womb of its generation" <note>Meaning the place where it first arose, or is absorbed back into the source.</note> and is either transformed back into blood or converted into a morbid condition. Thus we see springs and streams of fresh water descend from the mountain summit into the valleys; by their flooding, meadows are sometimes rendered more fertile, and at other times they are converted into a marshy and putrid state. In exactly the same way, the **earth of the Microcosm** <note>The solid parts and organs of the human body.</note> is sometimes nourished by its moderate descent, provided that this flow is according to nature; at other times it is harmed, if the flow is excessive, constant, and contrary to the laws of nature. For then the liver is usually cooled too much and weakened, from which three types of **dropsy** <term>Dropsy: (Latin: hydropsis) A historical term for edema, the painful swelling of tissues due to excess fluid.</term> follow. Or, if it takes its course into the region of the lungs, it typically generates **Asthma**, **Phthisis** <note>original: "Phthisin," a term for pulmonary consumption or tuberculosis.</note>, **Orthopnea** <note>Difficulty breathing unless standing or sitting upright.</note>, **Pneumonia**, and other such diseases. Finally, if it exits through the sutures or other invisible pathways of the skull, whether through the mediation of the veins or outside of them, and passes through the muscles, it is observed to produce quinsy, pleurisy, gout, and various kinds of abscesses, depending on whether the nature of the "meteor" <note>Meteor: In this context, any fluid or vaporous phenomenon within the body, paralleling weather in the atmosphere.</note> is greater in moisture or heat.

But truly, that **salty humor** <note>original: "falsus ille humor," referring to urine.</note>, as it is usually heavier than the others, is observed to occupy the deeper seat of the microcosmic earth, namely the **bladder**. We see this also in the Macrocosm: the lower visible part of the sphere of moisture tends to possess the depths of the sea and penetrate almost to the center of the earth itself, so that it exists as the lowest part and, as it were, the foundation of the entire sphere of moisture—excepting only that dense and muddy humor which participates in the loamy substance of the earth itself, being a sort of mixture of dark earth with both fresh and salt water (of which we spoke in the fifth chapter). 

And, just as it is certain that the immense force of the sea’s action, combined with the heat of the sun and stars, extracts its subtle part from the entire sea so that the air may be filled by its change to sustain springs, fresh waters, and all creatures (and from this it happens that this huge mass of water is rendered salty and, as it were, scorched, just as chemists have observed that "scorched water" <note>Distilled or highly processed liquids.</note> is rendered thicker and denser, and have similarly discovered that scorched earth is most ready to yield its salt or internal nature to water through boiling); so also the **chylous substance** <note>Chyle: The milky fluid of food being digested.</note>, being too watery and void of vegetative form, is drawn into the veins through the **sieve of the liver**. By its agitation in the stream of the veins and the heat of the liver and blood, it is "scorched" and rendered salty, or it draws saltiness to itself from the more earthy mass of the blood. Then, filtered through the "sieves of the kidneys" and separated from the blood, it passes into its own sea, or the bladder.

As for the invisible part of the human sphere of moisture, or the air, it should be known that just as in the Macrocosm certain air tends more toward moisture (that which is near the water, whose moist nature is the nature of every living compound), so too that air which is nearer to fire or earth necessarily exists as more dry in its nature. This is due to the strong nature it receives from its extremes, in which there is no portion of moisture; consequently, dryness abounds there, being nothing other than the absence of moisture. Moisture, however, is nothing but that medium which consists between two extremes, namely earth and fire. Hence it happens that the air, or the substance of the invisible sphere of moisture, is drier where it moves around the extremes, due to participating in their natures; but other air is most moist where it dwells around the center of that sphere. 

Therefore, dry air of any kind, insofar as it is not fit to be condensed into a moist and watery meteor, always remains invisible and is called an **exhalation**; but that which is moist can be condensed by motion and cold into a visible thing, and this species is properly called **vapor**, being hot and moist (of which we have spoken more broadly before). That exhalation, which is properly hot and dry air, is also—improperly and by accident—called cold and dry air. We have called this species of exhalation "cold and dry air" improperly, first because air naturally participates in heat, and second because such an aerial exhalation can never be moved without internal heat naturally impelling that earthy smoke. This species of exhalation is properly involved in that **melancholic complexion** which arises from a humor naturally communicating with the earth. This natural melancholy exists for the most part, although sometimes such a disposition is observed to affect people preternaturally—especially those naturally weak or lacking natural heat. These are led into such a state or habit of body either by their diet or by the cares and disturbances of the mind, as I myself have observed in my practice among many men and women, as I intend to show more broadly below. From this it happens that it sometimes affects **Hypochondriacs** <note>Historically, "hypochondria" referred to physical ailments of the upper abdomen (the hypochondrium) believed to cause melancholy.</note> with either a stiffness of the whole body, or numbness of particular limbs, or coldness of the stomach, and other such symptoms. 

The other species of exhalation excites a **wind** <note>original: "flatum," gas or internal wind.</note> of a condition opposite to that cold one; for it participates in the hot and dry element of fire, and is as if of the nature of the supreme region of the air, which is never reduced to a cloud by condensation. This species, therefore, not only attacks the diaphragm with a hostile impulse, but also, because of its lightness, is elevated to the brain, harming the fantasy and [turning] the actions of reason into a deceptive sense...

# ON THE SECONDARY PRINCIPLES OF THE MICROCOSM

...perverting [everything], affecting the viscera and the entire **hypochondria** <term>Hypochondria: In early medicine, this refers to the upper part of the abdomen, specifically the regions under the ribs, thought to be the source of various "vapors."</term> with burning heat by turns, suppressing the action of breathing, and bringing with it many such grave symptoms, which are well observed by Doctors and will be continually felt by wretched patients, not without great dread.

And both these types of exhalations are called **flatulence and wind** <note>original: "flatus & ventus."</note>; which also concur in their motion toward one another and produce a **third meteor** <note>In this context, a "meteor" refers to any atmospheric or bodily phenomenon caused by vapors, such as clouds, rain, or in this case, internal fluids.</note>, namely generating a dense and thick cloud in the brain as if in the middle region of the air, not otherwise than the air in the **Great World** <note>The Macrocosm or Universe.</note> is accustomed to be condensed into a cloud by the mutual blowing of the North and South winds. Thus also, by the blowing of the hot exhalation from the liver, and likewise the cold exhalation springing from the spleen, the air is carried in the cavity of the stomach into the region of the brain; or both these winds meeting there are condensed into a dense cloud, and afterwards into raw and viscous water, sometimes generating **coryza** <term>Coryza: A head cold or runny nose.</term> and sometimes a **hawking up of phlegm** <note>original: "scereatum."</note>, which happens mostly to **Hypochondriacs** <note>Those suffering from "hypochondriacal" disorders, then believed to be caused by vapors from the upper abdomen.</note> for this same reason: Concerning these meteors of the first degree, we shall make broader mention below in their proper place. Regarding the spiritual water of the middle heaven of man, we say that its entire purpose, because of the ethereal spirit reigning in it, is toward life and the conservation of the composite [being] in a healthy and sound condition; whence all its instruments or organs lead only to life, and in no way to death or the alterations of corruption: For the lungs are ordained for the attraction of air, so that from that attracted air the substance of the invisible ethereal heaven may be extracted for the continuation of life, and retained for the sustenance of life; while the superfluous and useless is expelled. So also the heart is that excellent laboratory in which the subtle is separated from the thick, and it is like a kitchen in which the nourishment of life is prepared and cooked. Similarly, in the thinnest and most excellent spirit of the **principle of Mem** <note>original: "principij Mem." In Fludd's philosophy, the Hebrew letter Mem (מ) often represents the "watery" or maternal principle of the middle world.</note>, the origin of diseases or alterations is not found in itself; for it is of the nature of the **Empyrean heaven** <term>Empyrean: The highest, most celestial part of the heavens, associated with pure light and fire.</term>, in which action is so adapted to passion that both embrace each other with reciprocal love and are never infected by strife or contrariety. However, the reason why diseases arise in the chest and the region of the brain itself is not in the impediments of the spirit of that place, but in the most wicked usurpation and invasion of the humors or exhalations procreated in the lowest region into those regions of the **lesser world** <note>The Microcosm, or the human body.</note>, insofar as they are clothed in flesh; through whose porous substance those vapors are accustomed to ascend secretly and stealthily into the middle and supreme region, against the laws and order of nature. There they mostly produce hostile effects, and infect the spirit itself—or rather the place and habitation of the spirits—with disturbances and a poisonous nature. Thus indeed **Lucifer** and **Strife** <note>original: "Litigium."</note>, having been cast down, nevertheless attempted to strive upward to bring war against God himself and his angels, and to disturb the entire celestial spirit! Yet, he could have no power over the celestial spirits; and therefore, having been thrust down, he exercised his malice against the earthly mass, since he was the **Prince of Darkness**.

In clearly the same way, the wicked **meteors** <note>Vapors or fluids within the body.</note>, having arisen in the lowest kingdom of the Microcosm, struggle against the vital and rational spirit, and since they cannot bring the violence of death upon them, they do not cease to infest their tabernacle or organs—as if generated from the earth and harmful, corruptible humors—either with sickness or death. But truly the vital spirit, insofar as it is the heart of the human soul itself, and similarly the rational spirit as its head, do not fear the assaults of the lower things; nor indeed can they truly and in themselves either fall ill or die; since death and diseases are passions to which the body is subject along with its elements from which it is composed. Indeed, if these elements are clear—namely, the sphere of equality—they are the basis of the soul. And yet this basis is subject to every alteration, because it is the middle consistency, or rather the entire existence of the lower heaven of man, which is subject to every alteration, and becomes, through the subtlety of the evil spirits reigning in it, the cause of all evils that are accustomed to happen to the human body.

For indeed, since—as the Holy Scriptures witness—every plague of the earth is attributed to an avenging spirit, and a **Demon** of wicked disposition presides over every wind, and consequently **Satan** is the prince of this world by divine constitution—namely, the lower and elemental world—it is certainly no wonder that humors of this kind in the lower kingdom of the Microcosm (which correspond to all those in the Macrocosm) are sometimes fierce and cruel toward the dark composition of man through the instigation of Demons. For by their fury and madness, we see in the Macrocosm itself the whole machine of the lower region and the entire spirit constituting the elements vibrate and tremble; the earth moves and vomits **typhonic fires** <note>Volcanic or subterranean fires, named after the monster Typhon.</note> from its bosom, the seas swell up and with open mouth swallow and as it were absorb not only ships but even entire islands, the air roars with the violence of the winds and wages war against the trees and structures of the earth, raises the waves of the seas on high, and groans with a tremendous voice, the fire of lightning with violence—not without amazement and a horrendous crash—breaks through and tears apart the thick clouds, scorches portions of the earth, and kills some creatures by crushing them, **Comets** of every species infect the air of both the Macrocosm and Microcosm and bring slaughter and famine to the world, and likewise excite rains and floods both to the earth itself and its creatures, and induce infinite other such calamities, all of which it would be tedious to recount in this place. What doubt is there, then, but that Demons of this kind, according to their natures, enter into the humors and meteors [contrary] to nature...

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *Concerning the third Microcosmic Element, which is א Aleph;*

->denoting the divine light.<-

Aleph א, which is the third principle of man, is that character which denotes in the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</term> both the potential and actual principle of all things. For the "obscure Aleph" <note>original: "א Aleph obscurum"</note> denotes that God is the potential and material principle of the hidden waters; and again, the "lucid Aleph" <note>original: "א Aleph lucidum"</note> argues that God is the active and formal origin of souls: whose essence the waters are in potentiality, as they are in actuality. And this principle in man was that breath of life which the Creator of heaven and earth breathed into the face of the external man, by which he was led from the potentiality of a living and rational animal into actuality.

From which it is clear that the "breather" and the "breath" are like a father and a son proceeding from the father. For, just as the Son is the offspring immediately proceeding from the Father, so also that breathing was the fiery spirit of life going out from the Breather, or the first and immediate emanation gushing from the lucid source. Consequently, this breath of life is truly God, Mind, Word, Messiah, and the power of the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH).</term> in the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "Little World," meaning man as a reflection of the universe.</term>, sounding within him no differently than the "LET IT BE" <note>original: "FIAT"</note> in the Macrocosm, when the Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters, infusing them with the fiery force of life. Therefore, the lucid Aleph is the universal act of both the Macro- and Microcosm, bestowing and infusing all power into both. Because of its clarity, it is called the soul, and by the sacred writers, the candle of the living God—the soul, I say, of the Macrocosm and the lamp of Jehovah. Its burning wicks or matches are the celestial stars; the oil refreshing the flame is the rectified spirit of the ethereal heaven, which behaves like the quintessence <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence" or purest, most concentrated form of a substance.</term> of wine; its denser or more watery part is the sublunary spirit, compared to the phlegm of wine or weak "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitae," often referring to distilled alcohol or a vital medicinal spirit.</note>. The source of this is the earth itself, which is nothing other than the accumulation of dense or opaque spirits in the center of the universal machine, and it remains as the mother or universal matrix of the spirit, from which the universal spirit first arose.

In the Microcosm also, the soul is the lamp of Jehovah, whose wicks are the eyes and the interior senses dwelling in the ventricle of the brain; and at the same time the heart itself, whose natural fuel or nourishment are the spirits, both animal and natural. The denser and more visible part of these is that natural spirit holding dominion in the lowest region. The base and the "dead head" <term>Caput mortuum: A term from alchemy meaning the worthless residue or "dead head" left after a process; here, the material body.</term>, as it were, or the more unworthy part of man, is his earth, which covers all things. And the sacred writings also seem to affirm this, as we find in Proverbs 20:27, in express words, that the soul of man is the lamp of Jehovah, with which he searches all the interior and secret parts of man; or, as Jerome interprets it: *The lamp of the Lord is the breath of man, which searches all the secrets of the belly.* And in Psalm 18:29, we have these words: *For you light my candle; Jehovah my God, you make my darkness shine.* Similarly, the Prophet, understanding this candle, speaks in Psalm 84:12 in these words: *Jehovah God is a Sun, giving grace and glory;* that is, God is the light and the lamp, and the Sun of my life. Wherefore in Proverbs 13:9 it is said: *the light of the righteous shall be bright, but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out.* Hence also it is said in Psalm 27:1: *The light is the salvation of the righteous, and the strength of my life;* and in Psalm 18:29: *If you light my lamp, Jehovah my God, you make my darkness shine.* Also in Psalm 36:10 David says: *In the light of Jehovah we shall see light.*

By which it is certainly argued that the light of Jehovah, or his most holy emanation, is the lamp of life and of the divine mind. When God takes away this emanation, or hides his face, the spirit will first be disturbed and immediately expire, according to that in Psalm 104:24: *When God gives to them, the creatures gather; when he opens his hand, they are filled with good; when he hides his face, they are troubled; when he takes back their spirit, they expire.* And to this purpose the words of the Prophet in Psalm 30:6 sound well: *Life is in the favor of Jehovah;* and in Psalm 90:14, it is said that the prolongation of life is the kindness of God. From these things, therefore, we see that the life and soul of the Microcosm—and consequently also of the Macrocosm, as man was formed after its image and from its substance—is the lamp of Jehovah. The Evangelist John in Chapter 1 also seems to acknowledge this when he says that the life and light of man is in the Word. Therefore, the lucid Aleph is the lamp of the soul of the world, both greater and lesser. By its splendor, the entire spirit of the internal man is illuminated, no differently than a clear candle in the middle of a very dark house, or the rays of lightning in the most shadow-filled night. When this splendor and emanation recedes, it is necessary that the final day of both the Macrocosm and Microcosm should end, and the period of that final "PERISH" <note>original: "PEREAT"</note> be reached. Indeed, by the lessening of that divine splendor, man and every other creature languish and become most wretched, according to Psalm 9:11: *The span of life is wretched without the kindness of God.*

### CONCERNING THE SECONDARY PRINCIPLES OF THE MICROCOSM.

From this, it happens that—due both to the rebellion and resistance of the substance of the lower spirit, and to the vast distance of God's seat or throne from the location of the lowest region of the Spirit (since God's kindness is not as frequent there as it is in the higher spirits, which are more obedient to the actions of divine emanation)—many changes arise in the lower region of the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "Little World," or the human being viewed as a reflection of the entire universe.</term> tending toward corruption. This occurs unless the Lord God <note>original: "Deus Iehova"</note> favors man by His pure grace, in whom that dense and thick spiritual substance resides. Hence David said in *Psalm* 31:17: *Let your face shine upon your servant; save me in your kindness.* <note>original: "Luceat facies tua super servum tuum; serva me benignitate tua."</note> This can indeed be understood as referring to both internal and external adversities. Hence elsewhere, namely in *Psalm* 106:4: *God pursues His people with benevolence and with His salvation.* And in *Psalm* 106:5: *He whom God has visited with His salvation shall enjoy the good and the happiness of His chosen ones, so that they may rejoice with gladness.* This is certainly to be understood regarding the soul and the body: for life and its well-being exist by the benevolence of Jehovah (*Psalm* 30:6), with whom—as held in *Psalm* 36:8–9—is the fountain of life, and He indeed gives the children of men to drink from the torrent of His delights. Hence in *Psalm* 41:3, He is called the restorer of life; and in *Psalm* 87:7, the Psalmist says: *All the fountains of my life come from God;* and in *Psalm* 80:19, he says: *Keep us in life so that we may call upon your name.* Moreover, God is accustomed to grant this gift to the righteous, so that He may preserve their Spirit—which exists under the power of malignant and destroying spirits due to the sin of Adam—from the violent power of the avenger and imbue it with long life: <insert>As</insert> we read in *Psalm* 91:16: *With length of days I will satisfy him; finally, I will cause him to enjoy my salvation.* Indeed, He even exercises His mercy toward the unjust and grants length of days, preserving their more passive spirit from the rage of the destroyer through the presence of His rays, which are truly the flight of the Demon, according to that saying of Solomon in *Wisdom* 11:21: *Indeed, they could have fallen at a single breath, pursued by justice and scattered by the Spirit of your power: But you have disposed all things by measure, number, and weight; for that which you are greatly able to do is always present with you, etc. But you have mercy on all because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of men so that they might repent, etc. You spare all things, therefore, because they are yours, O Lord, lover of souls.*

By these words, the Wise Man certainly seems to indicate most excellently that the Lord can do all things by the virtue of His power; but that out of His kindness, tempering His power with mercy, He spares sinners and is accustomed to exercise the benevolence of life even toward them. And certainly, although one might very rightly object that only a single act is at work throughout the universe—namely, that act proceeding from the power of the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: The sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH), representing the ultimate source of all power.</term>—and consequently that the cause of a creature's destruction is the same as the cause of its conservation, we willingly grant this objection. However, we nevertheless say in the meantime that the actions of divine light are always good and healthy; but the subject receiving them poorly and perversely is accustomed to turn them into destruction. For example, we see that fire and its flame are always permanent while it burns, and thus the same in its faculty; and, if its acts are well-received by a subject, it acts benevolently, gently reviving and warming frozen and chilled limbs with a kind heat, or drying damp things without any destruction of the subject. And yet, if a body affected by cold and frost approaches the fire too closely, the fire burns and destroys it; and similarly, it also consumes damp cloth or wood, reducing them to ashes by burning, while meanwhile the act and virtue of the fire is always the same. So too is there a poor reception of the influences of Saturn and Mars, which converts their actions into the worst effects, though the essence of the influence is not the cause, which is always good. For example: if the influence of Saturn falls overwhelmingly upon a subject that is naturally "golden" <note>likely referring to a "solar" or sanguine temperament</note>, it is accustomed to disturb it by extinguishing its warm nature and congealing its moist nature; and conversely, the virtue of Mars, flowing into a cold and watery subject, burns the cold nature and renders it false, absorbing the moisture. Yet meanwhile, both Saturn and Mars act benevolently toward creatures who receive their influx benevolently. So we see the Sun is troublesome to a weak eye, but gracious to a strong one. And the same Sun warms very stiff limbs in winter time, but in the extreme, it burns, so that by the natural inclination of animals, shade is sought; yet nevertheless, the virtue of the Sun is always the same, never failing to act according to its benevolent nature.

We conclude, therefore, that the first act—by which force and virtue are granted and conferred upon Saturn and Mars as well as the Sun and every other creature—is always one and the same. But this is the indication of God's infinite goodness above all His other creatures: that He Himself, understanding that the presence of His face would painfully affect all creatures and even melt the mountains themselves, mercifully covered it with the veil of His goodness and appeared to creatures only through the effect—namely, the garment of light through which His rays penetrated. Indeed, He even mercifully spared His creatures who were poorly disposed to receive His acts, so that He might also preside over them without the destruction of the individual. Therefore, He relaxed His power for their sake and benefit, and reflected and turned back a portion of His strength into Himself. This is indeed clearly and abundantly argued by these words of the Wise Man in *Wisdom* 16:22: *Snow and ice sustained the force of fire and did not melt, so that they might know that the burning fire, flashing in the hail and rain, was destroying the fruits of the enemies; but this again happened so that the righteous might be nourished, for the fire even forgot its own virtue: For the creature, serving its Maker, burns fiercely for the torment of the unjust, and becomes lighter for doing good for those who trust in you: Because of this, all things, being transformed, served your all-nourishing grace according to the will of those whom you desired; so that your children, whom you loved, O Lord, might know that it is not the fruits of birth that feed men, but your word preserves those who have believed in you: For that which could not be destroyed by fire, immediately melted away by a tiny ray of the sun, etc.*

### SECTION I. PORTION II. PART II.

From this, God’s mercy is made clear; He is able, and often accustomed, to blunt and dull the powers of His avengers, or to sharpen them according to His will, so that objects or subjects poorly disposed to receive His actions are not harmed. In truth, God’s actions cannot cause harm unless the recipient <note>The "subject" or "passive" element receiving the action.</note> is ill-disposed to receive them. Hence, when Jehovah, the God of Hosts, wished to manifest His power and strength against the Egyptians and obtain a trophy of victory against Pharaoh, He is said *to have hardened his heart*, so that through the rebellion and perversity of that spirit's resistance, the divine power—which nothing can withstand—might have a stronger effect upon him. Thus, by his own obstinacy, not only Pharaoh himself but the entire people of the Egyptian kingdom fell into ruin.

This, then, is the nature of that most holy divine emanation, called the **Luminous Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often used in mystical texts to represent the primal divine will or light.</note>, which is known to act everywhere according to the capacity of the receiving spirit. For toward those who receive it with goodwill, it acts with a benevolent natural property, and yet even to those who receive it poorly, it is present with its grace and mercy. 

Hence, in the highest heaven <term>Empyrean spirit: The highest, most "fiery" or spiritual level of the universe, closest to the divine.</term>, it is called **Jah** <note>Hebrew: יה</note>, which is a name of kindness; for there it acts benevolently because of the excellent, obedient, and tender disposition of the Spirit that receives its luminous acts. 

In the middle region, or the **Etheric Spirit**, it is called **Jeho** <note>Hebrew: יהו</note>, which denotes a seal, because there is a greater resistance of the spirit there than in the highest heaven. Thus, impressions are made through **Emeth** <note>Hebrew for "Truth."</note> into the etheric spirit, like a seal into wax. For according to the Cabalists, *Emeth* (that is, Truth) is the seal of God, by which all characters, forms, and proportions of life in any creature are imprinted. This Spirit is like a second garment which the emanation from **Jod** <note>The letter Yod (י), the first letter of the Name of God, representing the initial point of creation.</note> puts on; it is very obedient to its creator, yet it carries a certain "malice" toward lower creatures insofar as it is the dwelling place of the fates, which deal both well and ill with lower beings. 

In the lowest heaven, or the lowest spirit of both worlds, it is called **Jehovah** <note>Hebrew: יהוה; the full Tetragrammaton.</note>. Here, because of the resistance and perverse obstinacy of the subject—namely the elements and the things made from them—Jehovah is said to act in His severity and wrath. Hence, that awesome name is said, in the dimensions of the Sephiroth <term>Sephiroth: The ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</term>, to indicate both severity and punishment as well as clemency and mercy. 

For this reason, it is said in *Psalm 6:2* and *38:2* that *the wrath of Jehovah is His heat*. 
And *Psalm 11:6*: *He shall rain burning coals upon the wicked.* 
*Psalm 18:8*: *By the kindled wrath of Jehovah the earth is shaken and moved, and the foundations of the mountains are troubled.* 
*Psalm 21:10* and *83:15*: *The wrath of Jehovah is like a consuming fire.* 
*Psalm 78:21*: *The fire of Jehovah was kindled against Jacob, and His wrath burned against Israel.* 
*Psalm 78:63*: *God consumes the impious with fire.* 
*Numbers 16:35*: *The fire of Jehovah consumed those 250 men, etc.* 
*Deuteronomy 32:22*: *A fire is kindled by my wrath, which shall burn even to the lowest grave, and shall consume the earth and its increase, and set fire to the foundations of the mountains, etc.*

All of these passages prove the wrath and severity of God—not indeed regarding His own nature, but because of the unworthiness of the receiving subject. Because of its rebellion and resistance, God is said to "examine" or "test" it (to use the words of the Holy Bible). This is the reason that this same divine action—the power of the emanation from *Jod*—acts more vehemently the deeper it penetrates downward, due to the compression of its rays in the density of matter. Thus, the fire of lightning burns violently when compressed by a cloud; artificial fire destroys when in dense air; and the fire of Gehenna <note>Hellfire.</note> is said to burn beyond human imagination because of its immense constriction and the resistance of the rebellious and dark spirit. 

For a flame of fire spread out everywhere becomes invisible and imperceptible, and because of its expansion or distribution, its burning is not felt. In the same way, we see a river spread wide flowing gently and smoothly without great violence; but if necessity forces it to pass through the narrow gap between two rocks, it produces the most vehement and rapid effects. 

From this, it is clear that the act of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note> is unique and indivisible, and that its difference lies only in the passive subject upon which that act operates. For all things are said to differ according to the greater or lesser resistance of the suffering spirit and the portion of the act it receives, even though in reality there is only one act extending itself into infinity, and one spirit that suffers. This is demonstrated by the fact that if God were to take away His countenance and turn His face from the spirit of the world, necessity would force all bodies, all waters, and all spirits to return into a single spiritual substance and potential matter alone, for lack of form.

We conclude, therefore, that this one and the same light is called:
*   In the **Empyrean heaven** of both worlds: **Intellectual light** acting upon the rational spirit.
*   In the **Middle heaven**: **Vital light** operating in the etheric spirit or the innate nature of creatures.
*   In the **Elementary spirit**: The **element of fire**, which reverberates through reflections and resistance in the highest region of the sphere of moisture, surrounding the passive elements and the things made from them. 

Because of the resistance of the passive material, this element acts perversely and is mostly occupied with the corruption of all things; whereas, conversely, celestial heat acts toward life and the preservation of health.

## CHAPTER IX.

### Concerning the element of fire, which arises from this principle of the Microcosm, namely, Yellow Bile.

Just as we have asserted regarding the Macrocosm <note>The "Greater World" or the universe at large.</note>, the element of fire is that sphere of the elementary region of the world which surrounds and stands above the sphere of moisture. We have nevertheless stated that this is nothing other than an excessive ignition of part of the sphere of moisture, caused by the reverberation and reflection of super-celestial rays. In the same way, within the Microcosm <note>The "Lesser World," meaning the human body.</note>, we find a fiery nature springing upward from the chylous substance <note>The milky fluid derived from food during digestion.</note>, lurking within the lighter fluid of the sphere of moisture, and converting all its liquid into a fiery color and nature. This region is situated in the concavity of the liver above the convexity of the stomach—where watery "meteors" <note>In this context, "meteors" refers to bodily vapors or fluids that behave like atmospheric phenomena.</note> are generated—that is to say, in the highest region of the "air" within the body. 

And although the substance of this element is visible and behaves contrary to the nature of the element of fire—insofar as it is moist and fluid, while the true disposition of fire is hot and dry—it must be understood clearly that the reason for this element's visibility in man is that it is coarser and more mixed in the Microcosm than in the Macrocosm. This is because the former is composed of the elements of the latter, and consequently possesses elements that are coarser and more visible. 

Furthermore, since the original Being of man is that general moisture which participates in an invisible way in every species of worldly moisture, it is necessary that all his elements consist of a moist substance. Consequently, a certain moist substance serves as a vehicle and receptacle for the tincture <note>A subtle quality or essence that "stains" or characterizes a substance.</note> and quality of the element of fire. Within this resides a quality or tincture that is bitter, sharp, stinging, acute, and, by its primary constitution, hot and dry according to the nature of fire, in which it participates. Thus, in jaundice <note>original: icteritia</note>, we discern in the skin not a humor, but a dry tincture; nor is it the humor itself (which is the carrier and vector of the fiery bile) that is observed to excite fevers, but rather the sharpness of its acrimony and its fiery heat. 

Therefore, this sharp, subtle, and light tincture exists within that thin substance of "congealed air" in no other way than the fire of the Macrocosm exists in its own airy vehicle. Yet here it is rendered visible in man because he is a "spermatic" humor <note>Meaning he grows from a fluid seed or essence.</note> from which man is born, and in whose portion this fiery power appears after the growth of the newborn. Without this, that power could not be brought into the light or rendered visible, any more than the light of the greater world is usually seen without a mediating subject or visible colored object fit to receive its rays visibly. For it is the colored thing that is seen, and by the vision of the colored thing—that is, by happenstance—light appears to the eye. 

However, the necessity of its use demanded that the power of this element be found in a slippery fluid within man. Its chief utility in the body is to migrate in a fluid manner through its own proper passage into the viscera or intestines, not only to make the excrement contained within them slippery, but also to stimulate the "expulsive faculty" by its stinging and sharp capability. 

Therefore, although this humor carrying the fiery power is in itself a waste product, as long as it is retained in its own proper vessel, it serves the benefit of health. However, when it exceeds its limits or the margins of its proper receptacle—that is, the gallbladder—it acts upon the body not toward health or according to nature, but rather against the laws of nature and violently. It is observed to produce diseases, such as jaundice, Erysipelas <note>A skin infection often called "St. Anthony's Fire" due to its burning redness.</note>, certain fevers, and especially that which is called the Icteroid fever <note>A fever associated with jaundice.</note>, along with many others. Indeed, that pronouncement of both Hippocrates and Galen <note>The two primary authorities of ancient Greek medicine.</note> is most true: it asserts that any humor, however natural, usually produces a disease-causing accident—that is, something contrary to nature—when it is outside its own proper place. 

It also happens sometimes, and indeed quite often, that the spirit of the bile, donning the invisible wings of the element of fire and carried by a poisonous and hidden spirit, leaves the colored humor behind and migrates through the veins and arteries. It infects the entire structure, including the heart itself, with an unnatural hot imbalance <note>original: intemperie</note>, delighting in polluting the vital spirits with its poisonous breath, and thus attacks both the airy and ethereal spirits with pestilential fire. 

Sometimes, under such an invisible form, it joins itself to a putrid humor and is known to excite a continuous fever <note>original: Synochum</note> and even a burning fever <note>original: cauſonidem</note>; but for the most part, it sheds its poisonous quality. Likewise, it induces tertian fevers <note>Fevers that spike every third day, often associated with malaria in the period.</note>, both the intermittent kind and those stirred up in the spirits, as well as infinite other "meteors" of its own or another kind, according to the nature and constitution of the other humor or element with which it joins. But we have decided to treat these matters more carefully in what follows. 

From these things, one can see that this element usually appears either in the visible humor destined for it by nature, or in an invisible spirit, in which it passes preternaturally—flying with wings of destruction and imbalance outside its natural seat—either into only one part of the body, harming its natural action, or into several members at once, or even invading the entire body at once with its fiery imbalance. 

And certainly, it is right that if this element of the human body should cross its limits, casting off its reins and holding dominion over the body, one should watch with great anxiety and fear. For it excels all other elements in danger and speed of action because, as Artephius <note>A medieval author of alchemical and medical texts, often cited as a legendary long-lived philosopher.</note> reports—and rightly so—the Devil himself very frequently joins himself with this kind of humor or element, and often excites and helps it toward the destruction of the composite whole <note>The "composite" is the human being, the union of body and soul.</note>. His words are as follows: "There are certain infirmities with which [the Devil] joins him—"

the Devil acts, as the humor emerges from its balanced state and disturbs health itself; and this happens especially in diseases arising from <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and aggression.</note>, etc. This also undoubtedly happens in melancholic diseases and malignant fevers, because that hot nature, joining itself with the fiery nature of the <term>Cacodæmon</term> <note>An evil spirit or demon.</note>, and penetrating into the smoke, breath, or wind <note>The "pneuma" or vital vapors of the body.</note>, moves it violently. Carried within that vapor, it not only invades the "camps" of the vital spirits and beats upon the chambers of the heart in a formidable manner—from which follow <term>Syncope</term> <note>Fainting or loss of consciousness.</note>, swooning, and trembling or palpitation of the heart—but it also rises up with a proud and ambitious force against the fortifications of the animal spirits. It does not cease to invade the palace of the Phantasy, and indeed even the divine temple of Reason itself. From this, in both fevers and Melancholy, there follow <term>Phrenitides</term> <note>Delirium or brain inflammation.</note>, Deliriums, Manias, <term>Lycanthropies</term> <note>A form of madness where the patient believes they are a wolf.</note>, and other similar species of alienation, such as Despair, the appearance of empty visions, etc.; likewise a love of solitude, cares and anxieties, fears and suspicions without cause, sighing, and infinite other symptoms.

We conclude, therefore, that just as this humor, along with its wicked "soul" <note>Here "soul" refers to the active, spiritual agent within the physical fluid.</note>, brings very little utility to the body, so indeed it provides a huge proof of harm and evil. For this reason, there is need for the industry of the best Physician, and the medicines of a scientific Artist, by which that humor, with its soul or agent, may be confined to its own proper seat as if by chains or secure bonds. For when it is outside its place—whether in its own physical substance or only by the spirit and breath of its formal soul—it not only renders other humors (which are otherwise mild enough in their natures as they wander through the body) ferocious and makes them the authors of infirmities, but it even stands among them like a leader of all evil, giving movement to its power for doing harm. It is no different than how fire gives flame and life to a lamp or to turpentine, which before was quiet and innocent, possessing only the potential for burning or causing harm. And truly, if we examine the nature of the element of fire in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The Universe or "Great World."</note> well, we will eventually perceive that it is the author and origin of every movement toward corruption and alteration in this lower world; just as, conversely, solar or celestial fire is the evident cause of generation, health, and conservation, and is as it were the father of the life of inferior creatures, as will appear more clearly in the experiment described in the following chapter.

### CHAPTER X.

->*The key to our entire Philosophy, both Macro- and Microcosmic,*<-
->*or a most clear demonstration.*<-

Since a certain secret Treatise of ours, which we are to publish, relates primarily to the purpose of our intention and to the clear explanation of this doctrine—a Treatise to which we have given the title *The Key of Philosophy* or *An Ocular Mirror of Certain Physical Mysteries*—we shall therefore make a brief and summarized account of that secret in this chapter. By this, your wits may be sharpened and prepared to more rightly and easily understand this work of ours, both Macrocosmic and Microcosmic. I saw, therefore, a principal creature chosen from the vegetable kingdom, which is considered thoroughly necessary for human nourishment, first exposed to natural putrefaction, and then by the <term>Vulcanian art</term> <note>Alchemy or the use of fire in chemistry.</note> excited or elevated upward into a huge cloud. When this cloud, by the virtue of cold, was reduced into golden water, I discovered in the very center of that water a very black mass, not unlike the limbs of the dark <term>Chaos</term> <note>The formless state of matter before creation.</note> itself, being viscous. Thus it is said by <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>: <note>original: "cum omnia in mundi creatione perturbata essent, umbra horrenda obliqua revolutione fuerit subterlapsa in humidam naturam"</note> "When all things were disturbed in the creation of the world, a horrendous shadow by an oblique revolution slipped down into the moist nature." And Moses says: "The Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters." Augustine, however, says that "the Spirit of the Lord, which was carried over the waters, imparted to them a fiery vigor." For thus the water was tinted, which in this experiment of ours covered the dark mass. And, as Chaos in the creation of the world was a mass containing within itself the mysteries of the third and fourth days of creation, which the watery matter of both heavens (namely the first and second day's work) covered; so also in our practice, the blackest mass, overwhelmed by the illuminated waters, contained within itself the four elements of the lowest heaven (the works of the third day) and the <term>quintessence</term> and solar matter (the work of the fourth day). These things, after the completion of the second day's work, were deformed and existed only in potentiality toward being anything in act. Therefore, we extracted the four elements from our obscure Chaos in that manner expressed in the *History of the Macrocosm, Book 1, Chapter 10*. For water first arose, then the substance of air, which was so familiar both to the water and to the fire that it united itself naturally to both as a medium, participating in both extremes. Furthermore, I noticed that that golden liquid was a certain middle substance between water and fire; for it is a species of water, light and vegetable, which is like a volatile salt taking on the form of crystalline water, so familiar to the solar rays,

In that experiment, I observed two things worthy of note: namely, the reason for growth in plants, and indeed in animals themselves. This growth occurs because of the abundance of the vivifying soul or ethereal light, whose source is the **solar tabernacle** <note>original: "tabernaculum solare"; a Hermetic term for the sun as the dwelling place of divine light.</note>. This <term>latex</term> <note>A liquid or fluid substance; here referring to a specific alchemical preparation.</note> or liquor usually attracts that light to itself by a certain magnetic and occult power, after it has been liberated from its "seminal prison" through the natural rot (putrefaction) that takes place in the earth. I shall explain this more fully in the flowing style of the aforementioned Treatise, as I have found it to be true in a most noble practice.

The second observation is that this fluid substance alone, separated from water by the "Alchemy of Nature" in the liver and veins, is what creates blood in the human body. Indeed, after separation, it is so well-suited and inclined that, by the exertion of natural heat, it is transmuted into a red liquor. This is also because it is the cause of growth, nutrition, and increase, as we declared in the preceding demonstration. However, the water which—during the "second digestion" by the power of the liver and the glands that strain and separate the blood—is divided from this vegetative and bloody portion in the kidneys, becomes the matter for both urine and sometimes sweat. These are considered superfluous things and are expelled through the urinary or sweat-producing tracts because of their uselessness.

We found the third element, namely the fiery one, to be foul-smelling, putrid, and stinking most terribly. Therefore, I observed that this portion of "chaos" was the formal cause of corruption and rot in every body beneath the moon. Thus, all things close to rot and corruption are affected by a notable stench because of the dominance of this element within them. Its color is like that of the most intense bile or <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors, associated with fire and heat.</note>, and it carries with it a sharp bitterness and heat. So great is the friendship between this element (the fiery fluid of this plant) and the darkness, that although I had, by the art and method of common chemists, rendered this same element into a transparent and beautiful ruby specimen, within the space of a few days it gradually attracted to itself a dark and opaque "rust of shadows." It did this so thoroughly that all its clarity was as if snatched away, and it became plainly dark. 

From this, I gathered that the **Devil** (whose hidden nature is a "dark fire") most easily joins himself to this element when it leaves its natural seat—following the opinions of **Artephius** <note>A 12th-century alchemist often cited in Hermetic literature.</note>, and those of **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellos, a Byzantine philosopher known for his work on demonology.</note> and others which I shall mention later. Therefore, I concluded with a steady mind that this fiery humor is the chief cause of diseases and infirmities, since it is found by its very nature to be the origin of corruption and unnatural changes. Furthermore, because of the proximity of the **Evil Demon** <note>original: "Cacodæmonis"</note> to its nature, its malice is more to be feared.

Finally, once this fiery substance was extracted from its dark prison, there followed the vital humor of the plant, which I drew out with the greatest caution and patience, and finally cleansed from its filth (without which it cannot be found). I discovered this fluid to be of a marvelous nature and condition, for it was most clear, like a white crystalline spirit equal to solar rays adorned on all sides. For in its composition, I observed three testimonies of an ethereal nature: 

The first is a most clear spirit sprinkled everywhere with rays of light. In this way, we see the Sun decorating the blue substance of the sky with its rays, and yet the substance of the spirit remains visible to the eye. Secondly, the equality of its composition in light and spirit denotes that this humor participates in the "sphere of equality." The last is that it excels all other elements in the goodness and pleasantness of its scent, differing from them entirely; for they, by comparison, smell foul.

Therefore, the first testimony denotes the nature of the "innate heat" and "radical moisture" of life itself, both in the vegetable and animal kingdoms. For without doubt, that clear fluid—in which **Cupid** <note>Representing active, solar light.</note> lies with his **Psyche** <note>Representing passive, lunar moisture.</note> (or the "moist Psyche")—is that passive moisture well-disposed to receive the act of life. And that ray or light, delighting itself in that "bath of nature," is the act of life which works upon its passive partner to impart the faculty of life to creatures. I have also observed this through a notable experiment, the conclusion of which I shall explain at length in the Treatise cited above. 

The effect of the experiment was this: by placing a portion of this substance into common water and mixing it, I saw within a few days that innumerable worms of a marvelous nature were procreated. By this very thing, I was finally made certain that this <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; the purest element or "ether" that transcends the four terrestrial elements.</note> is the vital cause in both animals and plants. I saw that worms and other animals produced from rot take their origin of living from this kind of heavenly humor when it is loosened and freed from its bonds. Consequently, even the life of man is prolonged and successively continued by this same heavenly nature lurking in the air and continuously drawn in through the lungs. Similarly, this same nature, hidden centrally in food of every kind, contributes to the multiplication and preservation of the vital spirits and arterial blood, just as the "airy" part of the food itself leads to the increase of the venous blood and the strengthening of the natural faculty. 

The second testimony of its heavenly nature is the equality of the proportion of the spiritual moisture with the heat of the light. This is declared by the fact that neither the heat of the light existing in that spirit is enough to cause its continuous liquefaction, nor is the moisture of the spirit so powerful that it can hide the rays of its light. From this, it happens that this humor congeals by itself like crystal, or rather a stone...

...working <note>original: "operantibus"; completing the word from the previous page</note> in such a way that, if it is exposed to the hot sun for a space of only three hours, it attracts the **tincture of its rays** with as much desire as a woman attracts a man. # SECTION I. PORTION II. PART II.

...of a hyacinth-like color <note>original: "Jacinthini"; a deep reddish-orange or purplish-blue color, here likely referring to the gemstone zircon</note>, and it appears in its essence like water or a dry and fixed spirit. Nevertheless, it melts with even the slightest heat, and once melted, it retains an intense yellow color throughout the entire duration of its liquefaction. But indeed, as soon as it cools, it hardens likewise and returns to its original color. From these things, therefore, it is clear enough that this substance is a certain hidden influence from the sphere of equality or the soul through which the sun passes; and consequently, that a spirit of this kind is poured out for the generation and continuation of life from the source of life, which is the solar substance. 

Finally, the ultimate evidence argues that this humor is neither of the earth, nor of water, nor of air, nor even of the element of fire; insofar as it differs from all of these, both in odor and in the state of its substance. From this it is concluded that it is something above the "fourth essence," and hence that which is called the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; in alchemy, the purest, celestial element beyond the four physical elements</note> by the Chemists. 

Finally, the earth—or the darker part, acting like a deformed **dead head** <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>an alchemical term for the useless, inert residue left over after distillation or chemical reaction</note> of the entire mass—lies at the bottom of the vessel or gourd like a "shunner of light" <note>original: "Lucifugi"</note> destitute of all celestial grace. Nor can it be raised from that state by any violence of fire, except for the fact that it retains a certain fixed salt in its center. 

And thus you have all five elements from a single **Chaos**, or a single deformed mass, derived from a certain vegetable matter that preeminently nourishes the human body. But truly, since it is certain that all nourishment is converted into the substance of the one being nourished—as like is nourished by its like—it is probable that every element of the nourishing vegetable matter regards its own similar element in the nourished body. Consequently, the element of one nature corresponds to the nature of the element of the other. 

And because the more airy part of the nourishment is converted into the nature of the body's element of air, it follows that there is a very great relationship between both of these elements; since, according to that old axiom of the Philosophers: *that which makes a thing such, is itself even more so.* 

It follows, therefore, that the earthy element of this vegetable food contributes something to the **melancholic juice**, the water to the **phlegm** and urine, the air to the **blood**, the fire to the increase of **bile**, and the **fifth essence** to the succession of the **vital spirits** and arterial blood. Therefore, the substance of the Heavens in the plant nourishes its like in the animal—namely, the vital parts. Fire, air, water, and earth, however, nourish its body through the mixing of blood with the mass by means of attachment, union, and coagulation. 

In this way, the body is maintained at the same level of growth without diminishing, specifically because of the continuous supply of blood which arises from these elements of nourishment. Indeed, through the natural predominance of these elements in the blood, different **complexions** <note>original: "complexiones"; the specific balance of the four humors that determined a person’s physical and mental temperament</note> are produced. Hence, if bile—due to the liver's tendency to generate this kind of humor—gains dominance in the blood, it makes a man naturally **bilious or choleric**; if phlegm dominates, it makes him **phlegmatic**; and if melancholy dominates, **melancholic**. But if the action of the liver tends toward moderation, it produces a **sanguine** complexion. 

And yet, whatever a man’s complexion may be, vessels are ordained by the Creator to handle the excessive superfluity of any dominant humor, such as the **gallbladder**, **Spleen**, **Stomach**, **Intestines**, and **Bladder**. 

By these things, therefore, we are clearly taught that through the observation of this true visual demonstration of ours, it is very easy to understand what blood is, what phlegm is, what melancholy is, and finally (which is indeed the most difficult of all) what that hidden mystery of heaven is, by which life is prolonged and nourished in the human body. Finally, concerning this experimental secret, we shall make mention abundantly and copiously in its proper place, by the favor of divine grace.

Concerning the primary or Metaphysical and uncreated Principles; likewise concerning those secondary or Physical and created ones, from which two primary qualities—namely heat and cold—arise; and again, by their mutual action, another two more passive qualities—namely moisture and dryness—are produced. By the action and passion of these qualities upon one another, those four substances are procreated in the world, which are commonly called **Elements** <note>original: "Elementa"</note>. We have indeed made a sufficiently open and clear discourse on these matters in the preceding pages. The **Pagans** <note>original: "Ethnici"; refers to the pre-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers</note> never, or at least only very sparingly, engaged with the primary and uncreated principles of things; whence it also happened that they were accustomed to report on secondary Principles like blind men talking about colors—with the exception (I say) of a very few to whom the title of divinity was attributed on account of their divine insight into abstruse and mystical principles. **Aristotle**, therefore, sang of his Principles in an obscure manner, regarding the true and primary Physical foundations—namely Darkness, Waters, and Light—under a dark veil and robe, as it were, and treating them under the names of **Privation, Matter, and Form** <note>Aristotle's three principles of change. Fludd argues these are merely abstract names for the biblical elements of creation</note>. But in truth, he was ignorant of those primary and uncreated principles, for he considered the world to be uncreated and eternal. **Galen** and **Hippocrates** made their primary principles the four highest qualities, namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; which qualities, if they are within matter, they say firmly constitute the four elements. So it is that these men also (as appears from their writings) did not know those highest and uncreated principles from which all things were primordially made, nor did they even regard Darkness, Light, and Water (from which the four aforementioned qualities were produced). And this was the reason for such great uncertainty and inconstancy in the sciences, as much in Philosophy as in Medicine: namely, because when the Principles—or the uncreated or **Archetypal** <note>original: "Archetypicis"; referring to the divine blueprint or original model in the mind of God</note> causes—are unknown, it is impossible to judge rightly of those things which are "principled" or caused. We, however, are taught by the revelation of the prior principles flowing from a single source, that there are yet other principles closer to a complete composition (or a perfectly mixed body) than either Darkness, Light, Water, Earth, Fire, or the sphere of moisture, which are the three elements of composition. For as we see in the first creation, "otherness"—or the composition of the angel—nay indeed, even the consistency of the whole world, namely Light and...

## SECTION I. PORTION II. PART III.

Just as water (which constitutes **duality**) was procreated from **unity**, we likewise say that in the simplicity of the elements, a progression toward an **imperfect mixture** occurs before one may arrive at the **perfection of composition**. Thus, just as there was a progression from the essence of the **monad** <note>The Monad represents the number one, symbolizing the singular, divine source of all things.</note> to duality—namely, Light and Water—toward the perfect creation of the world in the likeness of a **trinity**; so too from light and water (both the dark and the clear) were heaven and earth made, from which the three elements (which others count as four) are derived.

Similarly, a mixture cannot be made from only one of these elements, much less a **composition** (which is more perfect than an incomplete mixture). Rather, that "middle mixture" is usually formed from two, and sometimes three, elements; it is called "imperfect" because it has not yet reached the fulfillment of composition. Hence, philosophers properly give the name **imperfectly mixed** <note>original: "imperfecte mistum"</note> to that which exists between the exact simplicity of the elements and their complete mixture, which we quite appropriately call **composition**.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that an imperfectly mixed body is closer to the simplicity of the elements than a perfectly composed one. Consequently, it follows that the imperfect mixture is a principle closer to the composite than the element itself is. For example, we see that for the production of the number three (**ternary**), the number two (**binary**) is a closer cause than the number one (**unity**). This is the reason why duality is considered an imperfect number, insofar as it is the middle point between most perfect simplicity and the exact composition made from units.

In this way, an element is like a "one," by the doubling of which an imperfect mixture is usually procreated. Nevertheless, from that mixture—through the labor and industry of Nature—complete composition and perfect generation are usually achieved. However, when that composition fails, there is an immediate reduction back into its nearest principle or "imperfect mixture," which is frequently observed to happen in the **corruption** <note>In this context, "corruption" refers to the natural process of decay or breaking down into constituent parts.</note> of things. From this, it is clearly evident that both the generation of a composition and its corruption move from that imperfect middle point and return to it again. Hence the axiom so often proclaimed by Philosophers: *No thing that is composed can be truly dissolved unless it is first reduced to its primary matter—that is, its next and most immediate origin.* Therefore, in every generation, there is a progression from the **starting point** <note>original: "termino à quo"</note> through the **middle** to the **end point** <note>original: "terminum ad quem"</note> in this manner:

**1.** is the starting point. **3.** is the end point in **generation**. But in **corruption**, **3.** is the starting point, just as the **1.** in the West is its end point. Thus, when the Moon is in the East, it waxes and the sea flows until it reaches the point of noon; from which, as the Moon declines toward its setting, the sea ebbs and decreases. Thus, by multiplication and increase, generation occurs; and by failure and decrease, the corruption of things occurs.

Therefore, progression in Generation happens from the simple perfection of **1.** in the East to the vigor or complete perfection of **3.** at Noon, passing through the **imperfectly mixed 2.**; and in this way, the exact generation of a composite is made. Here we see that **2.** is closer in place and number to **3.** than **1.** is. Hence, **1.** in the East can be called the **remote principle** in composition or generation, and **2.** the **proximate principle** of the same.

## CHAPTER II.

### *That the seed of any composite is an imperfectly mixed body, and consequently of the nature of the Meteors of the Macrocosm.*

In the category of such "imperfectly mixed" bodies, one finds the principles of composite things. These are contained between the raw elements themselves and the completely "elementated" <note>Bodies that have been fully formed from the elements.</note> bodies. These are properly those bodies, whether visible or invisible, which—by the addition of parts or by perfection (that is, through a complete movement from a starting point to an endpoint)—constitute and generate perfectly mixed bodies, including animals, plants, and minerals. 

For what else was the distant matter or the "proximate principle" <note>The "proximate principle" refers to the immediate building block of a substance.</note> of a metal or any other mineral, if not a smoke or a refined water mixed with fire? And what is the proximate principle? Is it not **sulfur and quicksilver** <note>original: "sulphur & argentum vivum." These are the two primary alchemical principles believed to form all metals.</note>—that is, a vapor mixed with an exhalation? What is the first nature of an animal besides water and light? And what is the second, if not air (or a thin smoke) and a hidden fire? What is the proximate and final cause? Is it not the **seed** <note>original: "sperma." Here used to mean the generative essence or "starting material" of life.</note>, or a thick vapor enclosing a subtle fire within its condensed body? 

Indeed, this seed is that "imperfectly mixed" body which passes immediately into the nature of a perfect composition. Certainly, the vegetable matter (or the cause of the vegetative body, whether distant or proximate) does not seem to differ from that of the animal, except that the animal version is more airy and fiery, while the vegetable participates more in water—just as mineral matter seems to claim a larger portion of heavy and earthy water for itself. Yet, the matter of these perfectly mixed things is always the same in kind: namely, **water**, which appears to differ in the number of its parts either by thickness or by thinness. The "acting form," however, comes from the subtlety of fire; by its greater or lesser presence, the "spermatic" matter becomes either thicker or thinner, and consequently, according to its proportion, it constitutes either an animal, a plant, or a mineral.

From these things it is clearly established that the **seed**—which is the proximate matter of the imperfect mixture, or the "tertiary principle" of that thing which it immediately constitutes—becomes an imperfectly mixed body. That is, it is a substance that stands midway between the element from which it moves and the "exactly mixed" body <note>A fully formed, stable organism or object.</note> which it proceeds to procreate and perfect in its movement. Just as the movement from unity to trinity is a progression from simple perfection to a perfect mixture, so must this movement proceed through a middle point, without which there is no absolute measure. 

But since **duality** is called an "imperfect number" (inasmuch as it is the middle between 1 and 3, but does not have a "middle" within its own proportion since only two terms are assigned between 1 and 2), it follows that the **seed** is like an imperfect body or an imperfectly mixed substance consisting between the simple element and the body that is to be completely mixed. Therefore, the seeds of all things (which we call the final and tertiary principles) are those intermediate or "imperfectly mixed" bodies. They are like those smokes, vapors, or dense and visible exhalations reduced into the form of a cloud or a thick or thin mist, which philosophers—not without reason—called ***meteors*** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, clouds, and wind, not just falling stars.</note>, because they are often raised high in the air. They define such bodies as "imperfectly mixed," and say they are generated in the air by the power of the stars from "smoke" (which they divide into two types: vapor and exhalation).

Hence we are taught that every thing composed of elements was originally from that middle substance called an **imperfectly mixed body**—that is, existing in a state of middle motion between perfect simplicity and complete composition. But we must carefully consider this: if such an imperfectly mixed body were the first principle in the generation and production of a composite thing, it is also necessary that, when corruption does its work, the composite returns again into this same matter or middle substance. This follows the saying of the ancient sages quoted above: *“The true dissolution of all things is the reduction of them into their first and proximate matter.”* <note>original: "Vera rerum omnium dissolutio est ipsarum in primam & propinquam materiam reductio."</note>

If this did not happen, it would be impossible for any composition—when resolution and putrefaction <note>The breaking down of a substance into its components.</note> take over—to move backward through the middle stage into its four primary elements. For it is impossible to return from the "endpoint" of generation to the "starting point" unless it is done through the middle point of imperfection. In this way—by extending its perfection and progressing back into imperfection (as the reins of the composition are loosened)—the perfectly mixed body wastes away and is gradually destroyed. For in all corruption, the thing subject to decay is first resolved into the nature of the **seed** (both male and female), through which it passed during generation toward the completion of its composition, although be-

Through the freedom of that state, and with corruption leading the way, it draws to itself—by a certain magnetic force—the multiplying power from the <note>original: "Sole occulto"</note> **hidden Sun** and the higher spirits. Through this middle state, I say, happen composition, resolution, or decomposition; generation and corruption; life and death of the body; and health and disease, both in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the entire universe.</note> and the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," meaning the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. This occurs by the admirable effect and operation of the divine act upon moist nature in perfectly mixed bodies, as will be explained more clearly in what follows.

It is manifest, therefore, that the "imperfectly mixed" is that medium through which the transition to the exact generation of a perfect composite is made. It is also that into which the regression from the point of generation occurs when the form is changed and corruption is at work. Thus, in the Macrocosm, the seeds of all things are nothing other than "meteors," which, being mere fumes, appear as they are through condensation. Therefore, in both the Macrocosm and Microcosm, all such imperfect materials procreated from fumes of both kinds can be called "meteors." The vehicle in which they subsist—or that "philosophical sea" in which they swim—is that aerial spirit possessing all the miracles of the world, both the manifest and the secret. ### CHAPTER III.

->*That every created and generated thing, or corrupted thing, receives its motion toward its perfection from the principles by way of the meteorological medium, that is, the imperfectly mixed body.*<-

There was never, therefore, any movement in the world—whether toward perfect creation, generation, or corruption—that was not made through the meteorological medium (that is, the imperfectly mixed). For just as the completion of a melody usually requires a middle, internal, and less-than-perfect harmony, so also in creation we see the **number two** <note>original: "numerum binarium"</note> interposed between the Creator and the created thing, so that the creature may be led to the perfection of its creation. For example, in the progression from the uncreated **Unity** (1), we arrive at **Duality** (2), denoting matter and form, or water and light. By their union, mediated by the bond of the **spirit of the third order** (3), the complete creature was procreated from those primary elements on the first day of creation, endowed with an angelic form. By similar reasoning, between Duality (2) and its square, **Four** (4), there stands the **Three** (3), which is like the imperfectly mixed or the medium between 2 and 4. Such is the substance of the middle heaven, whose substance (3) is matter, but whose form is the super-celestial duality (2). Thus, the 2 united to the 3 gives this heaven the name of <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence," a pure substance superior to the four physical elements (earth, water, air, fire).</note>. The perfect creature arising from these is the Sun and the other stars, which fulfill the roles of the square (4). Similarly, the form of the middle heaven—which is the entire nature of the higher heaven joined with such a spirit—is like an imperfectly mixed body or a "meteor" in respect to the perfection of the stellar creature which is procreated and perfected from it, even though it is very perfect in its own nature. And again, the star stands in the same relationship to the terrestrial creature, in whose composition all the elements concur. In these examples, one may see the nature of the "rotation of the elements" toward generation and corruption via imperfectly mixed media. **THERE** will be no occasion for doubting that two things concur for the procreation of the <term>Microcosm<note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe or Macrocosm.</note></term>, both internal and external: one is the spirit imbued with human form, and the other is the body produced to the perfection of the compound.
