...it will be lawful to do so. For example, on **Tuesday** I observe the rising sun. From this, I declare its nature to be Martial <note>original: "Martialem"; relating to the planet Mars.</note>; therefore, in the arc of Mars, I ascend as far as the <term>Sephirah</term> <note>One of the ten divine emanations or attributes in Kabbalah.</note> **Geburah**. This I know to signify strength and power joined with severity and punishment. Because its influences are guided by the Angel **Samael**, they denote violence, rapacity, cruelty, and other such traits once they are enclosed within an animal body. Furthermore, its aspect is a <term>quintile</term> <note>An astrological aspect where planets are 72 degrees apart.</note>, whose origin or triplicity is **Chokhmah** <note>original: "Hochma"; the Sephirah of Wisdom.</note> or **Jehovah**, an aspect in which severity threatens. 

But truly, at that same moment of the Sun's rising, we find that **Jupiter** holds several dignities in the heavens. The source of its <term>Sephirah</term> or influence is **Chesed** <note>The Sephirah of Mercy or Loving-kindness.</note>, which is presided over by the divine name **El**. This is indeed an aspect of the airy and benevolent triplicity, whose head is **Chesed**, in which love abounds. From this source, the **Seraphim** <note>The highest order of angels, associated with fire and love.</note> draw their amorous virtue or favor. **Chesed**, therefore, signifies clemency, for the sacred influences from **El** are most full of clemency and kindness. They pour that virtue into the <term>Dominations</term> <note>An order of angels (Dominions) that regulates the duties of lower angels.</note>, which the good angel **Zadkiel** finally receives and conducts downward into the region of **Jupiter**. Jupiter’s spirits <note>original: "dæmones"; here referring to intermediary planetary intelligences rather than evil beings.</note> then conduct these in various ways into the lower realms. 

In this way, the burning and violent influences of **Geburah** are tempered by the opposite property of the good and benevolent influences of **Chesed** itself. The fiery force of the one is soothed by the airy sweetness of the other; the malevolent acts and violent effects of **Samael** are mitigated by the benevolent virtue of **Zadkiel**. Indeed, the Martial spirits are bridled and in some way restrained by the industry of the spheres of **Jupiter**. The impulsive force is held within the limits of peace by the natural bond of love. Thus, the misfortune of one is corrected by the fortune of the other. 

Nevertheless, in the life of one born under such conditions, there will be the greatest instability; for his passage will be like a ship tossed upon an inconstant sea. If the virtue of **Jupiter** in the heavens is weak while that of **Mars** is strong, then the misfortunes of life pursue the newborn, which are again suppressed by the <term>exaltation</term> <note>A state where a planet's influence is particularly strengthened.</note> of **Jupiter**. Next, one must seek the dominant star of the **Horoscope** <note>original: "Horoscopi"; in this period, this refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, its Sephirah, its aspect, and its natures—concerning the secret of which I shall not speak further in this place. 

Nor let the scrupulous man say that many who are born at the same instant differ in complexion and nature; for the reason for that fact, once the secret is known, will be very easily demonstrated. Furthermore, even if two opposite planets of a bad disposition concur at birth—for example, if the Sun is rising on a **Saturday** with **Mars** governing in the heavens—it very often denotes the extreme misfortune of the newborn. it signifies a narrow constriction and imprisonment of the vital and natural spirit, unless the Lord of the Horoscope (that is, the hour preceding the birth) moderates it through its influences. 

But on the other hand, if the Sun rises on a **Thursday** with **Venus** predominating in the sky and the Lord of the Horoscope looking on with a favorable omen, it denotes a contrary disposition of the newborn’s fortune; thus, moderate influences produce a moderate fortune. And always, the nature of the divine property, of the same **Sephirah**, its triplicity and aspect, as well as the order of Angels, the angelic leader of influences, and finally—as the more immediate cause—the planet itself with its <term>Olympic spirits</term> <note>original: "dæmonibus Olympicis"; a specific group of seven planetary spirits common in Renaissance magic.</note> who are subject to the aforesaid leader, must be observed with the greatest diligence. Many other things occur in this divination which we shall clarify elsewhere, God willing. 

Here we would also have you observe with a diligent gaze that in this place I am teaching how to ascend from the latter things to the former; that is, from what is better known to us to what is better known to nature. Specifically, from the wandering star known to us to that fountain from which the drops of influence trickle down into these lower regions. For God is discerned through His wonderful works, from which we must ascend—not by a mathematical or linear ascension, but by a **formal sublimation** before we reach the fountain of the highest good. Thus we say a Horoscope is "exalted," even if it is not raised by mathematical height, but by formal dignity without changing its place or dimension. What this most occult exaltation may be is revealed to those "Children of the Sun" who, being exalted in mind, are permitted to gaze upon the vision of truth. 

But let us return to the matter at hand. We say that if a birth occurs while the Sun is running beneath the earth <note>i.e., at night.</note>, the wandering star assigned to the place of the Sun's setting is attributed to it, and the more noble planet of the lower hemisphere is considered for the same reason stated above. Many things of great moment are required to clarify the mysteries of this Astrological art, which it seems necessary and right for us to omit in this place, since we have proposed to dedicate perhaps an entire volume to this business elsewhere, God favoring us.

### *Fifth Experiment: Concerning the knowledge of the elemental disposition and inclination, or the complexion of the body of the newborn, and the more immediate cause of their physical composition.*

In all things, one must proceed as before. We can elicit this partly in the elemental region under the arc of the Lord of the Horoscope, and partly under that planet predominating in the heavens. For example, let the planet predominating the Horoscope be **Mars**. Under its arc in the elemental world, we find that the immediate causes of composition are fiery—namely, sulphurous <term>meteors</term> <note>In historical science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including vapors and fumes.</note> of many degrees—from which they argue a fiery and bilious <note>original: "biliosam"; associated with the humor of yellow bile and a choleric temperament.</note> elemental composition. 

But **Jupiter**, holding a stronger place in the heavens, mixes itself with the fiery composition of **Mars**. From this, we say that the heat of Mars is moderated by much airy and life-giving spirit, since we find the elemental meteors of Jupiter to be part of the lower air. By its contact, the strengths of the elemental fire are mitigated, and it promises an abundance of the vapor of life, from which is generated the **Mercury of life** <note>An alchemical term for the vital principle or "spirit" found within the blood.</note> visible in the blood. But truly, since the fountain of life...

->*Concerning many other mysteries of divination which can be clarified through a true and formal inspection of this mirror.*<-

Many other questions or doubts of this kind can be resolved by the knowledge of this most true Astrology, provided the artist is skilled in it—not in the common way, which is to grasp the external appearances but omit the internal realities, or like Aesop’s dog, to choose the shadow and neglect the essential substance. For example: How is one to find the nature of the ruling Angel of any person born, as well as the nature of the <term>Olympic</term> <note>Referring to the seven planetary spirits often cited in Renaissance magic books like the Arbatel.</note> and elementary demon subject to them? Which act of the vital soul is stronger in the newborn? Which day will be more fortunate or unfortunate for a certain man? For this question, one must consider the <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten divine emanations in Kabbalistic thought.</note> of the lord of that man’s <term>Horoscope</term> <note>original: "Horoscopus"; here referring specifically to the rising sign or Ascendant at birth.</note> and the lord of the day under the requested ruler. Which of two men waging war or a lawsuit against each other will prevail in a contention on a fixed day? In this case, one must consider the strength and weakness of the Sephiroth of both their births along with the lord of the heavens on that given day. And many other weighty questions can be resolved by the power of this mirror, which (I know) would be ridiculous to explain to the vain common folk here, just like other things reported by us; therefore, I shall not strive to speak further of this universal mirror.

->*How this universal mirror is included within the four characters of the great name, the Tetragrammaton, along with the four mothers corresponding to them.*<-

The first sphere of the following mirror denotes the three primary or archetypal principles which the Mosaic fathers named <note>The "Mosaic fathers" refers to the authors of the Pentateuch or early Kabbalistic commentators.</note>, where one character or principle is repeated twice, namely **ה** (**He**) <note>The letter 'He' appears twice in the four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>: according to whose pattern the upper waters are divided from the lower waters, and to each thing in the creation a proper "mother" <note>A reference to the 'Mother Letters' of the Sefer Yetzirah—Aleph, Mem, and Shin—which represent the elements of Air, Water, and Fire.</note> is subjected. From these, the remaining subordinate principles—falling between pure simplicity and composition—are placed in their proper positions, each according to the logic of its own property: Where, with the illumination of the "starting" **Mem**, it begins from the luminous **Aleph**. For the world begins in the luminous **Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, א.</note>, through the starting **Mem** <note>The standard form of the letter Mem, מ.</note>, and ends through the final and closed **Mem** <note>The form of the letter Mem used at the end of words, ם.</note> in the dark **Aleph**. For when the supreme Sun sets, it is necessary that the light of the world be brought back again into darkness; hence, just as the small **Aleph** is the beginning of number (namely, unity), so also the great **Aleph** is the end, which denotes the number one thousand, beyond which there is no progression. Thus the world arose, and thus shall be its destruction, if only the luminous **Aleph** removes its own luminous spirit from the world by hiding itself in darkness.

In the preceding <term>Macrocosmic</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "Microcosm" or the human being.</note> mirror, it appears that the world began from the bright **Aleph**, for the "beginning **Mem**" is illuminated by the bright **Aleph**. The form of the world truly reaches its limit in the "final **Mem**," where light returns again into darkness; for by hiding itself, the bright **Aleph** is changed into the dark **Aleph**. 

**Aleph**, therefore, is the beginning of things, and it is also their ultimate end. It is the **Alpha** and the **Omega**; it is unity and it is the number one thousand, beyond which there is no further dimension in Arithmetic <note>In Hebrew numerology (Gematria), the letter Aleph represents 1, but can also signify 1,000 (Eleph). Just as the world was born in this way, its destruction will happen no differently—namely, by the bright **Aleph** removing its face from the worldly spirit and hiding itself in darkness. That is to say, the world migrates back from its divine **act** into divine **potential**. 

And from this, it is said that **Aleph**, in the manner of a <term>Hermaphrodite</term> <note>In Renaissance alchemy and mysticism, this term refers to a being that contains both active/male and passive/female principles, symbolizing the completeness of the primordial Creator.</note>, participates in the nature of both sexes: of the male, namely, insofar as it is **act** and **form**; and of the female, in respect to **potential** and **matter**. Hence <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> said in the *Pimander*, book 1:
> "Mind, being most full of the fecundity of both sexes, etc."

Thus the world was made in the image of the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, considered the blueprint of creation.</note>, and thus Man was created after the pattern of the world; for which reason both are, not without wisdom, called the "sons of God" by **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>Mercurio Trismegisto: The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings on magic, alchemy, and philosophy are attributed.</note>.

And so we bring this volume of ours to an end. The remaining two volumes that follow (of which we briefly reviewed the underlying summary at the beginning of this book) will, by the favor of the Divine Will, see the light in their proper order. But let it be permitted to me in the meantime—both for the sake of refreshing my body and soul, as well as out of a desire to attend to my worldly affairs necessary for life and livelihood—to catch my breath for a little while. I truly hope that this work of mine will receive a favorable and happy reception from the "sons of true doctrine" <note>A common phrase for initiated students of Hermetic or Alchemical wisdom.</note>; although I know for certain that my labors will be met with laughter and contempt by the ignorant and envious (whose nature it is to unjustly attack anyone raised above their understanding with curses and insults) rather than being crowned with the honor of a just reward. However things may turn out, bolstered by patience and fortified by a secure conscience, I shall rejoice in my peaceful mind. Content perhaps with my own things, and not at all covetous of the world's vain honors or wealth, I desire only to breathe in peace and truly serve my God, the Greatest and Best. I pray for this from that most holy Divinity, **Jehovah**, with prayers impressed upon my living spirit. In the shadow of whose wings I have sung until now, and shall sing always.

# ANALYTICAL DECLA-
# RATION,
## In which
### *EVERY PART OF THAT COMPARISON, which Johannes Kepler recently instituted at the end of his World Harmony, under the title of "Appendix," between that same harmony of his and my own World Harmony, is answered by the very arguments of truth.*

Painters who are more skillful in their craft are accustomed to cast the worst color, and that most unpleasant to the senses, outside the margins of their art, so that they might render the work more pleasing and delightful to the eyes and mind of the spectator. Yet, for all that, the intuition of the wise is not so veiled by their deceits or illusory shadows that they are less able to judge colors most correctly, and to distinguish the whiteness of the swan from the blackness of the crow even through that very veil of darkness. 

Nevertheless, this subtlety of painters has always been absent from me because of the simplicity of my mind, or (to speak more accurately) the thinness of my talent; namely, so that I might not cover over my errors (which I confess are perhaps not small) with a hard and bold forehead through the faulty obscurity of other colors; or, uplifted by vain glory or self-love <term>philautia: a Greek-derived term for excessive self-love or conceit</term>, extol my deeds or writings by some comparative degree to the detriment of another's praise or the depression of an honest reputation. 

The truly learned, I say, will undoubtedly perceive the discrepancy of each color, and the truly wise will weigh the cause of each in the scales of justice; nor will they consider it right or honest for anyone to be a judge in their own cause, or to celebrate the praises of their own works through injuries to others and to trumpet them abroad with an unjust mouth. Whatever I have done or exposed to the world in the public manner, I have woven to a happy conclusion (as I hope), simply indeed and with a mind full of sincerity, so that it might please learned people; and not indeed to affect anyone with evil or rash speech or calumnies by blaming them either secretly or openly, or to speak a reproach to anyone with a sharp tongue. For I have never aspired to act in the manner of a Cynic <note>The Cynics were a school of ancient Greek philosophers known for their biting criticism; Fludd implies he does not wish to be a "snarling" critic.</note>, by whose tooth or the rust of envy I might erode anyone's reputation, or build up a famous—nay, truly vain—glory for myself from the disgrace of another, and accumulate ill-gotten praises. 

Hence it is that I have proposed to myself in this place to reply in a few words, with all bitterness set aside, to the comparison made by Johannes Kepler between my *World Harmony* <note>original: "Harmoniam meam mundanam"</note> published not long ago, and his own recently brought to light; whereby I may more clearly hurl back at him those things subtly, and yet with a somewhat serene forehead, objected in the Appendix of Johannes Kepler, through direct means and indeed in successive order.

# ANALYSIS BY ROBERT FLUDD.

In a very similar way, I would have gladly ended this treatise of mine by omitting the Appendix, if a civil respect toward certain of my friends did not command me to grant them a similar favor. I felt urged by an honest necessity to defend my good reputation and satisfy them in many points concerning the comparison of Johannes’s <note>Johannes Kepler</note> Harmony with my own (where he seems to sharply, though secretly, accuse me of some sort of ignorance). Therefore, he himself seems to discuss in the following pages how great the sympathy or antipathy is between our Harmonies; and I, following his path step by step, have proposed to examine the very marrow of this subject, lightly perhaps, but down to the very kernel.

->Text II.<-

*That author promised two volumes, one of which, inscribed as being about the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or the universe as a whole</term>, now sees the light; the other, concerning the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "Little World," referring to a human being as a reflection of the universe</term>, is still awaited. The first volume, comprising two treatises, appeared at distinct times: for I saw the first treatise, on the threefold world, after the Frankfurt autumn book fairs of the year 1617; the second, on the arts which worldly nature calls "apes," I saw at the Easter fairs of the following year, 1618.*

### ANALYSIS.

Those two divided offspring of my first volume were certainly not published one after the other because they had not both been fully written before the year 1617; indeed, I would have the reader know that the subject of that first volume was completed and brought to a successful conclusion seven years before its public distribution. Nor did one portion of it reach the hands of the Printer without the other; but it was in his mind (as it seemed to me), whether for the sake of greater profit or compelled by the shortness of time, to publish one part of that volume after the other—that is, at successive fairs. 

As for what pertains to the first volume of my Microcosm, dealing with both nature and art, I certainly did not require an interval of 22 years for its complete composition—which Johannes Kepler confesses he took for the completion of his Harmony. Instead, I received <note>original: "accepi," likely meaning he began the formal draft or "received" the inspiration/structure</note> that work around the feast of Saint Michael <note>September 29</note> in the year 1618, and I successfully finished weaving it together before Lent of that same year. This was done solely through nightly labors, with no hindrance interfering in my daily profession and medical practice, but accompanied by peaceful contemplation. 

Therefore, let readers—uplifted by the wings of justice—forgive me if, in such a rapid accumulation of great matters, significant errors perhaps crept into that work of ours while I quickly bypassed arguments of great weight. Or perhaps it is not as exact in its method, or as purged of faults, as that work of Johannes Kepler, which was revised again and again over such a long passage of time, and examined and refined with so much "cementing" and "fermentation." For through the uncorrected passage of time, a work is rendered most correct; raw things are made ripe, and the imperfect are led completely to the goal of perfection. 

Nevertheless, I hope that I have not brought anything to light, either in the history of the Macrocosm or the Microcosm, which I am not capable of supporting with "Atlantic shoulders" <note>An allusion to Atlas holding up the heavens</note> and defending in public writings against anyone's oppositions. For almost everything said by me has been proven in those same works of mine to be right and sincere—partly by arguments packed with philosophy (insofar as it does not lack the certain supports of experience), partly by the authority of ancient Philosophers and the confirmation of theosophists, and finally (which is the most certain of all), by the testimonies of visual demonstrations and various experiences.

->Text III.<-

*In the second treatise, therefore, he placed Music among the arts and covered the material of my third book to some extent; but in the first treatise, which is completed in seven books, he destined the third book to "World Music," usurping the same title that I prefixed to my entire work: and he touched upon the material of my fourth and fifth books.*

### ANALYSIS.

Here the Author acts preposterously, by counting the tail before he makes any mention of the head, introducing my artificial Music where he should only have discussed that natural and physical—

### TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX.

...is being dealt with: For thus, amid the barrenness of the field or area in the subject of his Appendix, let my will stand for my reason <note>Original: "Stet igitur pro ratione voluntas," a Latin legal maxim implying that one's choice or determination is sufficient justification.</note>. He seems to divide this text into two small portions: namely, the comparison of my **Technical Music** <term>Technical Music (Musica artificialis): The practical study of human-made music, instruments, and composition</term> with the third book of his *Harmony*, which he graciously acknowledges agrees to some extent with his own purpose; and the investigation of my **Worldly Music** <term>Worldly Music (Musica mundana): The "Music of the Spheres," or the harmonious mathematical proportions governing the universe</term>. In that part of his text, he seems to indicate in a certain way that I gave the same title to the third book of my *Physics* as he gave to his entire treatise. For this reason, he used the term "usurpation" not only in the scope of this context, but also in other places of his Appendix. This word is usually taken in a negative sense, as when someone unworthily attempts to grant and assign to himself the title of another's dignity and honor. But I shall ensure, I hope, that the author—puffed up by his own self-love—understands that this title belongs and is due to me just as much as to him, by at least equal right.

As for the first part, where he teaches that my **Technical Music** embraces the matter or subject of his third book, we say that it includes and comprehends not only the force of that third book, but even the whole power or essence of the science of Music in the abstract, as well as both its theory and practice. In his third book, he seems to treat first of the invention of Music from the strikes of hammers <note>This refers to the legend of Pythagoras discovering musical proportions by listening to blacksmiths' hammers</note>, and then in a certain way of the proportion of strings. I also showed this briefly in the sixth book of my *Arithmetic*, where in chapters 1 and 2 I discussed the division of the **monochord** <term>Monochord: A scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals</term> string and treated the proportion of the sounding hammers. He himself, in chapter 2 of that same book, mentions the harmonic section of the string and many proportions, and indeed with far too many words. I, however, have uncovered all of this and infinite other mysteries of string division in the column of my **Temple of Music** in a **hieroglyphic** manner <note>Fludd uses "hieroglyphic" to mean symbolic diagrams and complex visual illustrations that reveal hidden truths</note>, and I explained it with few words in the third book of that same treatise. Even **harmonic means** <term>Harmonic means: Mathematical ratios used to determine the middle pitches between two notes</term> and their reasoning, which he only treats superficially in his chapter 3, I have treated most copiously in both that book and my fifth—though I have delivered it in more elegant words.

As for the judgment on the origin of the harmonious intervals, which I called simple and consonant—about which he speaks in Book 3, Chapter 4, and I in Chapters 1, 2, and 3 of my third book—the matter is still before the judge; therefore, we shall discuss the cause of this matter in its proper place below. He also thinks he can express the marrow of consonant intervals and tries to divide them into more harmonious intervals in Chapter 5 of that book. We, however, have done this same thing completely in Chapters 4, 5, and 6 of the same book, and—what is more—we have shown the most certain method of finding them from the examination of the monochord string, just as we have proven it most exactly by practice and experience.

There we also explained the entire power of his Chapter 7, where the sectioning of the **Octave** in both types of song is discussed, as well as the number and order of the smallest intervals of one **Diapason** <term>Diapason: The Greek term for an Octave</term>, which is the subject of his Chapter 8. This was likewise discussed in Rule 5, Chapter 1 of my 3rd book, along with the true discovery of the Diapason on the monochord, which he treated only obscurely in his string sectioning. We also completely divided the monochord into its proportions and consonances, expressing this in various ways in the same book. In this operation, we also condensed the power of his Chapter 9, which treats the **Diagram**—that is, the modern notation of strings or voices through the letters of the Alphabet and lines—where he also introduces the notes of the art along with the system. He delivers all these things with much talk, over many pages, and in a rather confused manner; I, however, reduced it to a small space, as if casting a highly polished mirror, in which one may see and behold with open eyes the entire method of musical consonances, proportions, and intervals.

The use of syllables <note>The "solmization" syllables: Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La</note>, which he mentioned in Chapter 10 of the same book, we have explained in the clearest words in Book 2 of the same subject, and we demonstrated their reasoning with a diagram that is not to be despised. The entire composition of the system, which he discusses in Chapter 11, I have most clearly extracted from the architecture of my **Temple**; its formula I have diagrammatically delineated in a significant form in Chapter 1 of my 2nd book. There you will find the scale, both "hard" and "soft" <note>This refers to the "Hexachordum durum" and "Hexachordum molle," using B-natural and B-flat</note>, with keys both sharp and grave, and with the application of the voice to one or the other. You will also find the most exact discovery of the **square B** and **round B** <note>Original: "B. quadrati & rotundi," referring to the symbols for B-natural (♮) and B-flat (♭)</note> on the monochord, and that more clearly than we find it in his work. The reasoning for **natural song** (which he treats in Chapter 13) is also found in my same little book; we have clearly depicted it in a hieroglyphic manner under the sharp tower in the structure of my temple. Regarding the modes of melodies, he mentions them in his own way in Chapters 14 and 15; I speak of them in my Book 4, Chapter 8. He teaches the harmony of song in Chapter 16 and similarly treats the three means in song; I show all of this from its effect throughout almost the whole of Book 5.

Therefore, what he expressed with many words and a long oration, I have contracted into brief points and explained with hieroglyphic and highly significant figures. I did this not because I delight in pictures (as he says elsewhere), but because I had decided to gather many things into a few, and in the manner of the **Chemists** <note>Fludd here links his work to Alchemy</note>—for he seems to hint below that I associate with Chemists and **Hermeticists** <term>Hermeticist: A follower of the mystical and philosophical teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</term>—to collect the extracted essence, while rejecting the dross-filled substance. I chose to place what is good in its own proper vessel, so that, once the secret of science was uncovered, the hidden might be made manifest. Thus, the internal nature of the thing, stripped of its clothing—like a precious gem set in a gold ring—would be enclosed in a figure more suited to its nature, in which its virtue might be seen by the eye and mind as if in a mirror, without a circuit of many words. Furthermore, the necessity of the subject, and reason itself, commanded and persuaded me to write about each science strictly and succinctly. These things having been gathered together, it is manifest that the subject of my **Technical Music** extends its margins wider than...

ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE.

...to have it more rightfully than for it to be comprised under the Author’s <note>Referring to Kepler</note> third book. But of these matters we shall speak more copiously *below*. There is no need to respond to the second part of his text in this place, because a most ample opportunity to satisfy the Reader in this matter will present itself in the *following sections*.

### TEXT IV.

> *Therefore, let us make a beginning from his Technical Music <term>Technical Music (Musica artificialis): The practical science of human music-making, instruments, and theory</term>. He delivers it in 7 books. In the first of these, he reviews authors, nomenclatures, and the power of music over the souls of men. Regarding the Authors or inventors of Music, I say nothing, or certainly very little; for my intent is to reveal the causes of natural things.*

### ANALYSIS.

But truly, since he contends at the end of that passage that his intention was to reveal the causes of natural things, and asserts below that he did not receive the subject of his Music from the ancients, but unearthed it from the nature of things and established it from the very foundations; why does he attempt to relate his physical or natural comparisons to technical ones, or to compare his **Natural Music** with mine (which he himself acknowledges in express words to be **Technical**), when no right relationship is usually made between the concrete and the abstract? 

He also relates that he dealt with the Authors either not at all or certainly very little, as if that were superfluous in my work. And yet—by his leave—we find in his own writings that he proposes more concerning the Authors of Music than I did. For in the *beginning of his third book*, he mentions **Jubal** <note>original: "Iubale"; a biblical figure described in Genesis as the ancestor of those who play the harp and flute</note>, whom **Moses** accounts as the first inventor of musical instruments or strings. He takes this Jubal to be **Apollo**; and makes his brother **Jabal** the inventor of the pipe. 

Next, he says that **Pythagoras** derived the musical consonances and proportions from the strikes of hammers, which he immediately transferred to the measurements and divisions of strings, or the differences of sounds. I also named these as the inventors of Music in my first book; and indeed for this reason, in my **Musical Temple**, I depicted Pythagoras beneath an arch supported by two columns, watching the blacksmiths striking the iron with hammers. Finally, I shall narrate more extensively *below* how the Author’s intention operated in the completion of the manifestation of natural things.

### TEXT V.

> *In the second book, the Author approaches the things themselves, which he calls Intervals and Times. Again, I have said nothing at all regarding times, or the length and brevity of sounds: for they are arbitrary, and do not require an investigation of causes.*

### ANALYSIS.

It is, however, agreeable to reason that we join **Times** <term>Times (Tempora): In this context, duration, rhythm, or the "measure" of a musical note</term> with **Harmonic Intervals**, for without them no symphonic motion occurs. For the most exact proportion must be observed as much in the measure of time as in the dimension of the string or line, since no motion—by whose action Music sounds—occurs without time. 

Whence time is not inaptly defined as *the measure of motion, not in the same moment, but according to before (that is, the past) and after (that is, the future), with its present flow*; that is, with the present moment or minute of time, which is called the **Now** <term>The Now (Nunc): A technical term in Aristotelian physics representing the instantaneous boundary between past and future</term>. 

Whence I wonder greatly that the Author, when he has dealt precisely with Music or Harmony, confesses that he said nothing at all regarding Times, or the length and brevity of sounds, since for the reason aforesaid nothing should be said of motion without time. Yet he acknowledges that the subject of his **Worldly Harmony** <term>Worldly Harmony (Harmonia Mundana): The mathematical ratios Fludd and Kepler believed governed the movements of the heavens</term> is the real motions of the Planets, both in the latter part of his *Appendix* and throughout his fifth book. 

Now, Physicists define motion as *the progression of a movable subject from potentiality into act*; which translation is indeed numbered by time. Why, therefore, did he omit the times or the length and brevity of sounds, when without them Music of any kind is plainly maimed and deficient, whether it be considered in the abstract (merely mathematical) or in the concrete (that is, in Physical things)? 

For with a diligent investigation of things leading the way, what usually produces harmony in the higher realms except the variety of the motions of the celestial bodies? Did he not himself attribute deep tones to **Saturn**, both in the beginning of his first book and in many places of the fifth? From which he assigned to it the **Cubic** figure <note>Fludd is referencing Kepler’s theory from "Mysterium Cosmographicum" where the Platonic solids are nested between planetary spheres</note> as being the "heaviest" of all because of the slowness of that star in motion and its kinship with the earth; and he placed the **Tetrahedron**, which in size comes closest to the Cube, between **Jupiter** and **Mars**. He made the **Octahedron** for **Mercury**, the **Icosahedron** for **Venus**, and the **Dodecahedron** for the **Earth**, as if destined in the creation, arguing from there the differences of the planetary consonances through the various proportions of those Geometric bodies. For from where did he gather the gravity <note>In a musical sense: the low pitch or "heaviness" of a sound</note> of Saturn, if not from its slow motion? Or the proximity of Jupiter to it because of the contact of the Cube, if not because Jupiter was nearest to Saturn in the gravity of its motion?

<summary>Fludd defends his inclusion of musical history and the concept of "Time" (rhythm and duration) against Kepler's criticisms, arguing that since Kepler studies planetary motion, he cannot logically ignore the time-based measurements that define harmony.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s critique of Johannes Kepler's astronomical model. Fludd is arguing that Kepler's "Natural Music" of the spheres is incomplete because it focuses only on the distances (intervals) between planets and ignores the complex proportions of musical time and rhythm. Fludd begins by reviewing the standard planetary periods to show that even in a Copernican or Tychonic system, the mathematical foundations of harmony must include the temporal dimension.</meta>

->TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX<-

...it would be, and so in the rest? We know that the natural motion of Saturn, according to the opinion of the ancients, is completed in a space of 30 years; that Jupiter finishes its journey in nearly twelve years; that Mars traverses the Zodiac in a space of almost two years and five months; that the Sun travels the ecliptic in 365 days and nearly six hours; that Venus passes through the Zodiac nearly at the motion of the Sun, as does Mercury; and that the Moon passes through all the degrees of the Zodiac in its natural motion in about 28 days. Furthermore, by the logic of the preceding motions, we know that the mean motion of Saturn—which was called by the ancients its <note>original: "motus ejus deferens"</note> **deferent motion** <term>Deferent: In pre-modern astronomy, the large circular path along which a planet (or the center of its smaller epicycle) moves.</term>—moves on its own axis, intersecting the axis of the Zodiac or ecliptic according to the succession of the signs, at nearly two minutes daily. 

But indeed, they maintain that the motion of the same planet, made on account of the spheres carrying the **Apogee** <term>Apogee (Augem): The point in a planet's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth (or Sun), and thus moves slowest.</term> of Saturn (which occurs proportionally upon the axis and poles of the ecliptic of the eighth sphere), happens at a rate of one degree and about twenty minutes every two hundred years. Thus they say the motion of Jupiter is nearly the same with respect to the spheres carrying its Apogee as that of Saturn, namely 1 degree and 28 minutes. Its deferent motion, however, on its own poles and axis, is far swifter than the mean motion of Saturn; for by this, Jupiter is moved naturally by nearly 5 minutes daily. By this proportion, it is necessary that it traverse the Zodiac in the aforementioned time, namely in the space of 12 years. 

Mars is also moved according to the motion of the carrying spheres in the same time as Saturn and Jupiter. But by its own motion, it completes about 30 minutes daily; by which proportion it is said to complete the circuit of the Zodiac in nearly two years and 5 months. They say the spheres carrying the Apogee of the Sun have the same motion as the other superior planets—namely Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. But its deferent motion on its own poles and axis, according to the succession of the signs, completes nearly 59 minutes and eight seconds; and thus the Sun finishes the entire Zodiac in 365 days and nearly 6 hours. And so it is in the other inferior planets, namely Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.

But let it be admitted that our Author <note>Referring to Kepler</note> here—along with Copernicus, Schöner, Brahe, and others of the same sort—altogether denies and attempts to remove the stationary and retrograde motion of the **Epicycle** <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one (the deferent), used to explain retrograde motion in older astronomy.</term> (for such appears to be the Author's mind in *Book 5, Chapter 4*), and requires peculiar orbits for the spheres carrying the Apogee, by which he wishes all Planets to be made **eccentric** <term>Eccentric: An orbital path where the center of motion is not the center of the Earth or Sun, resulting in changing distances.</term>; that is, to change their intervals from the Sun. Let this very thing, I say, be posited. Nevertheless, it will be necessary—insofar as the aforementioned Authors differ little or not at all from the ancients in the effect of the natural motion of the Planets—that the **Harmony** found in his Planetary System be made from motions of this kind, since the Author has placed his hope upon these same foundations. 

Since this is the case, it must be asked (and do not think this is said foolishly) why he has rejected the variety of times in their length and brevity, when the progression of these motions occurs only within physical time? Certainly, a single and simple species of time does not suffice for this work, but rather a manifold one, insofar as the motion of the Planets is manifold and diverse. From this it follows without a doubt that the motion of the Moon relates to the superior planets just as, in musical times, the shortest durations relate to the mean and longer ones. For the most exact proportion in the diversity of planetary motions is beyond any controversy: seeing as the progression of the Moon has a relation to the **Soprano** <note>original: "cantum excellentem"</note>, the motions of Mercury, Venus, and the Sun to the **Alto** and **Tenor** <note>original: "Altum & Medium"</note>, Mars occupies the place of the **Countertenor**, Jupiter the **Tenor**, and Saturn claims for itself the **Bass** in the greatest or "large" sounds on account of its slowness and gravity in motion. 

What, therefore, is the cause that our Author here, through an excessive investigation of intervals, has forgotten himself and so neglected the secrets of time that he is content to use only **semibreves** <term>Semibreve: In modern notation, a whole note. In Fludd's time, it was the basic unit of measurement, but he argues it is too simple to represent the heavens.</term> in his Harmony? Perhaps this is due to an ignorance of the manifold differences of triple times (since in that proportion of temporal numbers, his triangular bodies ought to form with the planes of other species), or perhaps he even desires to fall into a more blatant error by asserting that the durations of sounds are arbitrary and require no investigation of causes. 

They do indeed, I say, require a great investigation of causes, as will most easily appear from a diligent inspection and contemplation of my **Temporal Triangles** in *Book 4 of my Technical Music*. For it is a matter of no small moment to know which temporal notes are entirely perfect, which are once perfect, which twice, thrice, or four times perfect, and which, finally, are completely perfect. Similarly, to investigate the infinite unequal or disparate proportions of temporal notes to one another will require great inquiry: namely, which is simple and which is multiplex; and then among the simple, which is double, triple, or quadruple multiplex; which is **superparticular** <term>Superparticular: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one part of it (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3).</term>, **superbipartient** (relating to thirds, fifths, sevenths), or **supertripartient** (relating to fourths, fifths, sevenths), or **superquadrupartient**, etc. 

Similarly among the multiplexes: which is a double or triple superparticular, and from those, which are **sesquialtera** <term>Sesquialtera: A 3:2 ratio.</term>, **sesquitertia** <term>Sesquitertia: A 4:3 ratio.</term>, or **sesquiquarta** <term>Sesquiquarta: A 5:4 ratio.</term>; and in the quadruple, which are sesquialtera or sesquiquarta. And then afterwards, which is a double multiplex superbipartient of thirds or fifths, or supertripartient of fourths or fifths; which is a triple superbipartient of thirds or fifths, or supertripartient of fourths or fifths; and which is a quadruple superbipartient of thirds or fifths, and supertripartient of fourths or fifths. Finally, from the notes according to their proportions, it will be permitted to know from our **Temporal Triangle** which notes, in respect to one another, are duple, which sesquitertia, which sesquialtera, and which at last are triple. 

Furthermore, even **Rests**—which are silent or implied notes—require the greatest investigation because of the variation of the aforementioned proportions; and also the signs indicating the velocity or slowness, the duplicity or triplicity of the notes. Concerning all these things, although I spoke briefly in my 4th book, yet...

->ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE<-

The whole mystery of musical timings cannot indeed be contained within a single volume. And without a doubt, since this vocal and instrumental music is a kind of image and shadow of that true Music which thunders secondarily in the heavens, and primarily in the supersubstantial heaven itself (according to the divine sentiment of **Iamblichus** <note>original: "Jamblici"; Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the power of music and mathematics.</note>: *The soul in the intelligible world heard the divine harmony, which it remembers here when it hears melodies possessing a vestige of the divine; remembering it, the soul is vehemently affected toward it, if it is among the number of those souls that once especially contemplated the very idea of harmony in their homeland*), it is necessary to imagine that there is no variation in the music of the heavens where a variety of times is not also found, since the proportions of the intervals and the times are the same for both. And certainly, it will be hidden from no one versed in Astronomy that the motion of the stars is distinguished by number and time. Consequently, we say that if the true proportions of the celestial times and intervals are duly compared with one another, a vast understanding of **world harmony** <note>original: "harmoniae mundanae"</note> may be drawn and derived from them. For motion can never leave behind its companion, time. Wherefore it is certain that, just as **Pan** <note>In Fludd's philosophy, Pan represents the "Universal Nature" or the sum of all natural forces.</note>—or universal nature, whose act is the moving soul—is said to be the son of Chaos, so also Time itself is the son of **Eternity**, without which Pan cannot endure or move for even a moment’s space. From these things, it is clear that if Time and Interval relate to each other in this lower Music, it is necessary that they also observe the same relationship to each other in the heavens. For just as the **Octave** <term>Diapason: the interval of an eighth.</term>, the **Fifth** <term>Diapente: the interval of a fifth.</term>, and the **Fourth** <term>Diatesseron: the interval of a fourth.</term> are the harmonic intervals of artificial Music, so they also perform this same role in celestial things, and even in the **Archetype** <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original divine mind or blueprint of the universe in Fludd's Neoplatonic worldview.</note> itself. But truly, since no motion occurs from one interval to another (as from a starting point to an end) without time, it follows that times are found among the Planets themselves, in both unknown and known proportions. Therefore, we conclude—contrary to the intention of the author <note>Referring to Johannes Kepler.</note>, who estimated the investigation of times to be trivial—that the length and brevity of musical Time, or all its differences, require great investigation and are very necessary for the history of his own harmony. And therefore (as it seems to me), there is a very great error in the fact that he said nothing about Times or the length and brevity of sounds; and so the matter is far different than if the various dimensions of Time in length and brevity were merely arbitrary, for it follows that they require an investigation of their causes.

### TEXTUS VI.

> *He calls certain intervals "simple," which to me are the smallest discordant harmonies: the major Tone, minor Tone, semitone, and **diesis** <term>Diesis: An extremely small musical interval, smaller than a semitone.</term>. Others he wishes to be composed of these, which I call consonances. Yet I have expressly refuted this opinion of the ancients—that consonances are composed of smaller intervals as if they were prior by nature—in Chapter IV of my third book, where I showed that, on the contrary, the smaller intervals arise from the larger consonant ratios.*

### ANALYSIS.

If I called the smaller intervals "simple" according to the opinion of the ancients, it was certainly not done without consideration; and when I said the larger consonances were composed of them, I did not do that without a cause of no small weight. For a whole is usually composed of its parts, a multitude from its smaller members (the unit of which is sound), a line from its points, and mathematical bodies from their plane figures (the origin of which is the Triangle), and later things from prior things. I shall strive to defend this assertion of the Ancients with irrefragable arguments below in its proper place, and I will attempt to refute the arguments brought forward by the Author. But truly, because in this context he calls the smallest intervals—namely the Tone and Semitone—dissonant and not consonant, it seems that the matter turns out quite differently. Experience teaches that the same tone of one string, corresponding to another by identity of proportion, is called a **unison symphony** <note>original: "Symphoniam unisonam"</note>. Wherefore, without doubt, the Tone is a consonant interval, although in another respect it can be called dissonant. Furthermore, we find that the space of the minor Semitone is the cause of the difference between "soft" or "round" song and "hard" or "square" song <note>This refers to the historical "soft B" (B-flat, depicted as a rounded 'b') and "hard B" (B-natural, depicted as a square 'b', the ancestor of the natural and sharp signs).</note>. Thus, if the sign for **B-flat** <note>original: "b. mollis"</note> is expressed in the bass at the position of **B-natural** <note>original: "B. mij" referring to B-mi, the hard B.</note>, it is certain that if the same sign is also placed in the same interval of the Tenor, it produces a most exact consonant voice. From this it is clear that since the Semitone makes a consonance with its voice, it is a consonant interval. But this is also clear in the pronunciation of the voice in different strings of B-natural: where if the flat is expressed on the second line of one melody and not the other, the sound will be dissonant and incomplete; but if the flat is depicted in both intervals, the agreement of both will be consonant. And for this reason, the smaller intervals can be called consonant as much as they are

# TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX.

### TEXT VII.

> *The remaining four books of the author possess a practical application, which I do not even touch upon. For in Book IV, he teaches regarding the measurement of the beat, its various modes, and the value of the notes through them; about which I have said very little in my Book III, chapter XV, and Book IV, chapter III.*

### ANALYSIS.

But who can be well-versed in Theory, when both his own confession and the evidence of his works confirm that he is ignorant of practice? For according to the opinion of the Ancient Sages, **"The truth of practice must confirm the truth of Theory."** <note>original: "Veritas praxis veritatem Theoriæ confirmare debet"</note> Next, he says that he dealt with a few things regarding the measurement of the beat <note>original: "tactus"; the *tactus* was the physical hand motion used to keep time in Renaissance music</note> and its various modes and the value of the notes in his own Book 3, chapter 15, and Book 4, chapter 3. Having read through these, I found very little indeed on this subject, and almost nothing relevant to the proposal. But even if this were true, why does he say—contradicting himself here in Text 5—that he has said nothing at all about the Times, or the length and brevity of sounds? Nor have I observed, through the whole thread of his *Harmonies*, any temporal notes besides the single Semibreve <note>the "whole note" of the period</note>. From this it is clear that he has utterly omitted all proportions of temporal measure, which were certainly very necessary to the very marrow of the work itself.

---

### TEXT VIII.

> *It contains the rules for composing figured song, an art which I do not profess. In Book VI, he even wanders into various musical instruments, about which I have not even thought; finally, in the seventh, he reveals a new instrument himself.*

### ANALYSIS.

I have said before that this <term>figured song: "cantus figuratus," or complex polyphonic music with varying rhythms</term> and its composition is, as it were, the idea and image of the higher harmony, of both the first and second kind. This we have confirmed with the words of the most wise **Iamblichus** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, and we can prove from many passages of the Holy Scriptures how, namely, because of its closeness to the Harmony of the Archetype and the Ideal, that music composed by **David** was not only pleasing and acceptable to the Creator himself, but was even able to soothe the rage and fury of cruel demons. And how much harmony it produces in the souls of men is found everywhere in the Divine Bible. Moreover, as pertains to the agreement of celestial Music with the earthly, we are taught by that perfection attributed to **Apollo**, and by the song with which **Mercury**, by means of his pipe, lulled the monstrous Argus to sleep; and Medea’s physical symphony, which put the most watchful barbarian Dragon to rest.

But the "vulgar astronomers" <note>Fludd’s dismissive term for those like Kepler who focus only on physical observations rather than spiritual causes</note> are not granted the ability to understand musical species of this kind. Hence it is no wonder if they lack the faculty for composing the formal and essential qualities of such songs; for they, relying only on their own opinions, believe everything that seems to be so to them, even if it is not. But those things which *are* but are *not seen*, they reject as impossible, mock them, and hold them for nothing. In this way, like **Aesop’s dog**, they choose the shadow while neglecting the substance; they take, I say, the color for the substance, and are deceived.

---

### TEXT IX.

> *In these four last books, therefore, he differs from me as a Practitioner from a Theorist: For instead of the fact that he hands down instruments, I inquire into the causes of things or consonances; and instead of the fact that he teaches how to compose a melody of many voices, I arrange mathematical demonstrations of those things which are naturally present in both Choral and Figured song.*

### ANALYSIS.

And yet, nonetheless, in the preceding books, he confessed in Text 3 that he agreed with me on the "bond of Theory"—namely, in the scientific progression of finding consonances. Whence he seems to acknowledge that I am as powerful in Theory as I am in practice. It will be no disgrace to me to be well-versed in both parts of musical science; and consequently, it is certain that he who is so disposed is more excellent and stands above one imbued with Theory alone by as many degrees as the whole is greater than its half. For, as we said before, **The truth of practice**

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s aggressive defense of his "Pythagorean" approach to music and the cosmos against Johannes Kepler. Fludd is arguing that abstract mathematical theory is useless without physical, practical application, and he is beginning to counter Kepler's mockery of the elaborate engravings in Fludd's books.</meta>

# ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE.

*Practice usually corroborates the truth of Theory.* <note>original: "praxis veritatem Theoriæ corroborare solet"</note> *But where he says that, while I merely hand over the instruments, he himself searches for the causes of things or consonances, I leave it to your judgment, O eminent readers of learning, how poorly this agrees with the assertion he put forward in the preface to his third book.* For he says in that place that Pythagoras discovered the differences of low and high sounds from observing the weights of hammers; by which he finally revealed the harmonic intervals of voices or sounds. Later, he adapted these intervals more precisely to the lengths of strings, because through them the ears are accustomed to judge more perfectly which parts of the string harmonize with the whole, and which are dissonant from it. Furthermore, he himself filled the first and second chapters of that book with fragments of this kind of business, where he even draws out the ratios of consonances from various proportions of unequally cut strings. And yet, having neglected the consideration of instruments, he says that he is searching for the causes of consonances. How empty and frivolous this is clearly appears, because **a string without an instrument is worth no more than a bell without a hammer.** 

And we have shown in our third book that all consonances, and even the smaller intervals of Music, are derived from the exact division of the <term>Monochord</term> <note>A one-stringed scientific instrument used to demonstrate the relationship between mathematical ratios and musical intervals.</note>—that is, from the proportional partitioning of a string stretched over its own proper instrument. He himself admits this throughout the entire second chapter of his third book. Furthermore, he acknowledges in chapter 3 of the same book that deeper sounds arise in longer strings and sharper sounds in shorter strings, provided they are stretched equally. Therefore, he cannot explain consonances—whether in heaven or on earth—by any better way than by the proportion of strings in size or length. For we know higher things by the relationship we hold toward lower things. <note>Fludd is invoking the Hermetic principle of "As above, so below."</note> For what mortal has ever entered the heavens and afterwards returned to earth so that he could reveal their mysteries exactly as they are there? But the sect of the most excellent <term>Astrologers</term> <note>In Fludd’s time, "Astrologer" and "Astronomer" were often used interchangeably for those who studied the heavens.</note> has its own heavens and planets even here on earth, by which they are refreshed in both body and soul through the vision of truth itself, walking on the right path with all false opinions cast aside. 

Next, he says that while I teach how to compose a melody of several voices, he constructs mathematical demonstrations. And yet he said previously in Text 4 that his intent was to open up the causes of natural things. But how much <term>Mathematics</term> differs from <term>Physics</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Physics" or "Physic" referred to "Natural Philosophy"—the study of the living, physical world—whereas "Mathematics" was seen as more abstract and removed from material reality.</note> I leave to the more shrewd judgment of the learned reader, since the latter deals with things in the concrete, the former in the abstract. Those best versed in Philosophy know that demonstrations of causes are made from what is similar rather than what is foreign, since like rejoices in its like. And this is why the Physicists, without the help of Mathematics, conducted their investigation of secondary causes through prior principles; nor indeed did they run from one art to another to complete that business. For among Physicists, that axiom is most celebrated: *It is done in vain through many things which can be done through fewer.* <note>A version of Occam’s Razor, suggesting that the simplest natural explanation is the best.</note> 

Hence, therefore, we think it must be concluded that, just as Mathematical Music needs mathematical foundations for its discovery of causes, so also does Physical Harmony. Indeed, the logic of all audible Music, and even the origin of the intervals themselves, looks more toward Physics by reason of its occult nature than toward Mathematics, if we rightly inspect its internal principle. For its secret consists in the physical division of spiritual matter—whether thick or thin—whose divider is the soul, the act of one singing or playing, whether it be in the <term>Microcosm</term> [man] or finally in the <term>Macrocosm</term> [the universe]. But because it would be too deep and difficult for the grasp of the ignorant to think this out, the Sages were accustomed to explain and open up the nature and motion of true physical substance by mathematical reasoning (since this kind of demonstration is more familiar to the senses), touching in this way the marrow of divine Music with geometric and arithmetic shadows. By these shadows, so great an error has now crept into the art of Music that, by dragging it out from the belly and bowels of Nature, they have placed it among the Mathematical liberal arts. And by this path we conceive only a vain shadow, or we look at the tunic or bark of Music, but we are ignorant of its interior essence or nucleus. This essence is nonetheless the same in man as it is in the world, the same in the elements as in the planets, and finally the same in those as in the <term>Archetypal world</term> itself, from which the Harmony of the entire machine originally arose.

## TEXT X.

->*Therefore also in his work there are very many pictures, in mine mathematical diagrams provided with letters.*<-

### ANALYSIS.

**H**ere indeed his "Therefore also" <note>original: "Propterea etiam"</note> ought to infer the cause of something: But of what? I certainly do not see it from the preceding text. For this is his preceding statement in the text immediately before: *And instead of him teaching how to compose a melody, I construct mathematical demonstrations.* Then his reason follows: *Therefore also in his work there are very many pictures.* And why? Because I teach how to compose a melody? As if that could not be done without pictures! Furthermore, we have seen that he himself uses infinite mathematical pictures almost through his entire first book, and specifically on page 58 where he depicts his five mathematical bodies <note>The five Platonic Solids which Kepler used to explain the spacing of the planets.</note>, and on pages 61, 62, 64. And in Book 3, pages 5 and 6, where he composes figures out of units, and depicts lines for strings through the whole second chapter of Book 3. And Book 5, with mathematical figures demonstrating his harmonic configurations; and again on page 180.

181.182. He repeats the representations of his own [mathematical] bodies along with other inventions: *on folio 186*, he expressly represents the handle or arc of the motions of the Planets according to his intention, along with others concerning the conjunctions of plane figures; he expressed the structure of planetary harmony according to <term>B-durum</term> <note>original: "b. durum"; a musical system using B-natural, typically associated with "harder" or major qualities.</note> on *folio 209*, and another for <term>B-molle</term> <note>original: "b. molle"; a musical system using B-flat, associated with "softer" or minor qualities.</note> on *folio 210*, and a mixed structure on *folios 211 and 212*. But indeed, if he says concerning these latter works that his structures or systems are diagrams furnished with letters, I answer this same thing for my own. For in **my fifth book**, where I teach how to compose melody on *folio 210*, you will find a Triangular system—a most exact mathematical diagram indeed, furnished with letters and figures—in which the secret of the measures not only of the whole system but even of the intervals is opened most exactly, along with the locations of the visible keys. This same diagram, furnished with letters and figures but constructed by another method, can be found on *folios 212, 217, 218, 220, 222, and 224*. Although some of these are described in the form of a Triangle, with three windows and a staff or rule—partly for the sake of ornament and partly so that the parts of my **Temple of Music** might be well perceived—they nevertheless pertain more exactly to the matter and are explained there with a better method than any of the Author’s <note>Kepler's</note> demonstrations could possibly shame. Therefore, these are mere words of the Author and marks of envy or poetic fictions, rather than carrying any real importance. And this same thing must be said regarding my entire mathematical work; in which, although I have introduced many pictures, the Reader can clearly enough perceive that they are all very necessary for the demonstrations of my propositions and should in no way be omitted.

As for the pictures found in my physical works, although they were not produced in a mathematical manner, I am certain they were arranged in a "physical" manner—that is, the manner by which my physical works are demonstrated—not without good reason. For just as he himself, in his **prior book**, delineated many propositions for the production and manifestation of his mathematical bodies and many demonstrations of plane surfaces from which the bodies must be composed, so I also have used physical (and not mathematical) demonstrations for the explanation of my subject. Nor does it matter under what form or figure they are depicted, provided they lead to the uncovering of obscure and uncommon things. And indeed, Johannes himself ought to acknowledge that this was not foolishly done, since his own words tend toward this: *“He himself is very much delighted by the dark enigmas of things.”* For if this is so, there will indeed be a need for visual demonstration to explain hidden matters. Finally, it is noteworthy that in this place the author enjoys praising himself; this would be more decent in a reader of the work than in the writer himself. For if every man were a judge for himself and in his own cause, he would leave no discrepancy between the extreme blackness of the crow and the intense whiteness of the Swan. I, for my part, most willingly commend what is mine to the fair judgment of the benevolent and learned reader, and according to his verdict, I shall judge the good or bad in myself and my works.

## TEXT XI.

> *See also how he is very much delighted by the dark enigmas of things, while I strive to bring into the light of the intellect things themselves wrapped in obscurity. That [obscurity] is indeed familiar to Chemists, Hermeticists, and Paracelsians; this [clarity] is the proper possession of Mathematicians.*

### ANALYSIS.

Indeed, I do not grasp the man’s meaning in this place; rather, I see that he has understood my mind poorly and in a manner contrary to what I intended. I, who desire to unfold the mysteries of the Ancients and strive to reveal the hidden in a natural way, am not found to "delight in dark enigmas" for this reason: because I have spontaneously undertaken to manifest to the world and make known to men what was long hidden and buried in the monuments of secret doctrine. Therefore, one must conclude that the Author, seized by excessive contemplation of heavenly things, is raving—or rather, is insane with a kind of logic—because of the instability of this opinion. Certainly, a certain man of sound mind from the same nation as Kepler, a most learned man and one far deeper than the Author himself in the inspection of natural things (known to me only through letters), reports these things in his writings sent to me: *“Who would not commend your singular skill in the investigation of things, where you recall, as if from the Garden, the true principles of things, which Hippocrates once treated through shadows and superficially in some places, and which Paracelsus treats today, etc.”* Another Doctor, a Frenchman also unknown to me, wrote to me in these words: *“You do indeed what most becomes a good man and a Philosopher, holding out to all a beautiful specimen of your genius, learning, and industry, etc.”* And another German Doctor wrote to me thus: *“Your writings are greatly approved by the inner cultivators of the more secret Philosophy; it will therefore be your task to bring to completion the rest which seem to pertain to the <term>Macrocosm and Microcosm</term> <note>The Hermetic concept that the universe (Macrocosm) and the human being (Microcosm) are reflections of one another.</note>, etc.”* And I could produce many other testimonies of learned men in this place, all of whom are far from Kepler’s opinion—namely, that my delight is to hide the mysteries of the An-

...or that I delight in dark enigmas. On the contrary, I have manifested hidden things to the best of my ability, even though my intention is not subjected to mathematical demonstrations—inasmuch as fictions are usually far removed from the truth. What then? That I did even more in that first Volume in detecting the mysteries of nature than was fair, or becoming of a good Philosopher. For it is found that all Philosophers participating in the divine mystery have praised silence and the concealment of secret science. **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> (whom he calls **Hermes**) calls his own silence a "fertile pregnancy of goodness." And **Apuleius** <note>A Roman philosopher and author of *The Golden Ass*.</note> says: *“Be silent, be silent, for silence is the safeguard of speech; spare it,”* he says, *“lest you bring some harm upon yourself by an intemperate tongue.”* How much weight the silence of **Pythagoras** carried (whom he [Kepler] wishes to follow in his invention of the regular bodies) is hidden from no one versed in Philosophy. Even in the sacred scriptures, we find the commendation of silence: For **Solomon** says in *Proverbs 25:2* <note>Original text cites Prov. 24, but the quote "It is the glory of God to conceal a matter" is Prov. 25:2.</note>: *It is the honor of God to conceal a thing;* and in chapter 12:23: *A prudent man conceals knowledge.* And hence it is that the Wise Man has hidden his secrets under parables or proverbs; and the disciples were admonished by **Christ** himself to be *subtle as serpents;* and Christ did not want *pearls to be cast before swine, nor the children’s bread to be thrown to the dogs;* and he commanded the disciples to speak to the Jews allegorically and enigmatically, *so that they might have ears and not hear, and possess eyes but not see.* If, therefore, my delight is in dark enigmas of things, why did I strive to reveal the physical secret and make it known to the world? How great was the love of the Ancient Philosophers and Theosophers for dark enigmas; indeed, how abundantly did **Solomon**, the wisest of all, and **Christ**, the Creator and Savior of all, and Divine Wisdom itself, abound in such a desire—since they recognized the world to be unworthy of such great gifts.

He himself [Kepler] seems to be a follower or an "ape" <note>original: "simia"; a common Renaissance term for a close or derivative imitator.</note> of **Pythagoras** in his choice of the five regular bodies <note>The Platonic solids, which Kepler used to model the distances between planets in his *Mysterium Cosmographicum*.</note> to establish his **Cosmographical Mystery**; and yet he refuses silence in secret science. From this it is clear that his "secret" is to be considered more in name than seen in reality. Indeed, it matters nothing if he does not hesitate to publish his mystery to the world—he who is ignorant of what the secret of Nature truly is. Nor does it matter, nor will it cause envy to those skilled in Philosophy, if he strives to bring forth things wrapped in obscurity into the deceptive light of his own imaginary intellect; since vain things most rightly suit vain people.

"That," he says, *"is familiar to the Chemists, Hermeticists, and Paracelsians; but this is the property of Mathematicians."* And rightly so: for it is the way of vulgar mathematicians to occupy themselves with quantitative shadows; while **Chemists and Hermeticists** embrace the true marrow of natural bodies. Such a natural Chemist was **Moses** himself, who extracted the substance of the entire world from the dark abyss—which **Saint Peter** then affirmed to have been water—and by physical proportions, and not Mathematical ones, he brought it forth into light, into regions and spheres distinct in degree by the power of the Word (whose office it is to strengthen the heavens): namely, into the **Empyrean heaven** called light, and into the firmament dividing the waters, and into the earth and the sea. > Gird up your loins like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. ...and yet the fertile mother of all qualities, motions, and things. Let the vulgar Mathematicians croak and babble about their "profound knowledge of nature"; yet men are to be known by their effects. For nature is the trophy of the fruit, which she herself becomes in the true Artist. By exquisite mathematicians who deal with **formal mathematics** <note>Abstract geometry and arithmetic divorced from physical or spiritual substance.</note>, Nature is measured and revealed naked; but by the spurious and faulty, she remains invisible and hidden. These latter men measure shadows instead of substance and are nourished by vain opinions; the former, having rejected the shadow, embrace the substance and rejoice in the vision of truth. 

We conclude, therefore, against the opinion of **Johannes Kepler**, that such a thing is familiar to vain mathematicians, nourished by a feigned imagination and opinion. Indeed, they look at mathematical bodies in such a way that they forget the truly natural ones. This is contrary to the ministers of true Chemistry, whose task it is to manifest hidden things, to extract nature submerged in opaque bodies, and to liberate the hidden light from the prison of darkness—as if from the abyss of ignorance—by breaking the chains. Finally, I would also wish it to be noted here that the Author [Kepler] strives greatly in this place to trumpet the praises of his own work.

# ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE
