### ANALYSIS.

From this context, we gather three things worthy of note: the first is an extraordinary praise of his own work, or rather of himself; which the Author <note>Fludd is referring to Johannes Kepler here.</note> seems to exalt both by exposing the errors of my subject and by showing contempt for ancient authors, as if his Harmony flowed from his own invention or was a virgin birth, proceeding as if from the brain of a fertile **Minerva** <note>In Roman mythology, Minerva (goddess of wisdom) was born fully formed from the head of Jupiter; Fludd suggests Kepler thinks his ideas are similarly divine and self-generated.</note>. Hence, he attempts to utterly remove and subvert the opinions of the Ancients, the Philosophers, and indeed even the Mathematicians; and then, in the final place, he tries to broadcast my ignorance and lack of skill to the world. As for what concerns me (to begin backward), first he attributes nothing to my own invention, but asserts that everything written by me was extracted from the ancients: then he proceeds in his usual way, and for the sake of increasing that "error" of mine, he says that *what I received from those authors, I used in a confused and incorrect manner.* Regarding his first assertion on this matter, we concede and acknowledge that the axiom of the wise is most true: *Nothing is said now that was not said before* <note>original: "Nihil est jam dictum, quod non erat dictum prius." A famous line from the Roman playwright Terence.</note>. And yet, something is occasionally added or fashioned for the sake of a better and shorter method: if the author himself denies this, the foundation of his own work will be found too fragile and subject to ruin.

Truly, in my **Technical Music** <note>Referring to Fludd's *Musica utriusque cosmi*, part of his massive work on the macrocosm and microcosm.</note>, I reduced the entire mystery of Music—indeed, everything that can be devised in Music—into a methodical arrangement within a temple, or rather a hieroglyphic image of a temple; an invention which no one until now has ever devised. If I have produced the testimonies and authorities of the best ancient Philosophers and Mathematicians for the harmony of this structure, I considered that this should turn to my honor and praise, rather than any reproach arising against me for confirming their testimonies. But when the Author says I used the sayings of those authors in a "confused and incorrect" way, we take these sayings of his as mere words and wind born of a **dog-like envy** <note>original: "invidia canina." A common 17th-century metaphor for a biting, relentless jealousy.</note>, since he can produce no instance of either confusion or incorrectness. He condemns me, but he is ignorant of the reason of truth in his own law: he praises himself, and conversely, I find no testimony of any praise for him. He seems to distort my musical proportions in the *end of his appendix* with confused words; and yet no mortal led by justice can (I know well enough) find any fault in the proportions expressed in my temple. Therefore, these are empty words and absurd voices; nor can he truly be a musician who suffers from such a vice of antipathy. 

But if this "confusion and incorrectness" alleged by him consists in a poor investigation of concordant causes (as he wishes), which he tries to correct in both the ancients and in me, refuting our sayings in that matter, we shall indeed see to it that he perceives with open eyes in the *reply to the following text* that the matter stands far differently than he thought, where I hope I shall pay him back in his own coin. 

As for what concerns the testimonies of Authors, it is indeed the custom of Philosophers to join the opinions of other Philosophers to their own reasons. Look then and see; the Author falls into **Scylla** while striving to avoid **Charybdis** <note>A classical idiom meaning to fall into one danger while trying to escape another.</note>, for while he accuses another of imitating the opinions of others, he himself incurs the very same error (if it be one); insofar as he acknowledges that he received the invention of the **5 regular bodies** <note>The five Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron) which Kepler used to model the orbits of the planets.</note> from Pythagoras in the *Preface to Book 1*; he follows the teaching of Copernicus regarding the motion of the Planets and the position of the heavens, *as is held in Book 5, chapter 3;* and in many other places: he praises Schoner and confirms and embraces his teaching in the *Preface to Book 1*. The opinion of Proclus is confirmed in his view that the perception of the 5 regular bodies should be transferred from the five elements to the Planets and their intervals. *And in Book 2, proposition 25* he says: *It seems agreeable to me that the teaching concerning the 5 bodies was the same, but hidden in the manner of a sect.* He acknowledges and follows Aristarchus of Samos; he extols the hypotheses of Tycho Brahe in *chapter 3, book 5.* And yet he boasts that he draws the matter of his Harmony from the nature of things, and establishes it from the very foundations, proceeding in a natural order so that all things are corrected according to the laws of nature and confusion is avoided: and so he says that he does not apply his conclusions to the whims of the Ancients. See, I pray, how inconsistent he is with himself in his assertions.

In the middle part of this text, he detects "confusion" in the teaching of the Ancient Authors and introduces errors to be corrected, which he says arise because of a variation of opinions. But I, in my technical Music, have followed the opinions of Pythagoras, Boethius, and **Guido** <note>Guido of Arezzo, the medieval monk who invented modern musical notation.</note>; whose views I prefer to follow and embrace rather than those of a man who, in true science, must be placed many steps behind them. And certainly, nothing is more certain than this: if Johannes Kepler had rightly understood the depth of Pythagoras and Boethius in the mystery of Nature, he would immediately cry out, forced by the truth: "I have sinned; my Astronomy is false, nor is there any other besides that unique one of the **Sages** <note>original: "Sophorum." Referring to the ancient masters of wisdom.</note>; my Harmony is fictional and imaginary; since I now see that there is but one and the same harmony of the world, composed of various resistances of bodies procreating diverse consonances, and this in the progress of Nature from imperfection to perfection." For it is most absurd to say that a regression occurs from the perfect to the imperfect; but always, according to the laws of nature, the imperfect tends by its own motion toward perfection. It is therefore rash of him to condemn these truly learned Authors before he correctly conceives the sense of their own words from their own minds, and not in his own fashion. He desires to avoid confused things, and by this very curiosity of his, he confuses himself; he chooses the worse and refuses the better. This, then, is the reason that he, exalted in his own conceit, condemns Peter Ramus in the *Preface to Book 1*, makes Aristotle’s exposition of the five proportions of bodies into something vain, accuses Pythagoras himself of error in his harmonic numbers in the *Preface to Book 3*, and exposes the fault of Ptolemy concerning the number of Harmonies and concordant intervals. Finally, in *Book 5, chapter 3*, he damns the ancient Astronomical Hypotheses of Ptolemy along with the theories of Purbach, and altogether...

Here, Fludd examines the first three books of Kepler’s *Harmonice Mundi* (The Harmony of the World, 1619), arguing that Kepler’s "harmony" is merely abstract geometry rather than the living, spiritual harmony of the universe.</meta>

# TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX.

suggests they should be rejected. Good God, what a sharp edge of genius is in this man! After so many centuries have already passed, he has crept into and penetrated the very marrow of the teachings of such great men, only to observe their "sins," so that he might finally purge the world of errors that have remained hidden for so long. Or perhaps the contemplation of the ancient world was so crude that before this time it was unable to see the errors in the Astronomy and Music of the Ancients.

But let us return to his own self-love <note>original: "philautiam," from the Greek for "self-love" or vanity.</note> and his vast "inspection" of nature. We find two impressions of this matter in this context; the first is: *I extract the material of my harmony from the nature of things, and establish it from the very foundations.* The other: *I proceed by a natural order, so that all things are corrected according to the laws of nature, and confusion is avoided; thus I do not even apply my conclusions to the decrees of the Ancients, except where no confusion follows.* Since he boasts, therefore, that in the books of his *Worldly Harmony* he has opened the sanctuary of nature, and found in it the true and natural harmony of things above all others—having pulled it from the womb and foundations of nature—it will surely be permitted to leaf through his books. We shall see if such a revelation of nature has been made there or not; similarly, whether he proceeds by a method and order so natural as to correct the "confusions" of other Authors.

He distributes his **first book** into geometric definitions and propositions concerning multi-formed surfaces with equal sides, which he calls "regular." With these, he makes a more ready entry into the composition of his "regular bodies," from whose proportions he seems to elicit his harmony. These flat figures, which he treats in *this book*, he makes either perfectly regular—in which all sides and angles are equal—and these he again divides into primary and radical, or "augmented." These augmented figures are those that exceed their own sides by continuing the non-adjacent sides of some radical figure until they meet; these he calls **stars** <note>Kepler was the first to mathematically describe "stellated" polygons.</note>. Or he makes them less perfect or "semi-regular," which vary in their angles even though the sides are equal, such as Rhombi. Here he reviews many degrees of knowledge pertaining to angular figures. He also has many propositions pertaining to the sides of the **Square** <term>Tetragon: a four-sided figure</term>, the **Octagon** (eight-sided), the **Hexadecagon** (sixteen-sided), the **Triangle** <term>Trigon</term>, the **Hexagon** (six-sided), the **Heptagon** (seven-sided), the **Dodecagon** (twelve-sided), and his **Decagon star** with its star, the **Pentagon** with its star, and other regular angular figures of this kind. Similarly, he treats the circle and its various sections, and here he ends that book. In it, we find nothing pertaining to the true Harmony of worldly Nature; instead, he makes a certain Geometric comparison between one angular figure and another. If this be "harmony," it is indeed "analogical" and so-called only by similarity, and not in truth—or rather, it is a **Mathematical and imaginary Harmony**, not a **Natural** one. Natural harmony should exist between the benevolent actions and the perfectly disposed passions of the **World Soul** <note>The "Anima Mundi," a vital spirit Fludd believed animated the physical universe.</note> with its material substance. It was never the intention of the Philosophers that natural harmony should consist of Geometric dimensions, because the active soul does not submit to visible measurement.

In the **second book**, he deals with the "congruence" <note>Congruence here refers to how shapes fit together to fill a space, like tiles on a floor.</note> of figures, which he applies either to a plane—making this either "perfect," when the individual angles of several surfaces meet at a point so that no passage is left and all meetings are similar (this is the congruence of figures of the same species), or "imperfect," where there is a similar mixing of figures of different species. Or he applies it to solids. This is "most perfect" when the angles of figures—whether regular or semi-regular—of the same species meet; or "perfect" but of a lower degree, namely when figures meeting at angles are of different species; or it is "imperfect" congruence when, other things remaining, a larger figure is found no more than once or twice. In planes, therefore, he says the Triangle agrees with the square; so also the pentagon with its star; the Hexagons also agree; thus the Octagon and Decagon with their stars, and the Dodecagon with its star, etc. In semi-regular bodies, he describes congruence in **Propositions 27 and 28**. Regarding the most perfectly regular bodies, he speaks in **Propositions 25 and 26**. And in **Proposition 25**, he describes those five most perfect and regular bodies <note>The five "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>, whose properties the followers of **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on geometry and Plato’s "Timaeus."</note> sang of so much.

And here he believes the force of worldly harmony consists; thus, this is the thrust of his second book. Here we see that this "harmony" of his, which he calls the congruence of figures, is just as imaginary as his "stars" are fictional, and removed as far as possible from Physical nature. Nor does he even understand the intention of Pythagoras and Plato in their mystical allusion to those five regular bodies.

In the **third book**, he deals first with the invention of Music, Pythagorean numbers, and the Pythagorean **Tetractys** <note>A triangular figure of ten points, sacred to the Pythagoreans as a symbol of the organization of the universe.</note> through definitions, axioms, and many propositions to inquire into the causes of musical consonances in his own manner. Similarly, he treats the invention of harmonic proportions from various sections of a string. He also treats harmonic means, the origin of fitting intervals (where he strives to refute the opinions of the Ancients), the sectioning of consonant intervals into fitting ones, the types of Song (**Soft** and **Hard**) <note>Referring to "Molle" and "Durum," the precursors to minor and major keys.</note>, the number of intervals in the **Octave** <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave</term>, the sectioning of the **Monochord** <term>Monochord: a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical ratios</term>, the composition of systems, "adulterated" consonances, naturally fitting song, the modes of melodies, and other things of this sort. Thus, in this book, we find nothing except mere "artificial" Music culled from the books of many ancient Authors; we find nothing of his own here, except that he delights in contradicting the reasons of the Ancients' invention of intervals. In these **three prior books**, therefore, the Author has neither extracted the material of his harmony from the nature of things (as he promised), nor established it from the foundations; nor has he proceeded naturally so that anything might be corrected according to the laws of nature to avoid confusion. Let us proceed, therefore, to his **4th book**. In that, indeed, before he reaches the full flow of the same subject...

<meta>This page continues the "Analytical Discourse" where Robert Fludd critiques Johannes Kepler’s *Harmonice Mundi*. On the previous page, Fludd questioned Kepler's claim to have discovered a new, "natural" harmony. Here, Fludd summarizes Kepler's distinction between sensible and archetypal harmony, his theory of planetary "aspects" (angles) affecting the Earth's weather, and his controversial idea that the Earth itself is a living "animal" with a soul. Fludd then begins his rebuttal, arguing that weather comes from the Heavens and the Sun, not the Earth's soul.</meta>

### ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE

...comes to pass, he divides **Harmony** into the **sensible** (that which is perceived by the senses) and the **secret and pure** (removed from sensible things). He says that for the consistency and being of the former, four things must concur: namely, two sensible things of the same genus and quantity; a **Soul** <note>original: "Anima"</note> that compares or distinguishes, or the reception of sensible things; and a suitable proportion, which he calls **Harmony**. Thus, he explains at great length that the existence of sensible harmony requires a **counting Soul**, without which number is removed; he also teaches how external things are received into the soul, and explains the degrees of actions and passions. He teaches, too, that this kind of harmony is in some way abstracted from things.

But the other species of harmony, which he calls **secret, pure, and insensible**, he names the **Archetypes** or **Patterns** <note>original: "Archetypos seu Paradigmata"</note> of sensible harmonies. He maintains that these Archetypal harmonies are divided and many in number, and says they require two "terms," namely either a whole circle or some part or parts of it. Here, therefore, he seems to remove all harmony except for **circular harmony**. Furthermore, besides these terms, he also requires a **Mind** for the existence of such harmonies; and there he recounts how the "species" (or forms) of mathematical things exist within the soul. He presents the differences between **Aristotle, Plato, and Proclus** on this matter, along with their doctrines, and other such things that argue for a relationship between this mathematical harmony of his and the mind or soul. 

He then proceeds to shape the faculties of the Soul according to these harmonies. And finally, he arrives at the main subject of this book, which seems to pertain to what he calls **secret and pure harmony**. He insists that the same proportions found in sensible harmony must concur in this secret harmony, though they differ in name. For what is called an **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> in sounds, he wishes to be called an **Opposition** <note>The astrological aspect where two planets are 180 degrees apart</note> in the radiation of planetary aspects. Similarly, in this, he compares **Vocal Music** with **Worldly Music** <note>original: "Musica mundana"</note>; for just as in a musical system a human voice or the sound of an instrument is either higher or lower, sharper or deeper, so too is **Meteorology** manifold. For it arises either from the joining of Saturn, or Jupiter, or another, or from the equinoctial or tropical signs.

This **celestial harmony**, which he treats here, he says is a harmony of **angles**, which consists in motion just as sensible harmony consists in sound. For he says these harmonies reside in the angles formed on the Earth by the luminous rays emitted by two planets. Therefore, he makes this harmony of the world "mixed" with respect to that truly celestial harmony (as he says) created on Earth by the two rays of two planets. 

Then he proceeds to the causes of effective **configurations** <note>The geometric relationships between planets</note>; where he first deals with the angles that two planets make on Earth with their radiations; likewise concerning the kinship and congruence of radiations; then concerning the degrees of **aspects**.
- The first degree he makes **Conjunction** and **Opposition**.
- The second, the **Square** <note>90 degrees</note>.
- The third, the **Trine** <note>120 degrees</note>, **Sextile** <note>60 degrees</note>, and **Semi-sextile** <note>30 degrees</note>.
- The fourth, the **Quintile** <note>72 degrees</note>, **Biquintile** <note>144 degrees</note>, and **Quincunx** <note>150 degrees</note>.
- The fifth and last, which he makes the weakest of all, the **Decile**, **Tredecile**, **Octile**, and **Trioctile**.

He makes the **Sextile** correspond to the **minor third** <note>original: "Tertiae consonantiae molli"</note> consonance; the **Quintile** to the **major third** <note>original: "tertiae durae"</note>; the **Square** to the **Perfect Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>; the **Trine** to the **Perfect Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; the **Sesquadrate** to the **minor sixth**; the **Biquintile** to the **major sixth**; and the **Opposition** to the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. 

He claims that by the power of these aspects making various angles on Earth, because of a certain **peculiar soul**, vapors, smoke, and exhalations, storms, and "meteors"—whether watery, windy, or fiery—are excited in the air. He says that natural changes occur in the waters and the Earth itself, which he therefore dared to call an **animal**. 

This is indeed the essence of his fourth book, in which he seems to touch upon one species of natural harmony with a needle's point (as it were). Let us see, then, if in this matter of harmony he agrees with the truth of the thing, and whether he draws it from the fountain of natural things or not; and whether he proceeds by the order of nature, so that confusion may be avoided. As far as the harmony of radiations is concerned, let us inquire whether that most exact order of nature is in it, by which he boasted he would avoid confusion and correct the uncorrected.

First, therefore, it seems likely that the radiation of two planets making angles on Earth is **not** the cause of storms or changes in the air; but rather a certain **hidden and admirable power of influence**, bending the air here and there according to its nature and appetite. Here, indeed, the Wise Man said not inaptly:

> that the air, going round by the conversation of the sun, hastens, and the air returns according to its circuits. <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 1:6, referring to the movement of the wind and sun.</note>

From this it is clear that whatever motions of the air exist, they are not excited to move storms because of some imaginary **peculiar soul of the Earth** by reason of angles made on the Earth, but because of the virtues of the **Solar spirit**, or rather of **Wisdom** acting everywhere, according to its dispositions in the heavens toward other planets varying in nature and motion, to which it gives light, life, and soul. 

Hence the power of radiations is primarily in the **air**, as if in the lower spirit of the **World Soul** <note>original: "animae mundanae"</note>, or the receptacle of its action, prone to this or that disposition of working—whether fiery, watery, or windy. For the soul and life of the Earth are rather **from** the air and **in** the air, than that the motions of the air (whether natural or accidental) should proceed from the Earth. For the air gives life to the waters, life to the earth, and life to all things composed of them. We see also that winds are born in the air (though where they come from is most difficult to know, according to the word of the Scriptures, even if Aristotle makes them the "sighs of the earth"). We see, I say, that they afflict the seas in various ways and excite storms in them, and violently tear down the mountains, rocks, and trees of the earth. 

Is it characteristic of a "terrestrial soul" to be so cruelly opposed to itself, and to destroy and tear apart its own members? Rains, also, snows, thunders, and Comets (drawn forth from the "treasuries of God" according to the doctrine of the Holy Bible) are produced and arise in the air. It escapes no one what slaughter and ruin these stir up upon the earth, as well as upon the sea. Therefore, it would be a foul thing if such damages to the Earth were derived from its own soul; but rather from the universal [soul] of the world...

### TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX

...that soul of the world proceeds; inasmuch as it is accustomed to float and act abundantly in its **airy vehicle**, as if in a passive medium best suited for its actions. This is even more the case if a likeness of itself rains down from the heavens; for that influence is stronger and more diverse in its action when it is fortified by two views and radiations in the air (which is the common receptacle for celestial influxes) forming an angle. And the earth itself, which continually breathes out via magnetic force, receives that spirit and sometimes retains it for a long time; insofar as all its empty pores are filled with air, retaining it like seed in a woman’s womb, where, according to the powers of the influences, various things are procreated in the earth’s belly—or rather, upon its surface. Do we not also see in **marble**, the hardest and firmest part of the earth, that the air itself, burdened with humid influences, penetrates that compact body? And that its internal salt, dissolved by this moisture, emits "copious sweats," which are signs of future rains? <note>Fludd refers to the common early modern observation that stone floors or walls "sweat" when the humidity rises before a storm.</note> Do we not sometimes see the earth itself as if choked and submerged by an abundance of rain, laboring as if from dropsy? <note>Dropsy, or edema, is an old medical term for swelling caused by excess fluid.</note> From where comes such a quantity of water, if not from the air, since the earth cannot give more than it has? Nor does it come from the sea, because its size is not diminished. To produce the **Flood of Noah**, not only *were the abysses of the earth widened, but also the floodgates of heaven and its windows.* <note>original: "terrae abyssus dilatata est, sed etiam cataractae coeli & fenestrae eiusdem" — a reference to Genesis 7:11.</note> Moreover, we have shown in our *Macrocosmic Treatise* that clouds and rain are gathered from the condensation of the air. We conclude, therefore, that in the lower kingdom of the world, **Air** is the spirit of life, whose soul is **Fire**, and consequently it is the immediate receptor of whatever celestial influences and radiations exist, which it later pours into the bowels of the earth. And hence the wiser Philosophers did not ineptly make Fire and Air the "acting" elements, while Water and Earth are the "passive" ones. Thus, it would be a terrible error to believe that the passive elements act upon the active ones more than the active upon the passive. Nor indeed are these angles of radiation **mathematical**, as the Author [Kepler] wishes, but **physical**, and similar to corporeal or truly substantial pyramids; insofar as two lights possess the airy spirit from the base all the way to the cone, just as we see in the flame of a fire or a candle. We say, therefore, that in the beginning *the Spirit of the Lord, which is the soul of the whole, moved and was carried over the waters*, <note>original: "Spiritum Domini... movisse & vectum fuisse super aquas" — reference to Genesis 1:2.</note> and not in the darkness or the earth; whence it is probable that the angles of visible rays were made in the air, and not in the earth. We shall examine his opinions concerning the earth a little further down, and now I shall proceed to the natures and harmonies of the radiations.

I perceive that he exceeds the limit of the ancient Philosophers in the number of radiations, so that he can stretch the business of his "aspects" <note>In astrology, an "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between planets.</note> almost to the boundaries of his intended **Harmony**. The ancients recognized only the **Conjunction, Sextile, Square, Trine, and Opposition**. He adds the **Semisextile, Quintile, Biquintile, and Quincunx**; indeed even the **Decile, Tredecile, Bisextile, and Trisextile**; so that he seems to establish more radiations than there are integral parts in his Archetypal Zodiac, to which, according to his opinion, these aspects are dedicated and assigned. But he said this so that he could make a comparison between the regular mathematical solids and these radiations, in order to attribute the same harmonic proportions and consonances to them as he assigned to the solids. He therefore gives the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> to the **aspect of opposition** [180 degrees]. This, it seems to me, is incongruously done; because the Octave is the most complete, perfect, and consonant of all harmonies. Yet, it is proven by effect how lethal and violent the actions of this aspect are here on earth; for in the opposition of the Moon with the Sun—and indeed of other planets, especially the malevolent ones—we perceive the greatest danger of disease looming, and the bells in the churches are by no means silent <note>A reference to the tolling of funeral bells during a plague or crisis.</note>; which is common knowledge in places suffering from the plague. Hence this aspect should be esteemed as a place of **dissonance and antipathy** rather than of the most perfect consonance and sympathy. If the other consonances compared to the aspects were duly examined, they would have no better flavor. Nor indeed do we estimate that Astrologers need more than five radiations; for from their diligent observation the greater changes of the world may be elicited. It is far too scrupulous to track and consider fractions and minutiae in which the discrepancy of things is so small and obscure, when it is established that those significations are included and contained within the major ones.

But truly, to descend to his opinions about the Earth, on page 158 he says: *Since the rays of the Planets always meet in the earth, rains then fall rather if the rays of two Planets make angles of 60 degrees than 59 or 63.* I answer that the rays of the Planets meet first in the **air**, where they receive their mixtures, and not in the earth. Whence clouds are generated in the air before rain falls into the earth's womb for the sake of bringing forth fertility; nor does the vapor of a cloud arise from the earth. On page 160: *There must be a Soul which, warned and as if excited by an aspect, stirs up meteors and storms, etc.* It follows, then, that this soul, which stirs the air according to a prescribed aspect, is here on the earth. We answer that there is no such "peculiar" soul—and much less one of the earth, which is most friendly to rest and consequently contrary to the action of a soul—but only the single **Soul of the World**, which, floating invisibly in the elements and the airy spirit as if in its own vehicle, creates alterations. For as man, the **Microcosm**, has only one soul to direct his body, so also the **Macrocosm** is governed by that one divine spirit which was carried over the waters, exhibiting a fiery power to them universally. For the soul of the air—which is no more divided from the soul of the Sun than a ray is from its source—produces various effects by celestial instinct, no differently than the heaven does by an Archetypal, divine, and ideal influx; for the word "heaven" corresponds to both air and ether.

# 18 ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE

...[whether it] be a humid vapor, or some other dry and fiery spirit bubbling and exhaling from the earth, etc. We utterly deny this assertion of his. For we say that the matter of the aforementioned meteors is formed in the most hidden bosom of the elements, or the divine treasury in the air—where they sometimes appear so visibly, though for the most part they remain concealed. What need is there for the opinions of the Heathens, or those who describe the hidden natures of things only through imagination and after-the-fact reasoning? I have read and re-read all their writings on this matter just as well as the Author <note>Fludd refers to Kepler here.</note>; and yet I did not emerge from them any more learned. Therefore, turning my mind and eyes to the fountain of all Wisdom, namely the Holy Bible, I found in them more certain indications of these secrets of nature. For in *Job 37:10* <note>Original: "Job 27.9," likely a transcription error for 37:10.</note> I read: *By the breath of the mighty God, ice is produced.* And in *Exodus 9*: *Jehovah sent rain with hail upon the earth.* And in *Psalm 147*: *God sends snow upon the earth like wool, etc. As soon as He breathes out His wind, the waters flow.* And in *Job 37:15*: *Do you know when God disposes the clouds, that the light of His cloud might shine?* And in *Job 38:22*: *Have you entered the treasuries of the snow, or have you seen the treasuries of the hail?* And in verse 37: *Who can number the sapphire clouds by wisdom, and who can tip over the water-jars of heaven?* And in *Job 36*: *Can a man understand the differences or the spreadings of the sounds of the clouds, and the thunders or the crashes of the firmament, or the pavilion of Jehovah? God thunders marvelously with His voice. When He commands the snow, it is upon the earth; or the shower and the rain, they descend upon the earth, etc.* Do you know where the way is by which the exhalation is divided, which scatters the wind over the earth? Similarly, when God sent His spirit so that the waters of the flood might be calmed and diminished, according to *Genesis 8:1*, did this wind proceed from the earth—even though he <note>Kepler</note> asserts that wind is a hot and dry exhalation? Surely this is impossible, because the entire dry force of the earth was submerged in the immense violence of the humidity. Indeed, the very soul of the earth, which he calls a flame, would undoubtedly have been drowned and suffocated by such a quantity of water, if any such thing existed.

From these points, it is clear that rains, showers, snow, hail, thunder, chasms <note>term: chasmata/chasms; early meteorological term for openings or "gaps" in the sky that appeared during auroras or lightning.</note>, and winds are drawn out from the hidden treasuries of Jehovah by means of the Word, and not from the earth as he foolishly imagined. For either the Holy Scriptures are false, or his assertions are adulterated, since the Scripture testifies that *the heaven is the best treasury of Jehovah, which by opening He will give rain to the earth in its time (Deuteronomy 28:12)*; and by closing it, *there shall be no rain on the earth to produce crops for the wicked (Deuteronomy 11:17).* Are the winds not also called in *Exodus 15:8* the *blast of the nostrils of nature?* Therefore, there are in the air so many and such great hidden mysteries of Jehovah that it is impossible for human wit to recount them. Indeed, this air is His life or lucid soul, with the spirit that constantly and continually penetrates it and makes it live. This air, when contracted, is nothing other than fire in water, or a thick soul agitated in such a spirit toward this or that motion—namely, fiery or watery—in manifold ways according to the will of Jehovah.

**Folio 160.** Finally, **the globe of the earth will be such a body as that of some animal; for as an animal has a soul, so also the earth has a soul, whose presence and aspects move the storms.**

I respond that the earth does have a soul, just as the soul of the whole is said to be in any of its parts; but not that it has a soul distinct from that of the universal world, which he himself placed in the spiritual sun, whose soul is Metatron. <note>Metatron is a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition, often identified by Hermetic philosophers like Fludd as the active intelligence or "soul" of the sun.</note> Furthermore, I would have him understand that the internal part of each thing is heaven itself, which operates by itself without the harmony of the Great Heaven. Thus we see fire burn and act without any compulsion from celestial aspects.

**Folio 160. The earth is an animal, not like a dog ready at every command, but like an elephant or a bustard prone to anger.**

To this assertion of his, we say that he proves by this very point—contrary to Copernicus’s opinion—that the Earth is not fit to be carried around in the space of 24 hours, since it is naturally so sluggish and slow to move. Finally, he runs off into many vanities to prove the earth is an animal by making comparisons between the hair of an animal and grass or plants; between lice and caterpillars or locusts; between tears and amber; between drinking and the absorption of the sea. He grants the earth the sense of hearing because a stone thrown into its chasms or deep holes usually makes a sound—not considering that this sound proceeds from the trapped air. It is also by the hidden power of this air that storms are said to be stirred up by the commotion of certain lakes. He even ascribes diseases and ailments to the earth due to rawness and the imperfection of its "digestion." To which we say: its soul must be very wicked and malevolent if it is accustomed to afflict its own body with such infirmities.

**He asserts that the ebb and flow of the sea proves the inhalation and exhalation of the earth.**

To which we say: the body of this animal is miraculous indeed, for it must take in more water in one inhalation than its own volume. **For it is no small dispute whether the sea or the earth itself is larger. Folio 163. In the earth, the soul (which seems to be nourished by respiration and absorption) is proof of a perpetual and sensible subterranean heat.**

We say that if this were truly the case, it would be a wonder how that flame could have resisted the invasions of the Great Flood. I acknowledge, indeed, that the Archaeus <note>term: Archaeus; a Paracelsian term for the "inner master" or vital force that governs the functions of a living body or the earth.</note> in the center of the earth performs the works of nature there in its own way, and that there is a central sun which operates there and fulfills its duty; but that this sun or that Archaeus is a fiery flame, I utterly deny—though Typhonian flames <note>term: Typhonian; referring to Typhon, the mythological Greek monster associated with volcanic eruptions and destructive winds.</note> are sometimes perceived to rise from the earth. These, however, are recognized by the Wise Philosopher to happen for far different reasons, just as a flame comes from a dense cloud or a spark from a flint.

**Folio 163. God has not only geometric patterns with Him, etc.**

We deny that lines or surfaces can be imagined in God, who is Unity; although number, weight, and measure were known to Him. But that measure does not belong to common Geometry, but rather to that purely formal Geometry which no one is permitted to know unless formal numbers and letters are known to him.

**Folio 163. Therefore, in the soul of the earth there shines a certain image of the sensible Zodiac circle, and thus of the whole firmament—a bond of sympathy between celestial and terrestrial things.**

We also affirm that the imaginary, or if you prefer, the ideal figure of the Zodiac—[mate-]

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s critique of Johannes Kepler. Fludd has just finished arguing that weather and "meteors" are products of divine breath in the air rather than mere earthly vapors. He now turns his focus toward Kepler’s astronomical theories, specifically attacking Kepler's use of geometry and his support for the Copernican (heliocentric) model.</meta>

# TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX.

...the ideas of heaven are imprinted as much upon the stars and every other element as they are upon the earth. Therefore, since the idea of the Zodiac reaches the air before the earth itself, it is necessary that the air—because of its easy reception of these influences—be stirred by them first, whether for good or for evil, and that it then pours those influences into the terrestrial matrix. Here, this air (which is expanded fire outside the earth, and contracted fire within the earth) hastens to bring the infused seeds to maturity. And so it is with the rest. From these things, it appears clearer than the midday light how he <note>Johannes Kepler.</note>, who condemns everyone except himself, poorly extracts the material of his "harmony" from the nature of things, and how he holds confused opinions that stand in need of massive correction. Is this, then, proceeding in a natural order, amending everything according to the laws of nature, and avoiding confusion? But now we shall turn the thread of our discourse to his final book.

In that place, he prepares those five Pythagorean bodies—namely the **Cube**, the **Tetrahedron**, the **Dodecahedron**, the **Icosahedron**, and the **Octahedron** <note>These are the five Platonic solids, which Kepler used in his *Mysterium Cosmographicum* and *Harmonice Mundi* to explain the distances between planetary orbits.</note>—and adapts them to the intervals of his celestial Harmony. For this reason, at the beginning, he deduces the kinship of harmonic proportions with those bodies. He makes the first of these through their characters in relation to one another; the second from their origin, such as 1:2, 2:3, 3:4, and 4:5; the third from the number of the sides of the planes compared with the number of the sides of the figure, such as the Cubic proportion 4:12 (or 1:3), the Tetrahedric 3:6 (or 1:2), and so on. Furthermore, he even compares the bodies among themselves; afterward, he approaches the essence of his harmonic subject. Since he included the chief matter of this in Chapter 3 of Book 5, we shall proceed to a brief analysis of it.

First, he urges the reader to utterly reject and remove from their mind and consideration the ancient astronomical hypotheses of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the proponent of the geocentric model where the Earth is at the center of the universe.</note>, as they were explained by **Purbach** <note>Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), an influential astronomer whose work updated Ptolemaic theory.</note> and others. He does this for the reason that they supposedly do not provide the true disposition of the bodies of the world or the "policy" of their motions.

I respond that it is by no means fitting for a wise man to give place to such persuasions rashly and ill-advisedly. First, because we have never found anyone in the whole world more learned and skilled in Astronomy than Ptolemy. Why then should we reject him, so that we might follow the new inventions of **Copernicus**, **Tycho Brahe**, and **Kepler**? These were extorted from the regular bodies of Pythagoras, and were by no means correctly conceived according to the opinions of Pythagoras and Plato. Should we follow them unless a greater probability of the truth declared that ancient doctrine to be erroneous—which, even now, we can gather from Kepler's own writings?

The opinions of Ptolemy and of all the ancient astrologers and astronomers—indeed, with few exceptions, even the modern ones—approved of eccentric and concentric motion in their own way. For this reason, they established the *Auge* <note>original: "Augem." This refers to the apogee, the point in an orbit furthest from the center.</note> and its opposite. They recognized the *Auge* and the circle carrying the planet <note>The deferent circle.</note> with its own axis and poles, and another circle carrying the planet itself with the axis and poles of the ecliptic. They made one axis for carrying the Sun, and another for the world. For the other planets, they assigned an **Epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note> with its triple axis—namely of reflection, declination, and longitude—and likewise the triple motion of that circle: Direct, Stationary, and Retrograde. Indeed, by these observations, they composed calculations for the motions of the stars and tables of approved certainty; they published learned *Ephemerides* <note>Tables giving the predicted positions of celestial bodies.</note> that were most exact regarding the motions of the stars, through which they predicted changes of time excellently, even to the hour and minute. And certainly, if this doctrine of theirs is as "spurious" as Kepler seems to proclaim to the world, it would be wonderful indeed that they could produce so many certainties in their observations of the stars' motions. Therefore, let the learned not rashly desert the foundations of Ptolemy, lest—out of curiosity for inventions that are worse and of less weight—they acquire a "frog for a good fish" <note>A Latin idiom similar to "trading a diamond for a stone."</note> and infect more excellent things with the vice of ingratitude and the rust of neglect and oblivion.

Let us see, therefore, what the "marrow" of this doctrine is. He makes the earth one of the planets and says, along with Copernicus, that it is carried among the stars around an immobile Sun. He confirms this Copernican opinion there through the hypotheses of Tycho Brahe, asserting that the earth moves around the Sun with a real movement of its body, walking a middle path between the outer circle of Mars and the inner circle of Venus.

I say, first, that it seems the Sun can by no reason be immobile because of the abundance of its light, which exists as more mobile than all things. For the duty of a true Form (of which kind light is) and an Act is first to necessarily act; then, it is fitting that motion follows its actions, because the effect of an act is motion. Thus, it is marvelous that the Sun, which moves all things (for he calls it the "fountain of motion" in many places), should be immobile, and that the old axiom of the philosophers should thus be confounded: *That which makes a thing such, is itself more such.* <note>original: "Quod facit tale, id magis est tale." A standard Aristotelian principle: if the Sun causes motion in others, it must possess motion even more so.</note>

But if he understands the Sun to be God Himself, I grant it. For God alone is He who moves all things and is not moved, insofar as He is outside of all things. Otherwise, it is necessary that the Sun—since its form is the effect of a divine act—moves other things in the same way it is moved by God. For it is a physical body, which is naturally mobile. As for the diurnal motion of the Earth, nothing more absurd can be devised. I have given sufficient arguments regarding this matter in my physical *Treatise on the Macrocosm*, where in Book 5, Chapter 15, I attempted to refute this opinion of Copernicus.

Afterward, let whoever wishes follow those prophets: Heraclides of Pontus, Ecphantus, Nicetas of Syracuse, Aristarchus of Samos, and finally Copernicus and Kepler. As for me, I shall choose **Job**, **King David**, and **Solomon** himself as my prophets. They expressly forge this opinion: that the Sun is mobile, but the earth is immobile. When these things are correctly understood, the foundations of the Author’s "harmony" will be easily destroyed, and consequently, it will be discovered that he poorly extracts the material of his harmony from the nature of things and from the foundations...

Then he says that it is most certain among all people that all the Planets revolve around the Sun, except for the Moon, which has only the earth for its center: however, this is something I have not grasped to this day. For I possess another, more intimate Astronomy <note>Fludd refers to his own "Mosaic" or mystical astronomy, which was geocentric—placing the Earth at the center.</note> that truly teaches me all these things: for I do not believe that all the celestial orbs and the earth itself rotate around the Sun; and I shall prove that holding the Sun as the center of the world is hardly consistent with the truth. Furthermore, he asserts that the eccentricity of a Planet is the change of its intervals from the Sun, which he makes the center; and there he provides a visual demonstration of the proportions of the intervals of one Planet from another. 

Next, he argues that the number of Planets or orbits around the Sun was taken by the most wise Creator from the **five regular solid figures** <note>The Platonic solids: Cube, Tetrahedron, Octahedron, Dodecahedron, and Icosahedron.</note>. He claims that when the angles of the **Cube** are applied to the innermost circle of **Saturn**, the centers of its planes almost touch the middle circle of **Jupiter**. When the angles of the **Tetrahedron** <note>A four-sided pyramid.</note> rest upon the innermost circle of **Jupiter**, the centers of the Tetrahedron's planes almost touch the outermost circle of **Mars**. Likewise, when the angles of the **Octahedron** <note>An eight-sided figure.</note> rise from any circle of **Venus**, the centers of the Octahedral planes penetrate and descend deeper below the outermost circle of **Mercury**, yet do not reach the middle circle of Mercury (for he assigns three circles to every Planet, giving the Planet's eccentricity to the middle one). Finally, he claims that by the proportions of the **Dodecahedron** <note>A twelve-sided figure.</note> and **Icosahedron** <note>A twenty-sided figure.</note> orbs, being equal to each other, the proportions or intervals between the circles of **Mars** and **Earth**, and between those of **Earth** and **Venus**, are the closest of all, and these are equal to each other. Briefly, he makes the **Cube** and the **Octahedron** a pair, and likewise the **Dodecahedron** and the **Icosahedron**. 

We ask therefore—since the Author speaks so confidently that the number of planetary orbits was taken by the most wise Creator from these five bodies—that he provide testimony of this matter from Holy Scripture, since the fabric of the world is found therein with the greatest exactness. Upon these proportions of regular bodies, he then seems to build the consonances of his harmony. Hence, to **Saturn** and **Jupiter**, the ratio 1:2—that is, the **Diapason** <note>The interval of an Octave.</note> consonance—is attributed by him, related to the cube. But he makes the specific proportions of the extreme motions of Saturn and Jupiter 2:3, roughly a **Diapente** <note>The interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note>. To **Venus** and **Mercury**, he attributes a greater harmony of 1:4, because, just as the Cube is the first of the primary figures, so the Octahedron is the first of the secondary figures. And so it goes with the rest. To these he adds many rules concurring with this fictional, or rather highly analogical, doctrine; it would be far too long to review all of them here. From these, a wise man may see how far these inventions of the Author are from the true foundations of Philosophy, which he himself promises to follow with such effort and such exact order of Nature; about which he is clear in his final comparison of harmonies with one another. But now we shall hasten to his invention of fitting intervals.

### ANALYSIS.

This, then, is the controversy between him and the Ancients: namely, whether the smaller intervals, such as the **Tone**, **Semitone**, and **Diesis** <note>The "Diesis" is a very small interval, smaller than a semitone, used in ancient Greek music theory.</note> (which he calls "fitting"), are the simple elements from which—as if from causes, elements, or principles—the consonant intervals or major consonances arise. The Ancients affirm this; but **Johannes Kepler** denies it, and in Chapter 4 of his 3rd book, he attempts to refute their assertion with specific reasons. 

In reaching a solution to this doubt, he seems to propose this question: is there a minimum element common to all "fitting" and consonant intervals, like a simple unit, from which—when taken according to a certain number—any of the consonances and fitting intervals might be composed? This he utterly refuses to admit. The sole reason brought forward by him is of this kind: If the individuals of all species that differ in size consist of one common minimum, there would then be some minimum quantity of the human species; of which a certain number of midgets <note>original: "pusionum", meaning manikins or tiny units of a person.</note> would compose any man, as if from elements—a tall man from many, a dwarf from few. For in harmonics, that quality of "Consonance" informs the proportion of strings or the interval of voices no less than the human form informs that mass of matter which is enclosed by a man’s skin. 

Similarly, he cites a comparative reason from examples of incommensurable quantities <note>Quantities that cannot be measured by the same whole unit, like the diameter and circumference of a circle.</note> in Geometry of every kind, making a relationship between those and incommensurable intervals. From this, he then infers that consonant intervals are prior in Nature to the smaller intervals, which he calls "fitting"; and consequently, he argues that the former are not composed of the latter as if from elements or from some smaller quantity, but rather the reverse. He says that he does not take "composition" here to mean a quantitative division of a thing, but rather its natural origin; just as the limbs of a man did not exist before the body, nor was the body collected from them like a house from stones. Accepting "composition" in this way, he denies that consonant intervals are composed either of other consonances or of the "fitting" smaller intervals. He argues there that, although the causes of consonant intervals are related, they do not have the same cause, but different ones, insofar as each has its own distinct, proper cause. afterwards, that melodic <note>original: "concinna"</note> intervals arise from consonant intervals, and not that consonances arise from the addition of melodic ones. This, then, is the force of his arguments, by which he intends to prove that the smallest intervals flow from the largest in a natural order; and consequently, he teaches that these smallest intervals are by no means simple, but rather born from the simple. But I, adhering closely to the opinions of the ancients, shall not hesitate to refute this opinion of his—first by the way of Arithmetic; then by reasons drawn from the principles of Geometry; and then finally by the very principles of natural things. Lastly, I shall turn the force of all my arguments toward a musical examination of consonance.

First, therefore, to draw the thread of the discourse to Arithmetic, we see that according to a certain order of nature, its **unity** <note>The number 1, viewed by Fludd as a divine or fundamental starting point.</note> is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers, containing within itself every number however large, yet devoid of all multiplicity, always the same and immutable. Whence this unity, multiplied by itself, produces only itself: for it is its own root, square, and cube. It is therefore the beginning and end of all things. From the progression of this unity, the number **two** is produced in the first place, thus 1 1; in the second, the number **three**, thus 1 1 1. From this it is clear that the number **seven** (for from that many smaller or melodic intervals is the consonance of the **Octave** <term>Diapason: the interval of an eighth, considered the most perfect consonance</term> composed) will stand thus: 1 1 1 1 1 1 1. And so it is established from this that its origin—namely, the smallest element of the number seven from which it arises—is unity. Consequently, the same logic applies to the origin of smaller consonances, namely those consisting of 3 or 4 intervals. For we do not say, following the order of nature, that 1 proceeds and arises from the number seven as a principle, nor from three, nor finally from four. It is vain to imagine this in a natural progression toward generation—that is, in a progress from the prior to the posterior. But this can be said in the flow from composition to the dissolution of the whole compound into its original parts, of which unity is the source; that is, in a regression from the posterior, from the point of the end toward which, to the Prior or the starting point from which. We respond, therefore, to his prior reasoning: that formal physical unity, along with its material likeness as the smallest part, is the primary cause of an individual of the human species, which increases in its progression or diminishes according to the greatness or smallness of its mass. But as for why the soul of one is more active and another more dull, this does not happen on the part of the form (which is always the same), but from a more fit or sluggish preparation of the matter. Thus, the same fire is observed to act differently in a damp medium than in a dry one, in a melancholic body than in a sanguine one, in iron than in wood; and yet it is always the same thing, and in its form is no more changed than the source of light itself from which it proceeded. Similarly, against his assertion where he says that the causes of consonant intervals are related but not the same: it is clear from these points that in Arithmetical consideration, that smallest element is the original unity, which is the source of numbers and the origin of progression, proceeding from the starting point to the end, both in concrete unities (which are partly material and partly formal) and in abstract ones.

In Geometry also, the proportion of progressions is the same; namely, from the **point** to the **line**, from the line to the **triangle**, and from the triangle to other plane figures, from which one finally arrives at solid bodies. We say, therefore, that in Geometry the natural progression is from points to lines, which are nothing other than a flow or continuation of points. From these it is certain that the point is in Geometry what unity is in Arithmetic: by whose progression and multitude the line or that **string** <note>Fludd refers here to the string of a monochord, the primary tool for measuring musical intervals.</note> is made, by the division of which various intervals arise, differing in kind from one another. And just as in the composition of a line, the line itself is known to be greater the longer the flow of points is from its starting point; so also it is clear that the larger the consonant intervals are, the more deeply they immerse themselves into multiplicity. But truly, it was not so wisely said (as it seems to me) that points are derived from lines: for this would be to extract principles from the things they produced, which would surely happen contrary to the order of nature. Similarly, to proceed to more manifest Geometrical unities, we see that the constitutive parts of a triangle are lines: which lines again are usually distinguished into their sections or roots. Therefore, just as that triangular figure <note>original: "trigonea"</note> is prior by nature (that is, the principle of all other Geometric figures, from which as a principle the four-sided, five-sided, six-sided, and all other figures arise), so also all other figures are resolved back into it. Hence, as God, the principle of all, is compared to a **point** by the Wise, from whom all things proceed and into whom all return; so the **Triangle** is compared to the **Holy Trinity**. For the point is considered by itself and in itself without dimension; but the triangle denotes its properties in the measurement of the world. We can, therefore, most rightly compare the **Whole Tone** <note>original: "Tonum"</note> to the line. From lines the Triangle arises, which is the origin of all Geometric figures: for, unless the **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron: a musical interval spanning four scale steps</term> flowed from two proportions or longer lines and one shorter one (the Tones or lines), it would be impossible to arrive at the **Fifth** <term>Diapente: a musical interval spanning five scale steps</term> with its greater or lesser part, no less than reaching a square without the mediation of a triangle. From which it is evident that the Tone, related to the line, is the manifest principle of consonant intervals, the largest dimension of which is the **Octave**. After this progression, one arrives at the secondary ratio of composition; just as the hidden principle relates as a point to a line, in whose progression from the primordial point toward the lengths of the **Semitone**, the **Comma**, and the **Diesis** <note>Extremely small musical intervals used in tuning theory.</note> and other insensible intervals are derived. ### ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE

...sounds are produced, and not in the reverse order, as Johannes taught. But now we shall proceed to a deeper speculation of his **Cube**. The Cube, he says in Book 5, Chapter 1, is the outermost and most expansive, because it is original and holds the logic of the whole. And this seems to be the reason for his discovery in the production of melodic intervals <note>original: "concinnorum"</note> from consonances. And yet he knows very well that the Cube originally flows from the **Square**, and the Square from its root, which is the **Line**. For who, well-versed in Geometry, ever doubted whether a mathematical body arises from surfaces, as those do from lines, by the motion and order of nature’s consensus? For from two things—namely **light** and **water**—the four elements were produced by a double action; from the duplication of these, in turn, the Cube (or the composite made of the elements) came into the light. From this, Aristotle most rightly applied the Cube to the element of **Earth**, because it is more heavy, ponderous, and composite. 

We conclude, therefore, against Kepler's assertion: although consonant intervals may arise from Geometry, it does not follow that melodic intervals emanate from consonances. And thus it is clear that the Author himself, contrary to his promise, does not proceed in a natural order to amend all things according to the laws of nature so that confusion might be avoided—as will appear more clearly from the following reasoning. For we assert that, although the Cube is called "most expansive and original," this happens for a different reason than our present purpose, as shall be declared below.

We also draw from the pure fountain of Nature, by way of inquiring into the mystery of sounds and the voice, that **sound** is a certain multiplication of the "identity" of sound proceeding from a starting point to a goal. It is such that from the point of the striker to the goal where the voice tends, there is surely a progression from unity to multiplicity. 

For example: in **thunder**, we see the form emitting the noise is a fiery force leaping out from a cloud as if from the fountain of a moving soul—just as the voice of a living creature proceeds from the tabernacle of its soul. Or consider the crack of a **cannon** <note>original: "bombardæ"</note> from its mouth: where the fire is the moving form, the gunpowder is the matter receiving the force and violently pushing the medium, and the airy spirit itself, torn and divided, gives the crack and the sound. For the air resists the fiery power because of its own moisture; through this resistance it suffers, and by its "passion" <note>In the philosophical sense: "passion" refers to the act of being acted upon by an external force.</note> it emits a voice. 

It follows, then, that in sound, there occurs a "numbering" of the voice from the striking form to the limit of hearing. This numbering or motion occurs from the chaining and flow of "airy atoms" in a physical or concrete medium, just as the continuation and measurement of a line occurs from the flow of points in a mathematical medium. 

But truly, the **form** of the air itself is always the same and continuous with the **Universal Soul of the World** <note>The "Anima Mundi," a concept Fludd championed, suggesting a single spiritual essence connects all physical matter.</note>; no part of which can truly be divided from its whole, even if, due to the diversity of the subject in which it dwells, it is said to differ in relation to us. For indeed, not even a single ray of the **Sun** itself is ever separated from its body: for the soul of the whole is unique, the same, and entirely indivisible in itself. And this is indeed the sentiment and opinion of all the wise. 

But now, because this formal essence fills every part of the air, the air itself—if it is struck by a strong force—tends to react and resist by the power of its hidden form. And so it suffers a "fissure" or resistance in one part, and the striking force, by gradually reverberating, emits a sound, as can be seen in an **Echo**. Thus we see that a pipe emits a voice from breath alone, and a strike made upon the air with a wooden stick likewise gives a sound. And although the soul or form of the air is indivisible, yet the substance of the air—which is "subtle water"—is divided into the smallest parts, just as water (which is "thick air") is divided into drops. Through these drops, sound is "numbered" in the air, not unlike how a line is numbered through points.

Hence it happens that, just as a very small body requires a very small use of the universal form, so too a slight impulse gives a slight and brief sound, because it urges only a small portion of air; and vice versa. Furthermore, where there is greater resistance—either by reason of the thickness of the medium numbering the sound, or by reason of the thickness and bluntness of the substance striking the air—there the voice is rendered **heavier** <note>low-pitched</note>. But where the medium is thinner and the striking substance is sharper, there the voice becomes more **acute** <note>high-pitched</note>. 

Thus a sword penetrates the air more easily because of its edge than a stick, which is blunt; consequently, the stick cannot penetrate the air as easily, and for this reason, it renders a heavier and deeper sound. From this it follows that, just as a large stick emits a blunt and heavy noise when striking the air, so very small rods make sharper sounds, because the medium with its form does not resist as much. By a similar logic, two rods of the same size but unequal in length will produce the same effect relative to each other as a large and a tiny rod compared in their striking of the air. The reason is that a thicker and blunter rod pushes the same portion of air as a very small and subtle one; for the long one has as much air to resist it because of its length as the short one has because of its thickness. So too we see a thin but long string sound as heavily as a larger, blunter, and thicker string of shorter length, as we observe daily in the use of the **Lute** <note>original: "Barbiti," referring to the barbiton or a similar large stringed instrument.</note>.

With these things observed, we shall hasten toward the natural logic of finding consonances. From the aforementioned experience with rods, it will be very easy to divine how the various **hammers of Pythagoras** <note>A famous legend where Pythagoras discovered musical ratios by listening to hammers of different weights in a blacksmith's shop.</note> emitted sounds proportional to one another. The proportion of one in size or weight to another was as 12 to 6 (or 2 to 1); of another, as 8 to 6; and of a third, as 9 to 6. Here the proportions of **double** <note>the octave</note>, **sesquitertial** <note>the fourth, 4:3</note>, and **sesquialter** <note>the fifth, 3:2</note> are found, constituting the consonances of the **Octave** <note>Diapason</note>, **Fourth** <note>Diatessaron</note>, and **Fifth** <note>Diapente</note>.

From these things it is clear that, since the material of the small hammers was the same—namely iron—the proportion of their difference was in their size, which in this respect was the same as their weight. We say, therefore, that the smaller hammer made a smaller fissure in the air; whence the air, compressed against the anvil, leaped back in reverberation and, in the manner of an echo, emitted a sharper voice, because the opening or dimension of the instrument penetrating the air was...

Having previously discussed the mathematical origins of intervals, Fludd now transitions into a physical and geometric explanation of how sound is produced through the "fissure" or tearing of the air, using the famous experiment of Pythagoras’s hammers as a starting point.</meta>

...sharper than the others; even the middle-sized hammer <note>original: "marculus"</note> gave a deeper sound than that first one, because it made a wider fissure in the air than the previous one. Finally, the largest hammer produced the deepest sound because it made the air gape more widely and divided it with a greater strike <note>original: "pavore"; here referring to the violent displacement of the medium</note>. Furthermore, a larger hammer tends to penetrate the air more deeply by its own gravity than a smaller one, owing to its weightier action upon the air. Indeed, this proportion in the perforation of the air is best discerned in a war engine <note>original: "tormento bellico"; referring to a cannon</note>. For the wider its orifice is, the lower is its sound; it penetrates more deeply into the aerial medium, and the sound is heard from further away. 

That there is also a multiplication and resistance in the air's substance during the production of a voice—that is, that a sequential numbering <note>original: "numeratio"; the idea that sound moves in discrete, countable steps through the medium</note> and division occurs in infinite small portions, and that likewise the form of the air is continuous and not divisible—is evident in thunder. In thunder, because of the continuity of the visible fiery form in the cloud with that which is invisibly expanded everywhere through the air, the light of the lightning is perceived suddenly without any resistance from matter. Yet, because of the "numbering" of the air, which requires time, the crash reaches the ears much more slowly. 

Just as we see in the natural composition of iron or hammers an addition of parts of iron, by which they are reduced into one larger mass to produce such consonant sounds, so too do the smaller consonant parts require this for their perfection. For if that which produces the sound behaves according to the natural proportion of its composition, it is necessary that the result also behaves in that same way. For as is the dimension of the string, such will be the proportion of the sounding air in all things; as is the hammer, such is the response of the aerial form to the impelling force; as is the rod, such is the voice. Indeed, the universal form of the air conforms itself to the resistance of the form of the instrument attacking it. Thus, with force resisting and attacking force, the moist medium—suffering their powers, namely the action and the resistance or reaction—narrates and clearly indicates them by the "mouth of nature" adapting itself to any proportion. This is not unlike one human speaking to another; in that moment of responding to one another, they both perceive each other's will unanimously through the virtue of the resonant medium.

But now, to approach the mystery of the consonances of strings, we say that their proportions in Music do not differ from those we have related before. For although a hammer and a cannon make a fissure in the air that is not long but wide—that is, not so much linear as superficial <note>i.e., having surface area</note>—nevertheless, as we see in Geometry, a parallelogram of this kind <image-desc>rectangular box symbol</image-desc> does not have more area or capacity than a square <image-desc>circular symbol</image-desc>. <note>The text says "quadratum" (square) but the OCR indicates a circular symbol; Fludd often equates the area of different geometric shapes to show proportional harmony.</note> 

So also the length of a string will occupy no more in the dimension of the air than the plane of a hammer or the roundness of a bombard <note>a type of early cannon</note>. Furthermore, this is the reason why, between two strings where one is very thick and the other thin and small, the thick string sounds as deep—because of its wide command in the air—as that small string stretched to double or triple its length, even if both strings are extended to the same measure. For example: <image-desc>line symbol: |,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,|</image-desc> and <image-desc>line symbol: |,,|</image-desc> which occurs for the reason stated above; namely, that as the string is, so also is the fissure in the air. Thus, a wide but not very long fissure will equal one that is much thinner but much longer in the same air.

Having perceived these things in the physical consideration of sounds, I now descend to the origin of consonances. Just as we said a measure is made in a mathematical line from point to point, from the beginning of the line to its end, so too is the reason similar and the same in a physical line. However, the physical line behaves differently than the mathematical one; while the latter is imaginary and in the abstract, the former is real and in the concrete. Indeed, through the crash made by thunder, we have declared how a real numbering of motion occurs from the place from which to the place to which—or from the cloud to the earth—that is, a multiplication of real or physical units in the air from the starting point before the voice passes to the ears of the listener. 

We have said that the form carrying the sound is that universal and most occult essence of the mundane sea <note>the *anima mundi* or world-soul</note>, which is never divided in itself, though it appears to be divided according to the division of the matter in which it exists. We say, therefore, that in any sound made in the air, a triple motion occurs: namely, in length, width, and depth. The proportional shape of the agitated instrument creates the length or width; but the depth is adapted by the power of the impelling form. If this form is greater and more vehement, it penetrates more deeply; if smaller, it remains superficial. In each of these motions, there is a progression from a single Physical Unit, which is the starting point. But the strike <note>original: "plaga"</note> in length and width is the cause of the proportion of consonances; its depth, however, is the cause of either a longer continuation of the sound or of the sound being rendered more sonorous and distinct. 

Since it is certain that there is no real line in which a Geometric surface is not found, it is obvious that every material string contains within itself a parallelogram, either larger or smaller according to its greater or lesser density. From this it is manifest that, just as a surface in Geometry has its origin from lines, and a parallelogram first from triangles and then from lines (from which every square is generated in mathematical order), so too all those motions concurring for the natural production of the voice—designating such physical figures and lines—take their principle from prior units, from which every motion flowed as if from a starting point. 

Since every proportion of intervals is measured by motion, and every motion is measured by number, and every physical number is a real unity (just as a drop is held as the unit of water), the air is distinguished into atoms as its smallest quantities, just as a line is distinguished by points. Furthermore, just as water has its lines from the chaining together of drops, and air from the progressive congregation of atoms—from which again surfaces and bodies compacted from them arise (that is, the triple physical dimension)—so we say that in every striking of the air, motion occurs; because from a smaller...
