# ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE.

...multitude, and as if proceeding from one smallest element until, through multiplication, a progression toward a vast number is made. In that motion, therefore, from which a consonance is brought forth, let the measure of motion in the air be the same as the measure in the substance of the string that generates that motion. But indeed, that string, in its natural growth from smaller to larger, had its progression in the belly of an animal; and thus we also perceive hemp <note>original: "canabim"</note> growing taller every day, so that all progression in generation occurs from the smaller to the larger. Why, then, should it be doubted that in consonances—presented through physical consideration—the progression occurs from smaller to larger rather than from larger to smaller? 

We say, therefore, that in the measurement of the Octave <note>term: Diapason. The interval of an eighth.</note>, the Fifth <note>term: Diapente. The interval of a fifth.</note>, and the Fourth <note>term: Diatessaron. The interval of a fourth.</note>, the motion in the air must be considered from the starting point to the end point—that is, from the beginning of the Tone to the end of the measure of five whole tones with two Semitones for the completion of the Octave consonance. In this motion, the transition first occurs through all the intervals of the scale <note>original: "concinnæ"</note>, through the Schisma <note>a very small musical interval</note>, the Comma <note>another tiny interval used in tuning</note>, and the major and minor Semitones, before the completion of one Tone is reached; and thus, through the multiplication of the air, one proceeds to the goal of perfect consonance. In this motion, although the air is divided, nevertheless the acting form <note>the spiritual or organizing principle that Fludd believes shapes matter</note> within it is always the same, adapting itself proportionally to both the larger and smaller consonances. For it is ready to act in proportion to the part of its medium or vehicle that is urged to undergo the action. 

Furthermore, do we not see among the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicos"</note> that all things are composed from their principles as if from parts, and not as smaller things from larger? Yet John <note>Johannes Kepler</note> says that the internal cause of every consonance is diverse and distinct. This assertion of his is indirect, since the same acting form is in one proportion as in another, no differently than the same breath of a flutist is accustomed to produce various consonances in a pipe. Nothing is indeed less consistent with truth than that the Octave consonance—compared to God himself because of its extreme perfection—could be the principle of either imperfect consonances or incomplete intervals, which are even more imperfect when compared to the complete consonance. For who, being consistent with himself, would try to elicit imperfect things from the more-than-perfect? Either the Octave consonance is completely perfect, and then it has no imperfection in itself, or it is not completely perfect, and then perfection is wrongly said to be in a higher degree. 

From these things it is clear that, just as maturity proceeds from rawness, so perfection proceeds from imperfection. For this is the continuous action of nature: to lead the imperfect to the goal of perfection. Indeed, the true progression of nature is to make a thing that is obscure and tainted by raw darkness into something pure, formal, and lucid, like the Sun itself. For he who knows how to elicit a brighter Sun from the imperfect than is this celestial Sun, he will perfectly understand what the truest Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> of the worldly Harmony is; he will look with open eyes from imperfection toward the goal of perfection, and he will find the numerical progression from formal unity into the multitude of matter, and again the reduction of that same multitude back to unity. 

For thus was the world made: namely, from the one into the multitude; and so also by transfiguration, it shall be changed in the end so that it returns to the one. Such a man, therefore, will truly deserve the name of Musician; and such a man will obtain a clear insight into divine Astronomy, the most certain of all things. To him, neither the positions of the stars, nor their motions, nor the reason of the seasons, nor the order of times shall be hidden, but with the spirit of wisdom as his guide, he shall be directed on the certain and infallible way of knowledge.

### TEXT XIV.

> *Let us pass to another passage of the author, where he introduces Music into the world. Here, indeed, the difference between us is immense. First, those harmonies which he intends to teach are mere Symbolisms, of which I say the same as I do regarding the symbols of Ptolemy: that they are poetic or rhetorical rather than Philosophical or mathematical.*

### ANALYSIS.

It will not (I hope) be a disgrace to me to have fallen into the same error with Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer and music theorist</note> himself, a man so illustrious; rather, it shall be turned into an honor that I have thought something similar to Ptolemy. Granting that they are mere Poetic symbolisms, we nevertheless utterly deny that we have wandered from the threshold of the Philosophers for that reason. For I see that it escapes the Author <note>Kepler</note> how much mystery the symbols of Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, Virgil, Ovid, and other similar poets contain within themselves in Philosophy. But, to come to his own doctrine, were not those regular bodies <note>The five "Platonic solids" which Kepler used to model the orbits of the planets</note>—which he established as the foundations of his harmonic work—mere symbols, which Pythagoras himself adapted to true Philosophy, drawing from them great mysteries about the mutations of the elements from imperfection to perfection? Yet the

# TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX.

## TEXT XV.

> *In his first volume, he divides the entire world into three regions; where, according to that most famous axiom of* Hermes <note>A reference to Hermes Trismegistus and the Emerald Tablet, which contains the famous phrase "As above, so below."</note>, *he makes the things above similar or analogous to the things below. Yet, for this analogy to succeed in everything, the things being compared on both sides must often be "dragged by the hair"* <note>A Latin idiom (*crinibus trahere*) meaning to force an argument or make an unnatural connection.</note>.

### ANALYSIS.

<margin>Preface to Book 1.</margin>
Nay, we can retort this very point upon the Author [Kepler]; who, in order to twist the five regular solids <note>The five Platonic solids, which Kepler used to model the distances between planetary spheres.</note> to his own purpose, drags the intention of Aristotle and Pythagoras himself as if by the hair. He gathers infinite definitions, axioms, and propositions so that, striving with might and main—"with feet and hands," as the saying goes—he may establish his symbols to support his inventions, even against the intentions of those very philosophers. With what violence he urges Nature itself! He suddenly elevates our Earth to the stars, forcing a heavy object to tend upward. Likewise, he turns an opaque and unmoving body into a bright star, understood to move between the spheres of Mars and Mercury. He even claims it has its own soul <note>Kepler proposed a "world soul" or *anima terrae* to explain the Earth's physical reactions and its relationship to the stars.</note> to command the air and waters and stir up storms and the ether. Similarly, he makes the Sun fixed and immovable, yet nevertheless the source of motion and the center of the world, so that the Earth moves around it, etc. As for my own work, the outcome will justify the deeds.

---

## TEXT XVI.

> *Now, to come closer to the foundations upon which* Robert Fludd *builds his "Music of the World": first, he occupies the entire world and all three of its parts—the* Empyrean, Celestial, and Elemental; *I occupy only the celestial; and not even all of it, but only the motions of the planets as if beneath the Zodiac.*

### ANALYSIS.

Yet he makes his own "celestial" part, which he chooses for his Harmony, as wide as my celestial and elemental parts combined, since he counts the Earth among the stars of heaven. From this it follows that the elemental part of the world is nothing but a portion of his vast "heaven." As for the motion of the planets, to which he grants the power of the whole Harmony: he indeed acknowledges his Harmony in the heavens, but he does not wish to consider or attend to the descent of that Harmony to us. <margin>text. 5.</margin> Therefore, when he deals with the motions of the planets, he says almost nothing about the length and shortness of sounds, even though he saw that the times of the planets' motions are diverse, as was said in the *Analysis of text 5.* I, however, have established my discourses on ascending and descending harmony—that is, on the exaltation of things through harmony, first divine, and then mundane. For I know that I have heaven on earth, while he himself transfers and snatches his earth into heaven. Thus the Poets imagined that Hercules, Astraeus, the Pleiades, the Argo, and indeed the Golden Fleece, Orion, the Hydra, the North Wind, and other such things were snatched into heaven.

---

## TEXT XVII.

> *He, relying on the ancients who believed the power of harmonies came from abstract numbers, is satisfied if he can demonstrate a concordance between parts by grasping them in numbers in whatever way possible, with no care for what kind of units are accumulated in that number. I [Kepler] nowhere teach searching for harmonies where the things between which the harmonies exist cannot be measured by the same measure of quantity; so that the cause of the quantity—the proportion between them—is the same as that between two strings of the same tension caused by their length.*

### ANALYSIS.

In this place indeed, I see that the Author is utterly ignorant of the true numbers of natural harmony. If it were not so, I know he would never have burst forth into such words. For the triangle of Pythagoras <note>The Tetractys, a symbol of four rows of dots adding up to ten, representing the organization of space and the universe.</note>, described by him in Book 3, folio 4, is depicted not with mere mercantile figures <note>original: "figuris mercatorijs" - Fludd is contrasting practical arithmetic used in trade with the sacred, "formal" numbers of the philosophers.</note>, but with purely formal ones—

...will find depicted (if he wishes to consider the matter rightly) things which are far distant from abstractions. He [Kepler] himself attempts to flee from abstract numbers in his harmony; and yet, he seems to treat nothing in numbers with sincerity except abstractions, since mathematical numbers derived from lines, surfaces, and bodies—or roots, squares, and cubes—are no less abstract than those found in common <note>original: *Algorithmica vulgari* — the standard arithmetic used by merchants and accountants.</note> algorithmic arithmetic. The wiser philosophers, namely **Themistius**, **Boethius**, **Averroes**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato**, so extolled numbers that they thought no one could rightly philosophize without them. 

But the common accountant, who is skilled in the merchant’s art of numbering, or one who is merely practiced in common Music or Geometry and looks only at the surface, does not know what that most noble number of which those philosophers spoke intends, nor its distribution into members. Rather, it is known by him who seeks out **formal proportions**—namely, the degrees of the progression of form in nature from imperfection to the highest perfection. Therefore, those philosophers are not to be heard or understood as speaking of common, material, or sensible number, but of the **formal number**, which is truly fiery and most familiar to reason. 

For the **Pythagoreans**, the **Academics**, and **Augustine** himself cared nothing for those other [common] numbers. They called this species of number *Natural, formal, and rational*, through which great miracles are performed in both divine and natural realms. Time indeed consists of such numbers, as does every motion and action adapted to time; all things subject to time and motion are referred to them. Through these truly golden and formal numbers, the concords and voices in Music have their proportion and consistency. Finally, all species of natural things, and those which are above nature, are bound together by certain formal numbers. 

The mystery of these hidden numbers was best known by those most learned in science, who attributed the **Monad** <note>The number One, representing unity or the Creator.</note> or unity of workmanship to God; the **Dyad** or duality to watery Matter; and afterwards the act of the **Triad** to Form, or the light and universal soul, which they called the "Virgin." These, moreover, are those three fiery and formal numbers which first flowed from the properties of the most holy Trinity into the fabric of the world: for watery Matter is joined with the luminous Form by the "glue" of the divine Spirit, and is called **Heaven**. 

Then, to man and his life, they attributed the **Hexad** (6) and **Heptad** (7); and finally the **Ennad** (9) to all creatures. From this, the number **Ten** <note>The Decad.</note>, enclosing not only all the world’s consonances but even its dissonances, is attributed by the Sages to the ten **Sephiroth** <note>In Jewish Kabbalah, the Sephiroth are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>. They said ten names of God preside over these, expressing His ten properties in the world—sounding together in clemency as much as they clash in severity. For such is the progression of formal numbers, beyond which no other ever was, is, or shall be: **1, 2, 3, 4**. Where 1 and 2 added together make 3; and if 4 is added to those, they become **7** <note>This refers to the *Tetractys*, a triangular figure of ten points used by Pythagoreans, though Fludd here highlights the sum leading to seven.</note>. 

And this is that miraculous number in which the creation of the world was completed; for in it, the material or elementary square [4] is united to the formal root [3], and the appetite of worldly matter is so fulfilled that it rests, being filled with the highest good. Hence, in this respect, that number is given to the **Sabbath** or rest. Occasionally it is also the number of punishment, when the property of **Elohim** <note>A Hebrew name for God often associated with judgment or justice.</note> is turned into wrath considered in the number three; and thus it is dissonant:

And the Holy Scriptures recount infinite other mysteries. However, this naming of the number seven is understood not in the common way, but in the mystical and formal way. For, just as the letter kills but the spirit gives life, so too is there the same difference between common and spiritual number. 

But let us proceed with our purpose: 1, 2, and 3 make 6; to which if 4 is added (which is unity), it becomes 7; or by the addition of the number four in its full value to 6, **10** is produced. Beyond this, as **Aristotle** testifies, there is no further progression: for all numbers that follow are mere compositions of these. In these formal numbers, therefore, all things are comprehended. And thus, whoever knows how to join vocal and natural numbers with divine ones, and how to temper them into the same consonance, this person will be able to work wonders through such a number, and likewise to know them, just as those most skilled in **Natural Magic** have confidently written. For these are the true numbers in which lies the secret of the entire essence of Harmony, without the knowledge of which it is impossible to judge rightly of Music, whether it be of the world <note>*Musica mundana* — the music of the spheres.</note> or artificial. 

And certainly, although I acknowledge I am hardly worthy of the knowledge of such a great mystery, I have nonetheless labored mightily to adapt the proportion of these kinds of numbers in my works. Curious readers will perceive that I have treated these matters more copiously in my *Microcosmic Treatise*, in the little book on *Divine Numbers*. But I would not wish you to believe that I have turned the thread of my discourse there to common numbers, but rather to the proportions of the mystery of Nature. 

We say therefore to the Author [Kepler] that he perceives our intention poorly by guessing that I received the power of my Harmonies from abstract numbers. But indeed, I see that he is so puffed up in his own opinion that he either holds the more relaxed matters treated by us in contempt, or at least is quite unable to grasp them, or to look into their inner recesses with his "mathematical eyes." I say, therefore, that I have had a greater care for the accumulation of formal unities to explain and unenucleate <note>To pull out the kernel or clarify the core of an idea.</note> the truth of world harmony than he could have, who is occupied only with the "letter" of the matter and seems to savor nothing of the formal spirit. For how is it possible that he can judge world Music, when he is utterly ignorant of its essence? But let us return to his "excellence" in Music, which he seems to trumpet so loudly to the world. He himself does not admit harmonies where the things between which the harmonies exist cannot be measured by the same measure of quantity, so that the cause of quanti-

...of quantity, there is the same proportion between them as between two strings of the same tension because of their length. He produced this sort of proportion in *Chapter 4, Book 3*. Among strings equally stretched, those sounds are deeper which are longer, and those are sharper which are shorter: where he seems to admit no proportional Music unless there is a difference in length between strings of the same measure or width. However, common experience teaches that this is false; because two strings of equal tension and the same length, but of different or diverse thickness <term>grossities: thickness or mass</term> or magnitude, are accustomed to return various harmonies in the deep and the sharp; about which more is said in the *Analysis of Text 13*. Therefore, here the difference in length is not the cause, but the magnitude: Whence I also assigned lower and deeper sounds to the denser and thicker matter of the world, and sharper sounds to the thinner spirit of the world: for the sake of demonstrating which, we have not ineptly drawn the figure of a pyramid.

## Text XVIII.

> *For that reason, he divides the whole world according to the radius into three equal parts, knowing well enough that they are not equal at all: but only for the reason that the first unity is the Elemental world, the second the ethereal world, and the third the Empyrean: and truly units cannot be depicted otherwise than by equality of lines: but I, unless astronomy testifies to that same quantitative measure of units, shall in no way use them as units to count harmonic proportions.*

## ANALYSIS.

Here Johannes Kepler seems to rebuke me sharply because I distributed the diameter of the world-machine into three equal parts for the discovery of my Macrocosmic Harmony: For, he says, the first unity makes the Elemental world, the second the ethereal world, and the third the Empyrean; he concludes this is erroneous because units cannot be depicted otherwise than by equality of lines. It is very easy to answer this objection of his: For, if the ethereal heaven is held to be the male, and the elemental region the female, whose womb is the earth, it is necessary that the same and most exact proportion exists between the ethereal heaven and that which is below; since the passion in the female must respond in the most exact degree to the action in the male, through that infallible axiom of Plato; *Forms are given according to the merit of the matter* <note>original: "Secundum meritum materiæ dantur formæ"</note>: But there is no generation except among things compatible in nature: And truly the heaven acts upon the lower things and gives form; while the lower things suffer in equal respect, and receive the forms of the heaven, by which they may be shaped.

But, to come closer to the matter, he denies that my units are equal because they cannot be depicted or measured by the equality of lines. Here indeed the Author has betrayed his ignorance in the true knowledge of natural units, because he seems not to know the weights of nature, without which one can reach neither the secret of Harmony nor the mysteries of celestial motions: For Hermes says (and indeed most rightly;) *What is above is like that which is below, and vice versa* <note>A foundational Hermetic principle from the "Emerald Tablet"</note>; that is, a thick unity is the same as a subtle unity, and a subtle unity the same as a thick one; that is, a thin spiritual unity is the same as a moderately coarse unity, and this is the same as the terrestrial unity, the densest of all: Which unities are nonetheless not measured by a common and equal mathematical line, unless such a measure is for the sake of demonstration. 

For example: If we had two handfuls of earth, one of which was to be kept in its thick and terrestrial nature, the other to be reduced by thinning into water, certainly that one handful of earth left in its nature will be equal to the other single one reduced to water, by reason of weight, in which the proportions of the wise truly consist: And although that single handful is reduced by thinning into 10 handfuls of water, and consequently requires a larger place than it had before; yet its proportion in weight is the same, insofar as it can be reduced by art into the same earth as it was before. Similarly, that water reduced into air will require ten times as much place and space for its container as it had before; and yet in formal proportion it does not differ from one coarse handful; and so in the rest. 

Whence it must be concluded against that objection of the Author, that units of the same bulk and element require equality of mathematical lines in their dimension; but truly those same units, diverse in bulk and with their substances changed in thickness and thinness—namely, so that one of them remains thick, while the other is thinned—are not measured by the identity of mathematical lines but by weights: And this is partly what Hermes understands in his enigmatic speech, when he says, *the superior behaves like the inferior and vice versa*: that is, one subtle thing is the same as one coarse thing, or heaven the same as earth, and spiritual the same as corporal, and thin heaven the same as thick heaven; that is, to be counted by the formal measure, which is made by the proportions of mystical weights, and not by the identity of common or numerical, linear, superficial, or corporal measure, seeing that these measures are known to wander far from the intentions of the Wise. Therefore, the most exact measures of these things, from which their Harmonies, the mysteries of nature, and the motions of the world are elicited—

# ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE

...divided, are those which are called the **Weights of the Sages** <note>Latin: *pondera Sapientum*; a term referring to alchemical or mystical proportions rather than physical weight</note>; to which alone, and to no others, it is given to make mutations of nature from one element into another while the identity remains. Indeed, by these weights, out of one handful <note>Latin: *pugillo*; literally a fistful or small amount</note> of earth and nine of air, ten handfuls of water are made; and from one handful of water and nine of fire, ten handfuls of air are made, ascending through the scale of the **vivification** <note>The process of giving life or spiritualizing</note> of gross nature into that which is simple and high. For in this way, nature was accustomed to produce the heavens alone from a gross and earthly thing through the exaltation of the identity of the elements into the nature of the heavens. Then, from one handful of fire and nine of water, ten of "dead air" are made, which is "living water," and from nine of the element of earth, ten of "glorified water" are made. 

But these proportions of weights must be understood with wisdom; because this is that sole doctrine without which no measure, proportion, or temperament can be acquired. For this proportion is that **Golden Chain** <note>The *Catena Aurea*, a classical and alchemical concept of the interconnectedness of all levels of reality</note>, and the wheel of the circles of the whole age, through which Nature herself is governed in the rotation and revolution of all her instruments. Without this gift of wisdom, therefore, no one skilled in the science of Astronomy can rightly judge the position and motions of the stars; no one can know the constitution of the world, or the power of the elements, or the beginning, middle, and end of times, the changes of the solstices and the varieties of seasons, the circuit of the year, the natures of living creatures, the rages of wild beasts, the forces of winds and spirits, the reason of storms, the very thoughts of men, the differences of plants, and the faculties of roots, or whatever things are hidden or manifest, according to that passage in **Wisdom 7:22**. 

These are those exquisite gifts of wisdom, without which no one can rightly penetrate into any science from those **seven liberal foundations** <note>The Seven Liberal Arts: Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy</note> of universal knowledge; instead, men led by opinion fall into infinite errors. And hence it is said that "Wisdom has built her house by hewing out her seven columns" (**Proverbs 9:1**) and that she is to be preferred by the learned over money and the most choice excavated gold. Whence the wise man says: *Wisdom is better than Rubies, and all delights cannot be compared to her* (**Proverbs 8:11**). Truly, this wisdom is more beautiful than the Sun of **Kepler**, which he made the source of motion, and she is found prior to every arrangement of the stars. Nor is it a wonder, since she is a pure emanation of the brightness of Almighty God (**Wisdom 7**). 

Therefore, my "units" tend toward the investigation of this wisdom, so that I may reach the highest peak of that unity. For so the sages say, that all things are one and the same in God and through God; who is the sole truth, from whom all things proceed into multitude through multiplication and dispersion, and into whom likewise all things return through exaltation and resolution into simplicity. Although my philosophy may seem common, yet under its shadow better things will appear through right investigation. 

Regardless, I respond to the Author's <note>Referring to Johannes Kepler</note> objections thus: my units are not to be measured by the same or equal linear dimensions; rather, I used them so that, in the manner of a pyramid, I might more exactly describe the formula of the **subtiliation of matter** <note>The process of matter becoming thinner, lighter, or more spiritual</note>. But if I were to explain the dimension of the sphere of each of the elements and heavens according to its linear proportions (if indeed that were possible), no paper could have held my figures. We say, therefore, that if the elementary heaven were thinned into an ethereal nature, then that one unit would fill the immense space of the ethereal heaven. Nor does it follow that, because it does not occupy such an ample space, it is therefore not "one" in natural proportion (which consists in weight), even though it differs in linear dimension. 

And we, taught by experience, know that earth can be reduced back into heaven, and yet the nature of the proportion of its substance remains the same as it was before; just as a poor man exalted to the status of a Bishop is still the same person, and a little water reduced by distillation into a great vapor returns again into its prior quantitative nature by condensation—namely, so that although it occupies the greatest space in smoke but a tiny one in water, its "unity" in the smoke does not differ from its "unity" in the water, except in space alone. 

But why should I use more words in this cause? Doubtless all of this, indeed even the response itself to this objection of his, is best explained by me in **Chapter 16, Book 2, Treatise 1 of *The Fabric of the Macrocosm***, at **Experiment 3**; where we have described to a hair's breadth the reason for our units and their difference in thinness and thickness. If the Author had read that chapter, he might not have judged my units so rashly. From these things, therefore, we conclude that the Author betrays his own ignorance in this context rather than being able to justly impute any fault to me in this matter. For, as he seems to assert that units cannot be painted or described without equality of lines, it is evident from this that he inquires into things more **mathematically and quantitatively** than truly **physically**, or according to the essence of natural things—that is, according to the measure of light in spiritual matter, or of **sulfur in its mercury** <note>Alchemical principles: Sulfur represents the active/formal principle, and Mercury represents the passive/material principle</note>. Let his "imaginary Astronomy" testify to that same quantitative measure of units; I, content in my physical manner, will adhere to my natural measures, equipped with essential weights.

For the top of the Elemental region in this way is twice as far from the top of the Celestial as it is from the top of the Empyrean: And in...*

# TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX

*...by the division of the pyramid, with respect to its axis, three equal parts come to the three regions; but with respect to the triangle through the axis, one unit goes to the Empyrean, three to the Celestial, and five units to the Elementary <note>original: "Empyreo" appears twice in the Latin text here, but the context of the three regions suggests the third is the Elementary realm</note>; finally, with respect to the space or the thickness of the figure, one unit goes to the Empyrean, seven to the Celestial, and nineteen units to the Elementary. What shall I say now about the other, contrary Pyramid of Light, whose base is formed by the adorable Trinity itself at the highest summit of the Empyrean heaven, but whose vertex is placed upon the earth itself?*

---

### ANALYSIS.

In this context, like the most inconsistent Proteus <note>A shapeshifting sea god from Greek mythology; Fludd is accusing Kepler of being slippery and changing his arguments</note>, he seems to vary in his sayings; for he now deals with the equality of the division of the parts of the pyramid, now inquires after its length, and then finally examines its triple dimension with his mathematical industry; and in all these things he wanders away from my intention. We shall speak abundantly to the wise concerning the logic of our units in the analysis of the following text, where much will be said about this subject in a few words. Then he says that I have counted how many parts go to the Empyrean, how many to the Celestial, and how many to the Elementary; and in this also he is mistaken regarding my intention. 

For my demonstration is not intended to deal with the magnitude of the parts, but with the proportion of the thinning <note>Latin: *attenuationis*; the process of making matter less dense and more spiritual</note> of spiritualized matter, by saying that the more the matter of the world tends upward, it is always rendered more subtle, and in its nature purer and more spiritual. Therefore, my pyramidal proportions did not intend to show that there is less matter in one heaven than in another (for I have affirmed that the units are the same in weight in the elementary heaven as in the celestial and the Empyrean); rather, through the arrangement of the portions of the pyramid, I intended to indicate the proportion of the refinement and purity of matter in its ascent—for example, the degrees of proportion in the movement from imperfection toward perfection. 

He passes on to an examination of the axis of the pyramid; which examination, although it pertains to a mathematical pyramid, matters little here, no less than an inquiry into a solid pyramid with numbers. For who among the students or beginners in Geometry is ignorant of the numerical proportion of the parts of a solid pyramid to one another? But for the sake of demonstration, I brought forth a geometric figure into the light so that I might more easily show the world the progress of physical nature in worldly matter. I certainly did not do so so that the reader might immediately skip from my physical intention to the mathematical numbering of the pyramid; for I did not introduce the geometric pyramid in my demonstrations with the intent that you should consider the identity of its matter, or compare the parts of its solidity to each other, or measure its length. 

Instead, I used it so that you might observe its figure and its proportion in descending and ascending, and in moving from imperfection to the goal of perfection. For in this way, we understand the proportions of perfection through the degrees of heaven, and the scale of imperfection through the stations of the elements distant from each other, before the limits of perfection are reached. And since to the ocular sight a mathematical pyramid and all its parts are of the same matter—that is, one part is homogeneous with another—I therefore divided it into equal parts for the better explanation of the subject; although that matters little to my purpose, which was to explain the physical motion of physical matter from the coarse to the subtle. 

Therefore, what my intention is through the true physical pyramid, as it exists in the nature of things, we have expressed in Chapter 17, Book 5 of the *History of the Physics of the Macrocosm* <note>Latin: *Physicæ Macrocosmi historiæ*; Fludd's massive work describing the structure of the universe</note>. And since I perceived that the difficulty of my intention might have brought a poor opinion of my labors to the world, perhaps because of a less ready explanation of the truth, or of my mind and sense, I therefore made an entire book in the last volume of my *Technical History of the Microcosm* concerning the explanation of physical pyramids, both formal and material; there I fully unshelled and explained my intention regarding the natural pyramid. 

We say, therefore, that our pyramidal contemplation is more "formal" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "formal" refers to the "form" or soul/essence of a thing rather than its physical "matter"</note> than can be grasped under mathematical consideration, since it denotes the hidden progression of form within matter toward its purification, refinement, and its being led to maturity and perfection from imperfection, and from the coarse and dense to the thin. And in this indeed lies the entire mystical intention of the Sages regarding the harmony of proportions and measures; nor does it differ from the progression of nature in this world. 

I make the base of that formal pyramid the seat of God, because there the perfection of all matter is consumed, and matter itself is reduced to divine unity from worldly multitude. Such will be the consummation, or rather the transfiguration of the world, and such was its beginning. One may see, therefore, that just as a material pyramid is more powerful in its form the more it tends upward (as is right to gather from my figures), so also the world itself and all things in the world abound more in form the more they are moved toward purity and subtlety from impurity and coarseness. And so they always ascend, not indeed by mathematical measures from the bottom upward—that is, from place to place—but from imperfection to perfection, from the impure to purity, from a humble degree to an exalted state, from rawness to complete maturity, from darkness to light, from earth to heaven, from evil to good, and finally from the Devil to God. In this way a Bishop is exalted without his location being changed; and thus indeed...

### TEXT XX.

*Since he mixes these two pyramids with one another, and from that mixture draws out musical proportions, he attempts a thing most different from the purpose of my work. For he compares light (the giver of form and soul) and matter—two things most different from one another—to which quantities do not belong in the same respect. I, however, do not admit as terms for forming a Harmonic proportion in the world anything except those things which receive quantities in the same respect; for example, the daily motions of Mars and Jupiter.* <note>Kepler is arguing that you can only compare like-with-like, such as the speeds of two planets, rather than comparing a physical thing like "matter" to a spiritual thing like "light."</note>

### ANALYSIS.

As far as my consonances <note>musical harmonies</note> are concerned, he considers them false and most different from his own purpose because they arise from the mixing of light with matter, which he says are "most different." Consequently, he infers that the quantities of worldly matter and form are by no means present in the same respect. Indeed, this assertion of his indicates an even greater ignorance of the depth of natural science than the things that preceded it.

For first, this is certain and proved by all Philosophers: that the desire of matter is to be "informed" <term>Informed: in a philosophical sense, this means to be given a specific shape, nature, or "form" by a higher principle.</term> by light, just as it is the nature of light (or the lucid form) to inform matter itself. Therefore, when the worldly matter was completed, it was undoubtedly done through this "lucid information." From this it follows that matter in actuality (which is called "secondary" by Aristotle and "Water" by Moses <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis, where the "Spirit of God moved over the waters." Fludd equates the primordial waters with the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>) retains a sufficient portion of form to exist, by which it may live and remain as it is. 

Furthermore, it is said according to the opinion of Plato that forms are given according to the merit of the matter; nor indeed is there any generation <note>creation of a new thing</note> except from things that are compatible in the nature of both form and matter. From this it is clear that lowly matter possesses a lowly form, while exalted matter possesses an exalted one. We also say that matter "suffers" <note>original: "patiatur," meaning to be acted upon or to be passive</note> naturally, just as form "acts." There also occurs, as the Wise Man witnesses, the same union between matter and form as between a female and a male animal. 

Furthermore, we say that the matter of the element of Fire is more worthy than that of Air, because it retains a greater portion of form; for its material substance was more disposed to receiving a multitude of form than that of Air. Likewise, under the same proportion, the matter of Air is more worthy than Water, and Water more than the matter of Earth; and similarly, the Heavens are more worthy than the substance of Fire. From these things it is evident that matter in all things adapts itself to its form according to its own dignity, just as the form itself relates to the merit of the matter. For there is no diversity in matter except because of the greater or lesser proportion of form within it; for it receives the dignity of matter from the form, just as the form receives dominion from the matter over which it presides.

From these things it is clearly evident that a most exact natural proportion exists between form and matter. However, this consensus does not admit the same "quantities" insofar as form is not measured by the common measure of Geometry, but by an "ideal" measure. Since form (inasmuch as it is invisible, though it acts visibly) cannot be depicted by Geometric lines except through an analogical representation, its measure is nonetheless most certain. Just as there is a physical dimension and pyramidal shape of matter, so too is there a formal shape—namely, a pyramidal one—and of the same dimension. For the effect of formal action is rendered sensible through the alterations of its visible matter; for that which makes something "such-and-such" is itself "more such-and-such." 

But form gave such a shape to matter because of its own proportional presence within it. Therefore, the form itself, existing ideally in the material pyramid, is equal to it in both shape and dimension. In this way, we say the soul is in the whole and in every part of an animal's body; hence it shaped the dimension of the animal body according to its own hidden proportion. And this is also how the soul or form behaves while existing in the material pyramid, which can admit a Geometric or quantitative measure. Does the Author <note>Kepler</note> himself not seem 

<margin>In Book 3, folio 4, he acknowledges this in the description of the numerical pyramid.</margin>

to acknowledge this same thing in Book 3, folio 4, in his description of the numerical pyramid? There, he seems to attribute one side of the triangle—namely that of the odd numbers—to the soul or form, and the other side, equal to it and composed of even numbers, to matter. Thus, he makes the side of matter in the pyramidal triangle of equal quantity with the formal side. 

Pythagoras and Plato also handed down the Monad <note>The number one, representing unity or God</note> to God the Creator, the Dyad <note>The number two, representing duality or division</note> to matter, and the Triad <note>The number three</note> to form. And indeed, the ancient Sages knew that the whole mystery of Worldly Harmony lay hidden in these proportional numbers, which are purely formal. From these things it is also quite clear that watery matter and lucid form are not "most different," as he made them out to be, but that they agree perfectly in "action" and "passion," no differently than a man and a woman, by whose union natural generation occurs. And this indeed is the Worldly Harmony: namely, that it produces harmonic consonances, or proportions of actions and passions, between matter and form in every region of the world.

Fludd is responding to Kepler’s criticism that his "harmonic" theories—which relate music to the structure of the universe—improperly mix physical matter with metaphysical light. -> TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX <-

From here, he proceeds to the arrangement of his own harmonies, which he says he will not admit unless the quantities are received in the same respect; and by this path, he chooses the material proportions of the world, but seems to reject the "formal" ones <note>original: *formas*; here meaning the spiritual or organizational principles</note>, since they cannot be measured by a common quantity. And yet, he goes on to a "formal" example—namely, the daily motions of Mars and Jupiter. I ask you to notice how poorly these agree with what came before. For he says that my Harmony is most different from his own because I derive my foundations from light and matter; and yet he himself here seems to derive his Harmony from motion, which is nothing other than the effect of light. For from light arises "act" <term>Act: in Aristotelian philosophy, *actus* is the realization or functioning of a potential</term>, and from act, motion proceeds. Hence it is clear that the cause of *his* Harmony is merely the effect of *my* cause, just as heat is called the effect of fire. For light in the body of a Planet is that which moves it—that is, either by a greater or lesser proportion of motion. Specifically, it is driven at either a slower or faster pace according to the greater or lesser vigor of the light, or the "form," or the soul that moves and acts within the body of the Planet, which is present in a proportion suited to the arrangement of the material mass. Furthermore, regarding his claim that he does not admit any Harmonies except those that receive quantities in the same respect, we have already demonstrated above that this can be otherwise by using two strings of the same length and tension, but of varying or different thicknesses. We conclude, therefore, that his assertion in this context is inconsistent.

### TEXT XXI.

*There is no less a diversity between us in this: that he ascribes four degrees of obscurity and darkness to the Elemental region. For he says that any part has four quarters—surely no less than three thirds, or five fifths! And now he claims that four are in the Earth, three are in the water (which is why it is already transparent), two in the air, and one in the fire.* <note>Kepler is using sarcasm here to mock Fludd’s division of elements into "fractions" of darkness.</note>

### ANALYSIS.

In this place, the dignity of the number four <note>original: *numeri quaternarij*</note> is called into question. To defend it with "hands and feet" <note>a Latin idiom meaning to defend something with all one's might</note>, as far as my meager talent allows, I am urged by the opportunity the Author provides. For the Divinity has celebrated the excellence of this number above others as the highest, by which I am led to hold and recognize it as divine; but even Nature herself, the handmaid of Divinity, and the nobler Mathematical sciences—namely Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy—have declared its wonderful effects. 

Therefore, if we diligently search out its praises in divinity, we will perceive in the first place that this "square" number is adapted to God the Father, in whom the mystery of the entire sacrosanct Trinity is included. For the first and simple proportion of the quaternary—namely, one to one—denotes the symbol of the Monad <term>Monad: the indivisible "One" or the ultimate source of all being</term> of the super-substantial paternal essence, from which the second Monad proceeding begat a Son equal to Himself; and this second procession is also simple, as 1 from 1. However, the proportion of two to two, which is the second procession from the simple ones, denotes the Holy Spirit, from the two—namely, from the Father and the Son. These processions are clearly expressed in the number four by that ineffable name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHWH, the four-letter Hebrew name of God</note>: where the double *He* (ה) denotes the procession from *Yod* (י) the Father, and *Vau* (ו) the Son. Hence this name alone, expressing the essence of God and no other, is called the Tetragrammaton. And it is for this reason that this number is called by the Sages the head and fountain of the entire Divinity. 

Nature herself, who draws her origin from divinity, also claims this number for her own principle. This is the very thing the Pythagoreans sang, who called this number the perpetual fountain of Nature, as appears from these following verses by which the Pythagoreans were accustomed to swear:

> I swear to you by the holy four, with a pure mind,
> The fountain of eternal Nature and the parent of the soul.

But I will now say in a word how this is: The Pythagoreans made "Duality" <note>The number 2</note> not a number, but a confusion of units. Therefore, they established its square as the first even number; and this not without reason. For since one unit denotes form or divine act, and the other denotes divine power or matter, it is necessary that the power appear out of the darkness through the act. Of these units, the first was made through the bond of the triune Unity of the universal substance of the world, according to the property of the sacrosanct Trinity. But truly, since the first square was from the number two, the progression of nature was into that number four, which is the double proportion to the number two, or the square of two. By this path, the universal watery substance of the world was divided into 4 Elements, distinct from one another. From this primary even number, the progress is made to the first Cube in the nature of things, which is the number eight <note>original: *Octonarius*</note>, or the doubled quaternary, denoting compositions made from the Elements—just as the elements themselves, like a square, proceeded from the number two, which denotes simple matter and simple form divided from one another. Hence, therefore...

<meta>Continuing the defense of Fludd's harmonic system against Kepler. On this page, Fludd shifts from discussing planetary motion to a deep philosophical and mathematical defense of the "quaternary" (the number four) as the foundation of all reality—physical, mathematical, and musical.</meta>

### ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE

...there proceeded four degrees of nature related to the four Elements: namely, Being, Living, Feeling, and Understanding; the 4 Cardinal Points of the world; the 4 Triplicities in the heavens <note>In astrology, the 12 signs are divided into four "triplicities" based on the elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water.</note>; the 4 primary qualities beneath the heavens <note>Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness.</note>; and the 4 seasons of the year. Indeed, the whole of Nature is encompassed by 4 terms: namely, substance, quality, quantity, and motion. Finally, a fourfold disposition typically fills the entire natural world: namely, the seminal virtue <note>The hidden potential within a seed.</note>, natural budding, the adolescent form, and the completed composite. But one may also look to this property of the natural quaternary in the same cause through infinite other reasons. By these, we can clearly prove that the number four is more suitable for choosing the division and distinction of "moist nature" <note>Fludd often uses "moist nature" or "humid radical" to refer to the basic substance of the material world.</note> than either the number three or five.

Arithmetic also argues for the excellence of this number over others; specifically, through that science, its double proportion is best explained. The first of these is one to two, while the later is two to four; its origin is produced and born with a twin procession and proportion: namely, one to one and two to two. It begins, therefore, from unity and ends in the quaternary. Indeed, all other numbers are contained within this number: for one and one make 2; from 1 and 2 arises 3; and from three with unity, 4 is born. Thus stand 1, 2, 3, and 4, in which all mysteries of the whole world and of Nature herself, as well as the dimensions of Arithmetic, are contained. 

For from 3 and 4, the number seven comes forth, which, if considered formally, is clearly mystical and full of secrets. From 2 and 3, the number five results by addition; from 1, 2, and 3, the number six; from 1, 3, and 4, the number eight; from 2, 3, and 4, the number nine; and finally, from the gathering of the entire natural progression—1, 2, 3, 4—the number ten is produced <note>This is the Pythagorean "Tetractys," where 1+2+3+4=10, representing the universe.</note>, beyond the naming of which there is no further departure. From these progressions, therefore, all Geometric and Musical proportions arise, such as 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; and 1, 3, 6, 9; and 1, 4, 8. 

Indeed, he who rightly understands the use of this natural progression 1, 2, 3, 4 in formal speculation will not find the mystery of the 7 days of creation hidden from him, nor why the Sun was made on the fourth day, nor how 3 and 4 constitute the number seven, or ten, or the quaternary in rational numbers. He will see why the quaternary number is the day of the Sabbath or rest, and why it is the day of the sun. Likewise, he will understand how, in true natural operation, three denotes and constitutes the number six, signifying the six days in creation. He will fish out the reason for the "critical days" and "climacteric years" <note>In ancient medicine and astrology, these were specific years (like 63) or days in an illness thought to be turning points or dangerous periods.</note>; and indeed, by considering 4 as unity, he will see with eyes almost wide open the procreation of the seven Planets in the world, and many other wonders.

In Geometry, its power is infinite, insofar as it embraces this part of Mathematics with 4 terms: namely, the point, the line, the surface, and the body. From it, we also see that original Geometric Cube proceed, from the heart of which our Author <note>Likely referring to God as the Creator.</note> produced the rest, just as the 4 elements were produced from the belly of Chaos. For the Cube is produced from the multiplication of a square, which he recognized as primordial and possessing the logic of the whole. Since this is so, it was necessary that we choose the quaternary number in our divisions; for the Cube is resolved into it as if into its first elements—namely, squares—from which the triangle and pentagon are drawn out according to its own construction. Therefore, a composite natural thing related to the Cube ought to be divided into its fourths, as if into squares, rather than into 3 thirds or 5 fifths; for in corruption <note>The process of decay or breaking down.</note>, there is a resolution of the composite (or Cube) into 4 elements (or a square), just as conversely, in generation, there is a natural progression from the square to the Cube.

Finally, the power of this number is found most exactly in the science of Music, insofar as it contains within itself all the harmony of Music. For the <term>Diapason: the interval of an octave.</term> consists in the "double" ratio, as 1 to 2; the <term>Diapente: the interval of a perfect fifth.</term> consists in the <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 3:2.</term>; and the <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth.</term> behaves as the <term>sesquitertia: a ratio of 4:3.</term>. Furthermore, all proportions of composite consonances arise from the quaternary number and its root; for example, the Diapason with a Diapente relates in a "triple" ratio as 2, 4, 6. For between 2 and 6, the triple proportion is aggregated from the double (2 and 4) and the sesquialtera (4 and 6). But the "double Diapason" <note>A two-octave interval.</note> is found in the "quadruple" ratio, as 2, 4, 8. Moreover, the Diatessaron and the Diapente together constitute one Diapason, as 2, 3, 4. From these, one may see that all proportions in Music receive their virtues from the quaternary number and its root, and either fall into or rise from its dimensions.

Lastly, if we look to mystical Astronomy, we shall perceive the entire force of the quaternary number in it, and most clearly so; for its whole secret is contained in the **Hieroglyphic Monad**, which displays the symbols of the Moon, the Sun, the elements, and fire. These are the four things that act and are acted upon in the world to induce the constant changes by which both corruptions and generations occur within it. The figure is of this sort:

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram of the Monas Hieroglyphica, a famous symbol designed by the Elizabethan occultist John Dee. It consists of a crescent moon at the top, a circle with a central point representing the Sun, a cross representing the four Elements, and a base resembling the zodiac sign for Aries, which Fludd labels as representing Fire. Labels appear to the right: Moon, Sun, Elements, Fire.</image-desc>

In this symbolism, we see first the indication of the quaternary number in the cross, through the arrangement of four lines meeting at a common point. When this is joined to the ternary number <note>The number three.</note> denoting the Moon, Sun, and Fire, it produces the number seven. This can also be provided by the 4 elements. And yet, this number seven is in itself nothing other than the quaternary number formally considered.

<meta>catchword: Furthermore</meta>

# TO THE KEPLERIAN APPENDIX

Furthermore, even those skilled in common astronomy have observed a matter of great importance when they divided the Zodiac into 4 triplicities <note>In astrology, the 12 signs are grouped into four "triplicities" (groups of three) based on the elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water.</note>. We conclude, therefore, that the Sages called this number the **Tetractys** <note>original: "Tetractin". The Pythagorean "Tetractys" is the number four, which the ancients considered the root of all things because 1+2+3+4 equals the perfect number 10.</note>, and preferred it in power over all other numbers, seeing as it is the foundation and root of all other numbers, as has been said. Thus, all foundations—whether in artificial, natural, or even divine things—are squared <note>referring to the four-fold nature of stability and completeness</note>, as was declared in the preceding pages. It follows, then, that a division of a natural thing by the number four—which is the very order of Nature itself—is more excellent than a division by three or five, which are naturally secondary to the quaternary root. 

Finally, regarding the division of the earth into 4 parts, water into three, air into two, and fire into one: that distribution is not to be understood in the literal manner of the Author <note>Kepler</note>, as explained above, but rather with respect to the **formal proportion** <note>In Fludd's philosophy, "form" refers to the spiritual light or soul within an object, while "matter" is the physical container. A "formal proportion" describes the ratio of light to shadow in an element.</note> in those elements. For I strive to demonstrate that the nature of earth—insofar as it is the basis, and the source and "cube" of matter—has little or no form or life-giving light within itself. It is, as it were, the vessel or womb of Nature and the receiver of celestial influences. Thus, the light it possesses is there more by accident than by nature, because it is so far removed from the luminous source. Earth is the coldest of all elements, and that in the fourth degree; just as water is also cold, but in a milder degree, and therefore admits a single degree of light into itself; and so it goes for the rest. It would be the part of a wise man, therefore, to understand correctly before condemning thoughtlessly.

### TEXT XXII.

> *Again elsewhere, he subdivides every region of any Element or Heaven into three spaces: the highest, the middle, and the lowest, though the probability of the senses does not follow this everywhere. You see that his units are again arbitrary.*

### ANALYSIS.

We say that the image of the world is a reflection of the **Archetype** <note>The "Archetype" is the divine blueprint or the mind of God.</note>. Therefore, just as the Creator of all things expanded and revealed Himself by proceeding from His unity into three properties, by which the world was founded according to their dispositions, so too has He divided the world into three regions, corresponding to the processions and properties of the most Holy Trinity. The first region is attributed to the Father, to whom the fountain and origin of light is assigned; to the Father, therefore, the first heaven or the work of the first day was given. The second is given to the Son; hence it is said, "By the Word He established the heavens." The work of the third day, by which the elements of the lowest heaven were produced, corresponds to the Holy Spirit. 

By the standard of this very thing, and according to this order, every heaven is again subdivided. This is proved because it was handed down by the most wise "God-bearing" fathers <note>original: "Theophororum patribus". This likely refers to mystical theologians like Dionysius the Areopagite who wrote on the celestial hierarchies.</note> that the Empyrean heaven is divided into three hierarchies. And you yourself were forced to admit that, according to the opinion of the Ancients, the ethereal region is distinct in 9 spheres, which, when divided by 3, leave three distinct parts. 

But he <note>Kepler</note> denies the equality of the intervals of the planetary spheres. And yet, it will be more probable for me to affirm it than for him to deny it; therefore, let the dispute remain "under the judge" <note>original: "sub iudice lis sit", a legal term meaning the case is still undecided.</note>. Truly, he acknowledges that the same higher impressions are ideally present in the lower things—such as an "ideal Zodiac" on earth because it was ideally in heaven. Therefore, it is probable that the other portions of the celestial world also correspond to their impressions and "images" in the elements. 

In this, too, he misinterprets me: for his imagination leads his concepts toward quantitative dimensions <note>physical measurements like miles or kilometers</note>, while I understood **proportions** between matter and form in the regions of the world. I am not speaking of the dimensions of intervals, but of the proportion of actions and passions between matter and form, or between water and light. He, therefore, focuses on the material pyramid and its quantitative dimensions. I was not thinking of the material at all, except insofar as the "formal" <note>the spiritual/active principle</note> was mixed with it. Thus, my quantities were ideal and proportional in formal consideration, and not otherwise, although I used mathematical lines and distances for the sake of demonstration. Consequently, the probability of this dimension is not found in the senses, but rather in the intellect. You see, then, that his rejections are arbitrary and dissonant from the truth of the matter.

### TEXT XXIII.

> *Yet for that reason, he proceeds to establish a **Diatessaron** <note>A musical interval of a fourth (a ratio of 4:3).</note> between Earth and water, and to apply its three intervals—tone, tone, and semitone—to the three spaces (highest, middle, and lowest). While the former have certain quantities for their own reasons, the latter do not even have boundaries set by nature; indeed, their measurements are plainly indeterminate according to these most general principles. And so it goes for the rest. But to me, natural units are proposed in which I may seek Harmonies: namely, the two extreme motions of the Planets (whether daily or hourly, it makes no difference), expressed by nature in their certain quantities.*

### ANALYTICAL DISCOURSE
<meta>catchword: ANALY-</meta>

->*ANALYSIS.*<-

Hardly any of the philosophers have ever doubted the three regions of the earth, nor the differences between them, any more than they have doubted the mineral, vegetable, and animal kingdoms, which naturally correspond to those regions. Hence, just as there is a difference of degrees between the mineral and vegetable kingdoms, and also between the vegetable and animal—since one is more fixed, earthy, watery, airy, or fiery than the other—so, without a doubt, there are proportions between the activity of one region and another. We know that just as minerals are more compact, fixed, and heavy, so also the portion of the earth tending toward the center is more weight-laden. Likewise, just as vegetables are more volatile and naturally fluid and watery than minerals, so too the middle region of the earth abounds with the waters of springs, from which rivers flow. The superior part of the earth, however, is more like the animal nature, for in it the life of things abounds, and there is greater volatility and lightness. Therefore, just as there is a kindred difference between earth, water, and air, so there is a necessary concatenation <note>A chain-like connection.</note> in the proportions between the central, middle, and superficial regions of the earth.

These proportions do not proceed from the nature of matter, but depend on an occult form <note>In Fludd's view, "form" is the spiritual or divine light that gives shape to raw matter.</note> acting invisibly upon it. Thus, they are not established by optical dimension or quantitative measurement, as he <note>Kepler</note> supposed; nor does my harmony consist in such proportions, but rather in the proportions between the more intense action or the relaxation of the form, and a similar passion <note>In the philosophical sense, "passion" refers to the capacity of matter to be acted upon by a "form."</note> in the matter, by which one element in its whole and its parts differs from another with its portions. Thus, thick water imbued with saltiness is said to differ from sweet water, and that again from a cloud, or a mist, or a thick vapor; and so on for the rest.

For this reason, his harmonic motions differ from mine in this way: those which he embraces belong to the particular creatures of nature; mine, however, are the motions of Nature itself, tending toward perfection in an occult manner. Likewise, his planetary motions are more useful for distinguishing the seasons of the year (according to that passage in Genesis: *that they might be signs measuring times, days, and years*) and they have their own particular duties. But these motions of mine are universal, by which the nature of every thing and creature, whether elementary or celestial, is moved; and at the same time, the elements themselves are moved into alterations and, agitated by a desire for perfection, are constantly rotated. For Nature always and incessantly tends toward the goal of perfection, even if it is sometimes hindered in its motion. This, I say, is the difference between the reasoning of his Harmony and mine.

### TEXT XXIV.

> *He <note>Fludd</note> seeks harmonic proportions in the degrees of darkness and light, without regard for any motion: I <note>Kepler</note> seek harmonies only in motions.*

->*ANALYSIS.*<-

That he indeed errs in this assertion can be seen from what has preceded. For he himself thinks that I found my proportions with geometric compasses, and he is mistaken; because my Harmony consists in the truest and most certain actions of the luminous empress, Nature, as has been said quite often. Furthermore, how ridiculous this assertion of his is, is clear from the fact that light is a creature surpassing and excelling all others in activity. Therefore, since light and darkness are the subject of my harmony, it is necessary that my Harmony consists in the motion and action of light upon the matter of darkness, like an agent acting upon a patient <note>The "agent" is the active force (light), and the "patient" is the receptive material (darkness/matter).</note>. Consequently, that statement of the Author was very rash, and a manifest argument of envy, or at least of ignorance, in which he says that I seek harmonic proportions in the degrees of darkness and light without regard for any motion. But he looked at the subject of my Harmony with his eyes, and not with his mind, so that in grasping at the shadow and embracing the bark <note>The outer shell.</note>, he utterly missed the substance and the kernel.

### TEXT XXV.

> *He <note>Fludd</note> tastes only a few meager concordances, and he elicits them from a mixture of his own pyramids <note>A reference to Fludd’s famous "Pyramids of Light and Matter" diagrams, which Kepler found unscientific.</note>—by which he carries about the world painted privately in his own mind—or he proves they are represented by it. I <note>Kepler</note> have demonstrated that the whole body of harmonic tempering, with all its parts, exists in the proper extreme motions of the Planets, according to certain measures demonstrated by Astronomy. Thus, his subject is his own concept of the world; for me, the subject of Mundane Harmony is the World itself, or the real motions of the Planets within it.*

### ANALYSIS.

Although I have constructed the monochord from the axis of the pyramids, or according to the author's <note>Referring to himself, Fludd, or the specific text under discussion.</note> eighteenth section from the semidiameter of the machine, nevertheless that **world monochord** <term>monochordum mundanum: a single-stringed instrument used by Fludd as a mathematical and symbolic model to represent the harmony of the universe.</term> examines the universal harmony of the world no differently [than a musical one]. It tests all its intervals or differences in the harmonic action and passion occurring between matter and form through the entire physical disposition of the world, just as is done in the monochord of my **artificial Music**, in which all musical consonances and all intervals and proportions are explained that can ever be contained within a musical system, by counting from its head to its tail. For, if the string is pressed in the middle, it will exhibit a double consonance, an **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, by sounding against the open string; and again, if any of those consonances are similarly divided into two parts, it will produce a quadruple proportion; and so on, down to an ineffable division, as was most clearly declared in the division of my monochord in the second and third books of my *Temple of Music*.

We say, therefore, that the ratio is the same in a string having the length of one cubit as it is in a string produced from the circumference of the world to the center of the machine, with respect to the discovery of harmonic intervals, proportions, and consonances. For if the entire semidiameter of the world is divided into two parts, both of those parts will sound against the whole in a double proportion <note>An octave (2:1 ratio).</note>, and so on, just as was said regarding the artificial monochord. We say, furthermore, that *Art is the ape of Nature* <note>original: "Ars sit Naturæ simia." A common medieval and Renaissance proverb suggesting that human skill mimics the creative processes of the natural world.</note>; and this can indeed be most rightly affirmed in artificial Music, since it received its foundations from nature itself. For there is no proportion or interval in voices or sounds that is not found in the physical constitution of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "great world" or the universe as a whole, viewed as a reflection of the human "microcosm."</note>, which obtained the power of its Harmony from the perennial and supersubstantial source of Love; so that artificial Music is but a shadow or icon of worldly Harmony. And this [worldly harmony] is the image of that divine or Archetypal harmony which consists in the symphonic properties of the Trinity, contained within the number of the **Tetractys** <note>A mystical triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows; for Fludd, it represents the divine structure of reality.</note>.

Wherefore, although very few proportions of my Harmony may seem to the eye of the Author <note>Likely Kepler, who criticized Fludd's diagrams as being mathematically imprecise.</note> to be contained in the string or the common axis of each pyramid, nevertheless, the steps of consonances and proportions are innumerable and ineffable, being explained in the world monochord just as in the artificial one. Indeed, I would even dare to prove that every degree of the semidiameter line, even if divided into atoms, has its own proper virtues in the harmony of the world. To distinguish this with the physical eyes will indeed be impossible, but it is very easy to demonstrate to the eyes of reason. Therefore, this Harmony of mine is not so imaginary as to be painted only in my mind, since it consists of certain and infallible foundations, just as we can demonstrate in the artificial Monochord. Indeed, this harmony of ours is approved in the growth of vegetables, the generation and mutation of animals, and even in the constant ratio of the elements.

But that harmony of the Author's <note>Kepler's</note> is likened to vain chimeras imagined in the air. It is extracted from the mere accidents of natural creatures—namely, from **Planetary motions**—as if every soul of inferior things depended on the aspects or motions of the Planets. This is proven to be most false by an argument taken from creation: it is certain that the earth existed, and plants flourished upon it, and seeds had their multiplication, and the other elements moved in their natural motion before any of the Planets—and consequently their aspects or motions—possessed any power or existence in the heavens. For those things were created with their creatures on the **third day**, but the planets only on the following day <note>Fludd is using the Genesis creation story to argue that "harmony" (life and growth) existed before the stars and planets were created on the fourth day, thus undermining Kepler’s belief that harmony comes from planetary orbits.</note>. And yet, he admits no worldly harmony except from the motions of the Planets.

If this were granted to him, two absurdities follow: first, that there is greater power in the "thing created" than in the "creator" <note>original: "in naturato quam in naturante."</note>, or in a natural thing like a Planet than in Nature itself; and second, that before the rising of the Sun and Planets, there was no harmony in the world, even though it was completed on the third day. Whether it is right or just to say such a thing, I leave to be determined by your judgment, kind Readers. For if he teaches that the whole body of his harmonic contemplation, with all its parts, consists in the extreme motions of the Planets, it follows from this that there was no Harmony in the world before the positioning of the Planets in the heavens with their intervals in Cubic, Tetrahedral, Dodecahedral, Icosahedral, and Octahedral proportions <note>These are the five Platonic Solids, which Kepler famously used in his *Mysterium Cosmographicum* to explain the distances between planetary orbits.</note>. For without distinct proportions of intervals, no Harmony can exist in the world.

O, the extreme delirium of the man! He is forgetful of the matter of light and darkness—indeed, forgetful of Nature, the royal empress of faculties. Fleeing to the stars and the structures of nature like an idolater with the Heathens, he determines that the act and government of the world’s fabric flow from their essences. He neglects that true morning star, the very Carbuncle of Wisdom, which must be placed many degrees above the sun and celestial stars in beauty and clarity. He, therefore, establishes the celestial sun as the source of motion everywhere in his works; but I establish **Wisdom** itself as the liquid light pervading everywhere in the world.

If to some this opinion of mine—which agrees with the sacred text—does not seem likely or clear, let them, I say, enjoy that trophy of ignorance which has been fixed for many ages. Let these words of mine, which I have brought forth truly and from the source of truth, remain for a world overwhelmed by various ignorances. But I know there is a chorus of the wise who will determine that the world and its harmony, published in my manner, is not a painted or fantastic thing, but closest to reality and truth; nor will they judge that my concept of the world’s Harmony [is merely a dream...]

### TEXTUS XXVI.

> *From these few things I believe it is established: even if to understand the Mysteries packed with the deepest philosophy which* Robert <note>Robert Fludd refers to himself here in the third person, quoting Kepler's critique.</note> *teaches, a knowledge of harmonic proportions is entirely necessary: nevertheless, he who has thoroughly learned even my whole work will still be not a little further away from those most perplexed mysteries than those mysteries themselves have receded from the most accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations.*

### ANALYSIS.

Now this John of ours <note>Johannes Kepler.</note> longs to put an end to this Appendix of his with the grand publication of his victory, in which he (he thinks) builds an everlasting monument to his own praises. He proposes to thrust my reputation, such as it is, into the abyss of disgrace and to plunge it into the whirlpool of ignorance and unskillfulness, so that his triumph over my world might seem more glorious by my misfortune. And indeed, let him enjoy the trophy he hoped to fix, if he can. But truly, it will nevertheless be right that truth holds its place, and falsehood be banished into exile as far as the polar darkness. 

At last, he speaks of opening mysteries; these he says were poorly understood by me, seeing as I lack "demonstrations." This he says even though he himself published the *Macrocosmic Mystery* <note>original: "Mysterium Macrocosmicum," likely referring to Kepler's 1596 work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*.</note> twenty-two years ago, as he himself admits; there he recognizes that the whole mystery of Nature seems to lie hidden, though he does so in vain. But, because I remember that there is a double mystery in the world—namely, of truth and of injustice, as we gather from the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>—it must be seen whether his mystery is one tending toward delusion, or toward the vision of truth; toward a vain and false philosophy (which the Apostle mentions) or a true one. Indeed, he confesses that the power of that mystery of his is contained in the subject of this Harmony of his. 

What then shall we judge of it, when the foundations found in this work seem to differ so far from the truth? He judges my harmonic proportions, in his own fashion, to have "receded from the most accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations," because he is more practiced in vulgar mathematics; but of that natural and truly formal mathematics, he seems never to have even sipped or tasted. Since this is the case (as appears through his inquiry made in the Appendix), it will be deemed impossible by a Wise man that such a person could rightly judge colors, who is not only ignorant of the effects of light and darkness in the machinery of the world, but does not hesitate to deny them with a brazen face. 

But truly, as pertains to my mathematical proportions, which I published through demonstrations to explain my intentions regarding Nature, I know them to be as true and certain as I know for a certainty that he himself has wandered from the path of truth regarding my intention and mind in the knowledge of the hidden mystery of nature, or of light and water. Nor indeed (let him say what he pleases) can he find any fault in those demonstrations of mine. But here lies the whole difficulty: he devises the exterior motions of a thing's nature, while I consider the internal and essential acts flowing from nature itself; he holds the tail, I embrace the head; I notice the principal cause, while he notices its effects. And yet he, although his extreme motions are "real" (as he says), sticks more in the mud and mire of the impossibility of his own doctrine, and is bound by the most perplexed chains of obscurity, than that he might easily free himself from those snares with his honor intact, or redeem his understanding for even a tiny price; and thus he who made a pit for others has ignorantly fallen into it himself.
